text:
Upon the sixteen petals
The <term>cakra</term> <gloss>energy center</gloss> of enjoyment is perfectly situated.
The letter <term>Ya</term> is taught as the element of wind.
The <term>samaya</term> <gloss>sacred pledge</gloss> <term>mudra</term> <gloss>symbolic hand gesture</gloss> is the female liberator <note>referring to a specific tantric deity or yogini associated with the wind element</note>.
Upon the thirty-two petals of the lotus
The <term>cakra</term> of great bliss is situated.
Hearing is explained as the <term>sahaja</term> <gloss>co-emergent</gloss>.
One should distinguish them by their two-fold classification.

The yoga of the conventional deity
Is the aspect of the generation stage <note>the phase of tantric practice involving the visualization of deities</note>.
That which has the form of bliss free from obscuration
Is the meditation of the perfection stage <note>the advanced phase of tantric practice involving the subtle energy body</note>.
The Buddha's teaching of the doctrine
Relies perfectly upon the two truths.
As it has been said elsewhere:
The aspect of the generation stage,
And the perfection stage itself;
By relying on these two stages,
The <term>Vajradhara</term> <gloss>Vajra-Holder</gloss> performs the teaching.
Therefore, it was said: Thus have I heard at one time. This is the explanation of what was taught previously. There, in the midst of the retinue, the Blessed One gave the command.
If one asks what kind of distinction that has:
It is the essence of the body, speech, and mind of all the <term>Tathagatas</term> <gloss>Thus-Gone Ones</gloss>. It is the very deity who has become the vital essence.
For that very reason, the secret of all the <term>Tathagatas</term> is <term>Vajradhara</term>.
What is even more deeply secret than that is <term>Karuna-vajra</term> <gloss>Compassion Vajra</gloss>, which is not to be shown to the <term>Sravakas</term> <gloss>Listeners</gloss> and others.
Then, after the Blessed One had inspired the retinue who, knowing this to be something difficult to find, became faithful and joyful, he spoke: O, <term>Vajragarbha</term> <gloss>Vajra Essence</gloss>, and so forth.
The phrase "Listen!" is the engagement in hearing.
Regarding the phrase "Vajragarbha requested," if one asks what was requested:
He requested to ask about the three meanings.
The Blessed One commanded: "Vajra is called indivisible," and so forth.
It is called indivisible because it cannot be divided. It cannot be harmed by the arguments of oneself or others.
If one asks what that is: the <term>Dharma</term> <gloss>phenomena/doctrine</gloss>...

<summary>This page explains the anatomical locations of the subtle energy centers and differentiates between the generation and perfection stages of tantric practice. It identifies Vajradhara as the source of these secret teachings, which are characterized as indivisible and beyond conventional argument.</summary>
<keywords>cakra, generation stage, perfection stage, Vajradhara, two truths, Vajragarbha, indivisibility</keywords>

Through the complete ascertainment of the three <term>vajras</term> <gloss>indestructible realities of body, speech, and mind</gloss>, one realizes selflessness and thoroughly cuts through the delusions of worldly existence. When that very reality becomes one's own <term>mantra</term>, the means of excellence are easily found. For such a <term>vajra</term> holder, <term>siddhi</term> <gloss>spiritual accomplishment</gloss> resides in the very palm of their hand. This is what is taught in the passage beginning with those words.

Therefore, this is not just anything; because at the very time of the fourth empowerment, sentient beings with the sharpest faculties will achieve the accomplishment of <term>mahamudra</term> <gloss>the Great Seal</gloss>. For others, it is established that the pith instructions of the Great Seal should be shown.

Now, to further establish the meaning of empowerment through the passage beginning with "The nature of wisdom is <term>Lalana</term>," the divisions of the three <term>nadis</term> <gloss>subtle energy channels</gloss> will be shown:

<term>Lalana</term> is the left channel. It is the nature of the <term>ali</term> <gloss>the vowel series</gloss> and the essence of wisdom. 

<term>Rasana</term> is the right channel. It is the nature of the <term>kali</term> <gloss>the consonant series</gloss> and the essence of skillful means. 

That which exists in the central region as the essence of their union is the <term>Avadhuti</term>. 

<term>Lalana</term> is the <term>dharmakaya</term> <gloss>truth body</gloss>. <term>Rasana</term> is the <term>sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>enjoyment body</gloss>. <term>Avadhuti</term> is the <term>nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>emanation body</gloss>. In the same way, they appropriately correspond to body, speech, and mind. 

From the non-dual union of the three <term>chakras</term> <gloss>energy centers</gloss> and the three channels, <term>mahasukha</term> <gloss>great bliss</gloss> arises. If great bliss is realized, then the four empowerments, the moments, and the divisions of joy will also be understood. Just as the numerical order of the centers was established for the generation stage, it should be understood similarly for the empowerment stage. 

Regarding the Four Noble Truths and so forth, they also correspond respectively to the four empowerments: 
1. Thoroughly knowing suffering. 
2. Abandoning the origin. 
3. Manifesting cessation. 
4. Meditating on the path. 
These are the purifications. 

Likewise, there are four realities. Regarding the reality of the self: "In short, the five aggregates are well known as the five Buddhas. The <term>vajra</term> sense sources themselves are the <term>mandala</term> of the <term>Vajradakinis</term>," as it was said. Regarding the reality of the deity and so forth, in the Hevajra... <note>The text cuts off mid-title or mid-sentence referring to the Hevajra Tantra</note>

text:
The phrase **blazing in the navel** refers to the word **navel** as the center, specifically the <term>avadhuti</term> <gloss>central channel</gloss> between the other channels. The phrase **being burned** refers to the five <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates of being</gloss> being consumed by the fire of great passion. The phrase **Locana and the others** refers to the elements such as earth and so forth. Regarding the phrase **having burned**, it means the burning away of the ego and the sense of "mine" <note>the fixation on a self and its possessions</note>.

The phrase **the moon-holder <term>Ham</term> drips** refers to the arising of the <term>jnana</term> <gloss>primordial wisdom</gloss> of great bliss. This is explained as follows:

->The innate is not described by others, and is found nowhere at all;<-
->Through the timing shown by the Guru, and through one's own merit, it is known.<-

This is an explanation of the perfect realization. <term>Canda</term> <gloss>the fierce one</gloss> is <term>prajna</term> <gloss>transcendent wisdom</gloss>, which practices the <term>samadhi</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss> of the generation and completion stages. <term>Ali</term> is the mind characterized by great compassion. Therefore, emptiness and compassion are expressed by the term <term>Candali</term> <gloss>the fierce inner heat</gloss>.

The **navel** is their center, characterized by the <term>mahamudra</term> <gloss>Great Seal</gloss> of clear light. If one asks what is done there by the blazing of the <term>tummo</term> <gloss>inner heat</gloss> and the unsurpassed wisdom, the text says **the five Tathagatas** <gloss>Buddhas</gloss> and so forth. This includes Akshobhya and the others who are the lords of the mandala and the deities within the mandala, as well as Locana and the other consorts. **Burning** means they are consumed without even ash remaining.

Furthermore, the phrase **having burned, the moon-holder <term>Ham</term>** indicates that because there is nothing other than the mental proliferation of "self" and "mine," the "self" is realized as mind-only. If one asks what occurs through that burning, the text says **the moon-holder drips**. Therefore, the **moon-holder** is Vajradhara, who remains after arising from the meditative absorption of clear light. As it is said:

->The past, the future, and the present are the three worlds themselves;<-
->In that moment purified by clear light, they are all seen without exception.<-

Regarding the **Chapter on the Vajra Family**, **Vajra** here refers to Hevajra. **Family** <note>original: <term>kula</term></note> refers to the body. Alternatively, that which arises from it is the family. The chapter that makes this manifest is the Chapter on the Vajra Family. This is the commentary on the difficult points of the <term>Hevajra Tantra</term>.

<summary>This page explains the esoteric symbolism of the inner heat yoga within the Hevajra tradition, defining terms like Candali as the union of wisdom and compassion. It describes the transformation of the aggregates and the realization of the mind as clear light through the dripping of the syllable Ham.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra, Candali, inner heat, clear light, Vajradhara, five Tathagatas, avadhuti, mahamudra, prajna, compassion</keywords>

text:
One should recite <term>Om Hum Svaha</term> one hundred thousand times for the purpose of the preliminary ritual service. Afterward, on an unbaked clay vessel, write the syllable <term>Pam</term> using <term>steatite</term> <gloss>soapstone or magnesium silicate</gloss>. In the center of that, write <term>Om Hum Devadatta Stambhaya Hum Svaha</term> <note>Devadatta is a placeholder for the name of the target person to be paralyzed</note>. Fill the vessel with ashes from a cemetery and cover it with another unbaked clay vessel to form a joined pair. Upon this, draw a four-cornered mandala of the Great Powerful One <note>likely referring to Mahabala or a form of Hayagriva</note> beautifully adorned with <term>vajras</term> <gloss>ritual scepters or diamond-bolts</gloss>. Place this underground and press down upon it with your left foot. While remaining in the meditative absorption described previously, recite the mantra. If you recite <term>Om Hum Vajra Devadatta Stambhaya Hum Svaha</term> one hundred and eight or one thousand times, the person will be paralyzed.

Likewise, through the complete transformation of the syllable <term>I</term>, perform the yoga of the White Goddess <note>Gauri</note> who is the color of saffron and holds a noose and a hook. Meditate on the syllable <term>Am</term>, which is the color of a <term>bandhuka</term> flower <gloss>a bright red flower, Pentapetes phoenicea</gloss>, in your own heart. Recite the mantra <term>Om Am Svaha</term> one hundred thousand times for the preliminary service. Then, visualize the target person in front of you, red in color, naked, and with loose hair. Visualize a fire-colored syllable <term>Om</term> in her <term>bhaga</term> <gloss>vulva</gloss>. Alternatively, if it is a man, visualize it in his heart. Think that the person melts and becomes intoxicated by the light of the syllable <term>Am</term>. Recite <term>Om Am Gauri [Name] Me Vashamanaya Ham Svaha</term>. Visualize that the person is bound by the throat with a noose, pierced through the heart with a hook, and pulled completely until they arrive at your feet. If you do this, they will certainly be brought under your power.

Likewise, through the complete transformation of the syllable <term>I</term>, visualize the Water Goddess Yogini. She is blue in color and makes a hand gesture with the thumb and forefinger. In your heart, visualize a blue syllable <term>Kham</term> upon a sun disk. For the preliminary service, recite <term>Om Kham Svaha</term> one hundred thousand times. Visualize the target person naked, with disheveled hair, riding a blue camel. Visualize them facing south, agitated, and fleeing as they are struck with a stick. Recite the mantra: <term>Om A Kham Vira Yogini [Name] Ucchataya Kham Hum Hum Hum Phat</term>. Within seven days, they will certainly be expelled. Likewise, from the syllable <term>U</term> comes the Vajra Dakini <unclear>...</unclear>

<summary>This page details ritual instructions for the magical acts of paralyzing, enchanting for power, and expelling enemies. It describes specific visualizations of deities, syllables, and mantras combined with physical ritual objects like clay vessels and cemetery ashes.</summary>
<keywords>Vajrayana, ritual magic, mantras, Gauri, paralysis, enchantment, expulsion, yoga, visualization</keywords>

It is called a <term>sattva</term> <gloss>being</gloss>, which means that this very seed syllable is <term>Vajradhara</term> <gloss>the Vajra Holder</gloss>. If one asks what kind of special quality it possesses, it is described as having the nature of supreme joy. The phrase "radiating forth" means that from that very seed syllable, one should radiate various forms identical to the body of <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>Vajra of Joy</gloss> until they pervade everything. "Gathering them back into the heart" means that those very forms are gathered back together and absorbed into that same seed syllable.

Then, that practitioner, having become the embodiment of <term>Dvesha</term> <gloss>Anger</gloss> <note>a reference to the transformation of anger into wisdom</note>, arises in the form of <term>Heruka</term> <gloss>a wrathful deity</gloss> from the total transformation of the moon, the sun, the symbols, and the seed syllable. This constitutes the five aspects of manifest enlightenment. Regarding this, as stated in the eighth chapter:

The moon is the mirror-like wisdom.
The seventh of the seven <note>likely referring to the sun or a specific numerical sequence in the tantra</note> is the wisdom of equality.
The seed syllables and hand-symbols of the deities
Are described as the wisdom of discernment.
The unification of all these is the wisdom of perseverance.
The perfection is the purity of the <term>dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>sphere of reality</gloss>.

The three elements starting with "blue and sun" refer to the yoga of the single hero, which is common to all deities. Now, in order to briefly present the four types of Hevajra and the fourth yoga of <term>Nairatmya</term> <gloss>Lady of Egolessness</gloss>, which consists of the nature of the mandala circle, the text mentions "charnel ground" and so forth. Just as with the activities of the third yoga, one should view the fourth in the same way.

Inside the vajra-fence, within the celestial palace of the mandala of the eight terrifying charnel grounds, the Lord Hevajra is completely surrounded by the eight <term>yoginis</term> <gloss>female tantric practitioners</gloss> such as <term>Gauri</term>. The phrase "breath circulating" is an etymological explanation where the letters are elided from the phrase "because the corpse remains," meaning "the place of the corpse" <note>the charnel ground</note>. This summary is made using the term "charnel ground," which is also the perfection described in the eighth chapter.

The term "charnel ground" refers to the supreme nature of joy, the Lord, residing within the body which is devoid of self. If one asks how the body is a charnel ground, it is said:

By this reasoning of the "circulating breath,"
It is clearly called a charnel ground.

text:
The practicing <term>yogi</term> <gloss>practitioner of yoga</gloss> must not become intoxicated. Because delusion becomes primary, it creates a great obstacle to yoga. This is how one should train. This concludes the commentary on the sixth chapter, the Chapter on Conduct, from the <term>Hevajra Panjika Ratnamala</term> <gloss>The Precious Garland: A Commentary on the Difficult Points of the Hevajra Tantra</gloss>.

The <term>samaya</term> <gloss>symbolic signs</gloss> are the language of the <term>mleccha</term> <gloss>barbarians</gloss> through which the <term>yoginis</term> <gloss>female practitioners</gloss> indicate their realization. One should understand this as the supreme method itself. Therefore, the Chapter on Signs and so forth is taught. Regarding the chapter that clarifies the signs, it says the following. A brother is a <term>yogi</term>. A sister is a <term>yogini</term>. The phrase "one finger" refers to the forefinger; it means "Has he come?" The phrase "which one" means "Which one should be looked at?" The phrase "with two" refers to the forefinger and the middle finger together. "Showing the silk scarf" refers to the manner of binding a silk scarf with those two fingers. "Three points" refers to pressing the little finger with the thumb and extending the remaining three in the manner of three points. "The boundary" refers to the boundary of the crown of the head. "The wheel" shows the manner of a wheel. "Frowning" is the movement of the eyebrows. The explanation of "loosening the topknot" and so forth belongs to the interpretable meaning.

Regarding the phrase "showing one finger" and so forth: any mention of one finger refers to using the forefinger, or the middle and forefingers, to point to the <term>padma</term> <gloss>lotus/consort</gloss> of <term>prajna</term> <gloss>wisdom</gloss> to stir it. Regarding "that itself is the 'well-come' <note>original: "svagata"</note>," the term "well" refers to the fluid <note>seminal essence</note>, meaning it was brought down through the union of the fingers. Regarding the "mudra of illness" and so forth: the <term>mudra</term> <gloss>hand gesture</gloss> of illness is the accomplishment of the <term>dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>sphere of reality</gloss>, which is the ultimate limit of bliss; these are to be known. If one asks what that is like, it is said: "From grasping the left thumb" and so forth. "Left" refers to <term>prajna</term> <gloss>wisdom</gloss>, specifically the interior of her lotus. The "thumb" is the <term>vajra</term> <gloss>diamond/phallus</gloss>; when it reaches the state of emission, it is to be pressed. Regarding the "ring finger" and so forth: the ring finger is the primordial wisdom of <term>prajna</term>.

<summary>This page concludes the sixth chapter on conduct and begins the commentary on symbolic hand gestures and secret signs used between yogis and yoginis. It provides specific tantric decodings for physical gestures, interpreting them as metaphors for the union of wisdom and method.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra Tantra, Ratnamala, yogi, yogini, symbolic signs, mudra, prajna, lotus, vajra, tantric conduct</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
The lotus <note>referring to the female generative organ in tantric symbolism</note>. Wisdom <note>original: "prajñā"</note> refers to the vajra <note>referring to the male organ or the indestructible nature of reality</note>. Meditation <note>original: "bhāvanā"</note> refers to the application or entry into practice. These three are present at the beginning, while the two forms of the co-emergent <note>original: "sahaja"</note> are at the end. That which is to be meditated upon exists between these two. The act of meditative absorption is called equipoise <note>original: "samāpatti"</note>. The bliss arising from the cultivation and generation of that state is called "by its bliss."

The term "circle" <note>original: "cakra"</note> refers to what is called the circle of the Yogini, because all these elements are gathered within that very Great Bliss <note>original: "mahāsukha"</note>. If one asks what that bliss is like, it is described as "just as it is appropriate." This means self-awareness <note>original: "svasaṃvedana"</note>, which is the essence of knowing by oneself without depending on external conditions. That very self-awareness is awakening <note>original: "bodhi"</note>. The mind that has the nature of awakening is called the Mind of Awakening <note>original: "bodhicitta"</note>. The word "action" <note>original: "kriyā"</note> has the sense of gathering or collecting. Because it causes the body to remain, that itself is called the "deity" <note>original: "deva"</note>.

The phrase "how it arises" refers to arising according to the actual nature of reality; it arises without depending on a subject to grasp or an object to be grasped. Semen <note>original: "kunda"</note> refers to the form of the fluid which is like the jasmine flower or the moon. Why is it so? It is said, "The co-emergent is of two types," meaning there are two types of co-emergent joy.

If the co-emergent is like that, one might ask what are the "man" and "woman"? The text says, "The consort," and so forth. Regarding "among these," there are seven, which are the two types of joy. If one asks what they are, they are the relative and the ultimate. The essence of Great Bliss is the ultimate <note>original: "paramārtha"</note>. That which arises according to appearances is the relative <note>original: "saṃvṛti"</note>, because it possesses a mere portion of the relative itself. For that very reason, it is said "of the two types." The word "of the four" refers to the four types. "The distinction" refers to the general distinction of the co-emergent. 

If one objects, "Is it not elsewhere asserted that there are four joys? How is this different assertion not contradictory?" The text explains, "Thus, the co-emergent," and so forth. It means they arise through the sequence of the four, such as joy <note>original: "ānanda"</note> and supreme joy <note>original: "paramānanda"</note>, from the perspective of the generation stage <note>original: "utpattikrama"</note>.

<summary>This page provides a technical commentary on tantric terminology, defining the symbolic meanings of the lotus, vajra, and the two types of co-emergent joy within the context of the generation stage. It clarifies the relationship between relative and ultimate bliss and the role of self-awareness in achieving awakening.</summary>
<keywords>co-emergent, sahaja, Great Bliss, mahāsukha, Bodhicitta, self-awareness, svasaṃvedana, generation stage, four joys, yogini cakra</keywords>

text:
The six faculties are the eyes and so forth that reside in the body. The terms <term>stable</term> <gloss>stationary or inanimate</gloss> and <term>moving</term> <gloss>mobile or animate</gloss> refer to external things that either possess or lack a mind. Regarding the phrase "I myself am," this means that not only am I the Vajradhara <gloss>Holder of the Scepter</gloss> whose nature is uniquely Great Bliss, but that I encompass all.

The phrase "equal in sameness" refers to the essence of indivisibility. If one asks how that is so, the text says, "by meditating on that reality." The explanation for this is called <term>equal taste</term> <gloss>sameness of experience</gloss>. Furthermore, the explanation for this is "equality" and so forth, where "equality" means the state of becoming identical. The word "that" refers to things that are inferior, middling, and so on. The word "taste" refers to the essence, which is a synonym for "entity" or "thing." If one asks what that "taste" is, it refers to the innate nature characterized by Great Bliss atop the <term>cakras</term> <gloss>energy centers</gloss>. In order to show the summarized meaning, it is said: "The meditation is the equality of a single taste."

Furthermore, if one asks how to meditate on the equality of a single taste, the text says "from me" and so forth. The phrase "the practitioner knowing thus" means having understood this with certainty. "Extremely composed" <gloss>meditative equipoise</gloss> means remaining in that state at all times. To clarify that very point, the text mentions "eating and drinking" and so forth. The phrase "by nature" means engaging according to one's own natural disposition. Regarding "Mahamudra" <gloss>The Great Seal</gloss> and so forth, it means "for the sake of accomplishing the Great Seal." This demonstrates the yoga of superior devotion.

Now, in order to show the mind within this very context, the text says "all beings will be meditated upon" and so forth. "All beings" refers to sentient beings and the vessel-like world <gloss>the external environment</gloss>; all of these arise precisely from meditation. If one asks why, it is said "by the mind," meaning by the consciousness that possesses conceptual thought. If one objects that if things are not investigated, they cannot be meditated upon, the text says "all phenomena" and so forth. This means thoroughly knowing the innate essence.

<summary>This page provides a commentary on the nature of Great Bliss and the yoga of Mahamudra, explaining that all animate and inanimate phenomena share a single essence or taste. It emphasizes that the practitioner should maintain meditative equipoise during all activities, including eating and drinking, to realize the indivisibility of the mind and the world.</summary>
<keywords>Great Bliss, Vajradhara, equal taste, Mahamudra, meditative equipoise, innate essence, six faculties, conceptual thought</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: this text continues a discussion on the cognitive powers of a practitioner and the superiority of the Hevajra Tantra.</meta>

One knows the minds of oneself and others in the past, future, and present. Regarding the phrase "the realms of higher beings and the human world" <note>original: mtho ris mi yul</note> and so forth: "single form" refers to being of a single nature. The meaning of "the parts of oneself and others" has already been explained.

In order to demonstrate how the <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>The Joyful Vajra</gloss> is more distinguished than other scriptures, the text says, "the knower of all <term>Vedas</term> <gloss>Knowledge/Ancient Indian scriptures</gloss>," and so forth. The Vedas are the <term>Rig Veda</term> <gloss>hymns of praise</gloss>, the <term>Atharva Veda</term> <gloss>protection from existence</gloss>, the <term>Sama Veda</term> <gloss>chants</gloss>, and the <term>Yajur Veda</term> <gloss>sacrificial formulas</gloss>. <note>The Tibetan text uses descriptive names for the four Vedas: nges brjod, srid srung, snyan dngags, and mchod sbyin.</note>

"Tenets" <note>original: grub mtha'</note> refers to the views of the <term>Tirthikas</term> <gloss>non-Buddhist extremists</gloss> such as the <term>Vaisheshika</term> <gloss>Ancient school of atomism</gloss>, and the discourses <note>original: mdo sde</note> of the <term>Shravaka</term> <gloss>Hearer/Foundational vehicle</gloss> collections. These are called tenets because they serve to bring one to the "end of rebirth" <note>original: yang srid kྱི་ mtha'</note>. "Extensive rituals" refers to the <term>Kriya Tantra</term> <gloss>Action Tantra</gloss> and similar classes. Accomplishments <note>original: dngos grub; Sanskrit: siddhi</note> characterized by what is explained in these systems do not exist <note>meaning they do not lead to ultimate realization</note>.

One might ask: does such accomplishment exist in the <term>Paramitayana</term> <gloss>Vehicle of Perfection</gloss> or not? The text says, "existence will be purified," and so forth. It is "purified" because it exhausts the afflictions and the obscurations to knowledge. This refers to the path characterized by the six perfections. Through that purity, enlightenment will be attained; however, the phrase "at the end of existence" means it is attained by passing from one birth to another throughout three immeasurable eons.

If one then asks: "Since the <term>Yoga Tantras</term> also state that enlightenment is attained in this very life, how is this <note>the Hevajra system</note> superior?" The text says, "without that," and so forth. "That" refers to the <term>Sahaja</term> <gloss>Co-emergent/Innate</gloss> nature, characterized by self-knowing awareness. Without this, it is not taught that accomplishment exists in either this life or other lives.

If one then asks: "What is the difference between that system and this one?" The text says, "one who does not know the <term>Hevajra</term>," and so forth. Other tantras merely point toward the Innate, but this Hevajra Tantra explains it in a completely clear and vivid manner. Therefore, it is shown very clearly that for one who does not know the Hevajra, the hardships of hearing, contemplating, and meditating will be meaningless. If <unclear>one seeks the Bodhisattva path</unclear>

<summary>The text explains the superiority of the Hevajra Tantra over the Vedas, foundational Buddhist vehicles, and other Tantra classes by emphasizing its unique, vivid presentation of the Innate nature.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra Tantra, Vedas, Sahaja, Innate, Paramitayana, Yoga Tantra, Enlightenment, Tenets</keywords>

text:
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Hevajra Tantra, specifically focusing on the meaning of the mantra and the nature of ultimate reality in the context of empowerment.</meta>

The mantra is **Om Ah Hum Phat Svaha**. The phrase "offering and making requests" refers to the teacher. The phrase "in the same way as explained" refers to the *Compendium of Reality* <note>original: Tattvasamgraha</note> and other similar texts. "Vajrasattva" <gloss>the Adamantine Being</gloss> here refers to **Hevajra**. The phrase "afterward" means immediately following the empowerment. "Completely pure" means being purified of the stains of cyclic existence <term>samsara</term>. "Having the form of wisdom" means being equal to the wisdom of the All-Knowing One.

Regarding the phrase "cyclic existence and complete purification": This refers to that wisdom in which there is not even the slightest distinction between existence <term>samsara</term> and liberation <term>nirvana</term>. It is said to be "surpassing" because it is completely beyond all conceptual elaboration <term>prapancha</term>. 

This very point will be clearly demonstrated by the two verses beginning with "in supreme joy." "Supreme joy" is the highest transcendent wisdom <term>prajna</term>, which is the wisdom characterized by clear light. 

The phrase "there is no meditation" means there is not even the slightest thing to be meditated upon. The "meditator" is the mind, and that too does not exist. "Body" refers to the physical body. "The apprehended" refers to the objects that appear. "The apprehender" refers to the eyes and the other sense faculties. Similarly, flesh, blood, and so forth also do not exist. 

Having established that the obscuration of disturbing emotions <term>klesha-avarana</term> does not exist in this way, in order to show that the obscuration to knowledge <term>jneyavarana</term> also does not exist, the text says "there is no seeing" and so on. This means that external objects such as things to be seen do not exist. 

In the phrase "without waves," "waves" refers to conceptual thoughts. When those are exhausted, it is "without waves." "Manifold" refers to appearing in various different forms. When that is absent, it is "without the manifold." 

The expression "these words" refers to the words spoken by the Blessed One. "Asked" refers to the request made by **Vajragarbha**. What was the meaning of the request? He said, "For what reason?" and so forth. The intended meaning is this: the nature of the Co-emergent <term>sahaja</term> is inherently pure.

<summary>This page provides a philosophical commentary on the non-dual nature of Vajrasattva and the lack of inherent existence in meditation, the body, and sensory perception. It explains that ultimate wisdom is free from conceptual "waves" and the distinction between samsara and nirvana.</summary>

<keywords>Vajrasattva, Hevajra, wisdom, non-duality, emptiness, meditation, Vajragarbha, clear light, sahaja</keywords>

text:
Just as those who speak of the <term>Alayavijnana</term> <gloss>all-basis consciousness</gloss> assert that it is the holder of the seeds of all wandering beings, so too is the Great Bliss <note>original: "mahasukha"</note> realized through the empowerment of primordial wisdom and insight. That which is characterized as the emptiness of all phenomena is praised in the <term>Mantrayana</term> <gloss>Secret Mantra vehicle</gloss> of the <term>Mahayana</term> <gloss>Great Vehicle</gloss> as being the very foundation of all phenomena. To accomplish that very state, the text says "Great Bliss" and so forth. "Union" refers to the meditative equipoise of method and insight. "Entity" refers to the nature of the five Buddhas. "Non-entity" refers to the very state of being free from conceptual elaboration.

How does one come to have the essence of bliss within the mandala of Shri Hevajra, which is the nature of method and insight? The text says "Vajrasattva" and so forth. This refers to the <term>vajra</term> <gloss>scepter symbol</gloss> as the hand symbol arising from the seed produced by the perfect union of the sun and moon, which are the nature of method and insight. The seed residing in the center of that is the <term>sattva</term> <gloss>being</gloss>. The being who possesses the vajra is Vajrasattva. This very state is called Bliss.

Regarding the phrase "Vajragarbha asked," for what purpose did he ask? Because the Blessed One praised the reality of the generation stage as being the very essence of bliss. The text says "perfection" and so forth. "Meditation" refers to the meditation on the deity itself. "What is the need for a non-existent generation?" means that there is no such need. This is the intended meaning: what is the use of this effort in meditating on the mandala circle if one aspires to Great Bliss? If one thinks that the desired goal will be achieved through Great Bliss alone, then to show respect, the text says "degenerated by the force of faith." In this context, being "degenerated" despite having respect for the generation stage means actually abandoning the generation stage. The phrase "the non-entity of the body" refers to that very generation stage.

<summary>This page explains the relationship between the all-basis consciousness and Great Bliss within the Hevajra Tantra tradition. It defines Vajrasattva as the union of method and insight and discusses the necessity of the generation stage in spiritual practice.</summary>
<keywords>Vajrasattva, Great Bliss, Alayavijnana, Hevajra Tantra, generation stage, method and insight, emptiness, Mahayana</keywords>

text:
The buddha-field of the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>One Gone Thus</gloss> Amitabha is called Sukhavati <gloss>The Blissful</gloss>. Here, however, the <term>bhaga</term> <gloss>source of phenomena/womb</gloss> of Nairatmya <gloss>She Who Realizes Selflessness</gloss> and the other goddesses is called "the Blissful." This is because it protects the unsurpassed bliss of the essential nature in its condensed form; I abide there. In order to symbolize all phenomena as being one with the form of Great Bliss, it says: "The appearance of the form is in the shape of the letter E."

The state of Buddhahood itself is the Jewel. Its casket is the place where it is deposited. Now, in order to show the greatness of such a nature, the text says: "I am the teacher," and so forth. This means I am the one who explains such teachings as the Hevajra Tantra. "The listener" refers to the disciple possessed of good qualities. "The goal to be accomplished is myself" refers to what was explained previously. The one who accomplishes that is also the self. "The teacher of the world" refers to the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Complete Enjoyment Body</gloss> forms, which are my own self.

Regarding the phrase "the worldly and the transcendent," that which arises from the conceptual elaboration of both is the worldly. The transcendent is the <term>bodhicitta</term> <gloss>enlightened mind/seminal essence</gloss> in the form of fluid, which acts as the cause for those very states. Because this is necessary for the world and because its essence is the <term>Sambhogakaya</term>, it is my own self.

If one asks: "If you are primarily the essence of Great Bliss, what is that like?" the text says: "Co-emergent Joy," and so forth. If one asks: "What is the specific character of that co-emergent joy?" the text says: "The end of the supreme," and so forth. The meaning is that it is the very point where Supreme Joy ends and the Joy of Cessation begins.

Previously it was stated: "You are the very nature of all Great Bliss that is to be accomplished." If that is so, then since the co-emergent bliss of worldly beings is not the goal to be accomplished, how could that be you? In response, the text says: "Even so, by a child," and so forth. The word "even" <note>original: "kyang"</note> functions as a logical reason. This is because that very bliss is primarily shown through examples.

<summary>This page provides a tantric commentary on the nature of Great Bliss and the symbolism of the letter E. It identifies the teacher, the listener, and the goal of practice as expressions of the internal enlightened nature.</summary>
<keywords>Amitabha, Sukhavati, Nairatmya, bhaga, Great Bliss, Hevajra, Sambhogakaya, bodhicitta, Co-emergent Joy</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: establishing the relationship between the example and the actual realization</meta>

By using the example of that which is similar, the actual nature is established. Therefore, that very nature is the primary teaching, while this <note>referring to the example used</note> is a conventional designation. To demonstrate this very point, it is said: *Like a lamp in the darkness*, and so forth. Just as some objects like a vase or a cloth located in a dark area are made visible and established by a lamp, so too should one view this. The great bliss, which is the quality to be established, is established by means of the exemplary worldly <term>sahaja</term> <gloss>co-emergent</gloss> bliss.

Regarding the phrase *in the abode of bliss* and so forth, in order to clarify what was previously stated, it says: *thirty-two*, and so forth. This refers to the body blazing with the major and minor marks of a Buddha. The *Lord* refers to the Master of the Buddha-Dharma. The *Consort* is the example, namely the <term>Vajra</term> <gloss>Diamond</gloss> Consort. The phrase *fluid in her womb* <note>original: "bhaga"</note> means residing in oneself. *Fluid* is bliss, specifically the external fluid. The phrase *without that* means if that fluid is absent. Because bliss arises in dependence upon the fluid, if the fluid is absent, such bliss cannot be produced by any other cause. 

Therefore, it is said that bliss will also arise from the <term>deity yoga</term> <gloss>meditative union with a divine form</gloss>. One who desires that same great bliss must certainly practice the deity yoga. Its path is neither a thing nor a non-thing, because it is the essential nature of both the fluid and the bliss. The Buddha, who is the fruit of that path, is also neither a thing nor a non-thing. How is this so? The text says: *possessing the aspect of faces and hands*, and so forth. The essence of the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Complete Enjoyment Body</gloss> is formed. Due to the very <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body</gloss> of supreme bliss, it is formless. Therefore, because it is a non-abiding formed nature, it is said: *It is not formed, yet not formless*; it does not remain in either state. Why is it so? For that reason, *all beings are co-emergent*, which refers to all sentient beings. Co-emergent...

<summary>This page explains the relationship between worldly bliss and the Great Bliss of enlightenment using the metaphor of a lamp in darkness. It clarifies that the Buddha's nature transcends the duality of existence and non-existence through the union of form and emptiness.</summary>
<keywords>Sahaja, Great Bliss, Deity Yoga, Sambhogakaya, Dharmakaya, Vajra Consort, Co-emergent</keywords>

text:
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the nature of the innate and the practice of deity yoga from the previous section of the Tengyur.</meta>

What is the meaning of the word "born"? It refers to the <term>Sahaja</term> <gloss>innate or co-emergent</gloss> nature. It is said, "It is called the co-emergent nature of all phenomena," which is a synonymous expression. That very nature is <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>transcendence of suffering</gloss>. 

If one asks how this is so, the text says: "By the mind that is of a completely pure aspect," and so forth. "Completely pure" means stainless, the very essence of <term>Prabhasvara</term> <gloss>clear light</gloss>. The meaning is that when the mind takes on that aspect, it becomes Nirvana.

One might ask: "If the world is the very nature of the Buddha because its essence is both existence and non-existence, why then should one meditate on the forms of deities?" To answer this, the text says, "While that is true, the form of the deity," and so forth. The mention of "face, limbs, and color" refers to the ordinary body. 

If one then argues that meditation is therefore useless, the text says, "Nonetheless," and so forth. This refers to the <term>Vasana</term> <gloss>habitual tendencies</gloss> of the ordinary body which remain as residues. The intention is that one should meditate on the divine body of the deity in order to discard those tendencies and to increase the tendencies of the <term>Anasrava</term> <gloss>uncontaminated</gloss> aggregates.

Now, it must be established that the meditation on the body is itself the cause of <term>Apratishthita Nirvana</term> <gloss>non-abiding nirvana</gloss>. Therefore, to prove this through various examples, the text says, "By that very knowledge of the poison," and so forth. To "extract" means to neutralize or overcome. 

How was it called "wind" previously? Because it is the movement of the breath. How is it reversed? Because it belongs to the same class. Testing that is what is beneficial. <term>Bhava</term> <gloss>existence</gloss> refers to <term>Samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of rebirth</gloss>. "Purity" refers to its total exhaustion. By saying "through existence itself," the meaning is that through the transformation of the sun, moon, hand-symbols, and seed-syllables, which constitute existence, those very things are exhausted by the aspect of the deity. 

"Conceptual thought" is Samsara. The meaning is that conceptual thought is exhausted by the "conceptualization" of the deity's form. It is like the example: "Just as when water has entered the ear," and so forth.

<summary>This page explains the Innate (Sahaja) as the pure, clear-light nature of mind and justifies deity meditation as a method to purify ordinary habitual tendencies. It uses the principle of using the cause of a problem as its cure, such as using conceptualization of a deity to exhaust ordinary conceptual thought.</summary>
<keywords>Sahaja, Innate, Nirvana, Clear Light, Deity Yoga, Vasana, Habitual Tendencies, Non-abiding Nirvana, Samsara, Purification</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
should be performed, because it is the very essence of the support for those <note>referring to the foundational nature of the yogic practices or deities mentioned previously</note>.

"Joy arises from that, distinguished by the division of moments," means that it is categorized by divisions such as "various" and so forth. If joy itself exists, one might ask, what is the purpose of distinguishing these moments?

The text says, "By knowing the moments..." and so forth. The intent is that if one knows the essence of the moments themselves, one will fully understand the functioning of bliss through the various joys. Otherwise, one will not.

To demonstrate those very divisions of the moments, the text says, "The various..." and so forth. "Various" <term>nana</term> <gloss>diverse or multifaceted</gloss> refers to being skilled in diversity, which is the activity of the Master <term>Acarya</term>. Regarding the section beginning with "Ripening" <term>vipaka</term> <gloss>the fruition of karma</gloss>, the phrase "reversing from that" means becoming unlike that <note>shifting from ordinary causal results to yogic experience</note>.

"Wisdom" <term>jnana</term> <gloss>primal awareness</gloss> refers to the wisdom of great bliss. "Eating that" means experiencing it. Regarding the section beginning with "Dissolution" <term>vimalabdha</term> <gloss>thoroughly agitated or refined</gloss>, the term "eaten" refers to the memory of what has just passed and ceased. Alternatively, the knowledge of individual realization is called "eaten," meaning the definite apprehension that "I have experienced bliss."

"Devoid of characteristics" refers to the three <note>moments or joys</note> previously explained. "Attachment and freedom from attachment" refers to being free from both existence <term>samsara</term> and passing beyond sorrow <term>nirvana</term>.

By the passage starting with "The various..." and so forth, the four joys are established as the four empowerments <term>abhiseka</term>. The intent is that through each respective joy, one attains what are called the Master, the Secret, the Wisdom, and the Fourth empowerments.

For that very reason, the text discusses the activities of joy and so forth. "In stages" refers to the following:
1. Joy is the Master Empowerment.
2. Supreme Joy is the Secret Empowerment.
3. Joyless Joy <note>also translated as 'freedom from joy' or 'extraordinary joy' depending on the tantric context</note> is the Wisdom Empowerment.
4. Co-emergent Joy is the Fourth Empowerment.

In this way, one should understand the application of the four empowerments, the four moments, and the four joys based on the oral instructions of the Guru. Thus, the enumeration of the four empowerments should be understood.

text:
The song should be sung. This is expressed in the phrase <term>malaya-ja</term> <gloss>born of the Malaya mountain/sandalwood</gloss> and so forth. <term>Kolla-iri</term> refers to the head. <term>Bolla</term> refers to the syllable <term>ham</term> which resides there. <term>Mumuni</term> refers to the gaze. <term>Kakkola</term> refers to the syllable <term>am</term>. The union of these two is <term>ghana</term>, meaning uninterrupted flow. <term>Kripita</term> is the indestructible sound. <term>Vajja</term> refers to the arising of all these. <term>Karuni</term> refers to the practitioner <note>yogin</note>. <term>Ka-a-i</term> refers to non-action. <term>Narola</term> refers to not engaging in external meditative absorption. <term>Tahin-bila</term> refers to the nature of selfhood. <term>Khajja-i</term> means that the self should not be observed <note>the realization of selflessness</note>. <term>Ma-ana-vija-a-i</term> means one should drink the drink of great bliss born from yoga. <term>Kalinja</term> refers to the vital wind <note>prana</note>. <term>Pani-a-i</term> refers to the wind entering inside. <term>Dudhura</term> refers to the afflictions such as attachment. <term>Causa-ma</term> refers to the aggregate of form. <term>Kacchuri</term> refers to the aggregate of feeling. <term>Sihla</term> refers to the aggregate of perception. <term>Kapura</term> refers to the aggregate of consciousness. <term>La-i-a-i</term> means to bring into union. <term>Mala-indhana</term> refers to the aggregate of formations. <term>Salija</term> refers to the nature of the pride of the self in all things. <term>Taham</term> means the practitioner should eat there, which means to make things natureless <note>void of inherent existence</note>. <term>Prenkhana-kheta</term>: <term>prenkhana</term> refers to the flow of the liquid bodhichitta from the state of great bliss, and <term>kheta</term> refers to its re-entry. <term>Shuddha-ashuddha</term> means not perceiving things as existing or non-existing. Therefore, <term>ramsu</term> is used because of its correspondence to that; <term>ramsu</term> refers to the drops of fluid. By that, <term>ambha</term>, which refers to the channels of the limbs of the body, should be arranged. <term>Tahin</term> means by such a union. The selflessness of all phenomena is <term>sarava</term>. <term>Pani-a-i</term> means that one should follow accordingly. <term>Malaya-ja</term> refers to the gathering of the channels <note>nadis</note>.

<keywords>twilight language, sandhyabhasha, yogic anatomy, five aggregates, bodhichitta, channels, great bliss, selflessness</keywords>

text:
She herself is <term>Nairatmya</term> <gloss>She Who Has No Self</gloss>. That very essence is the meaning of the phrase "mandala circle." If one asks what the reality of this "Selfless One" is, it is said that she possesses the nature of the <term>dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>sphere of ultimate reality</gloss>. This is the answer to the five questions.

When it is said, "Vajragarbha requested," what did he request? He requested the meaning of the <term>samvara</term> <gloss>union or binding vow</gloss>. Regarding the statement "situated in the center of the body of all yoginis," the center of the body refers to the navel. The phrase "in the form of the letter E" refers to the first vowel. "Abiding" means to dwell there eternally.

To demonstrate the meaning of the union, the text says, "Just as it is externally," and so forth. This means that just as one meditates on the external Nairatmya, the internal is no different. The intention is that because it is condensed within the body, it is called a "union." Furthermore, just as the mandala of Nairatmya is here, so too is the letter A situated at the navel.

Just as the letter A at the navel is the union of Nairatmya, the "Vajra Sense-base" refers to the letter <term>Hum</term>. The intention is that "by means of the method itself," the method is the union abiding in the heart of <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>Joyful Vajra</gloss>.

If one asks what results from this, the text mentions "Vajra bliss" and so forth. The intention is that the bliss of those two letters reaching the tip of the vajra becomes the cause for accomplishing the body of <term>Mahamudra</term> <gloss>the Great Seal</gloss>; therefore, it is called Mahamudra.

Regarding the phrase "by this," the "secret absorption" refers to the absorption characterized by the internal self. If one asks for an example of this, the text says "the two of the external two," which refers to the union of Nairatmya and Heruka.

Regarding the "three bodies" and so forth, the three bodies of the Buddhas are the three <term>kayas</term> <gloss>dimensions of awakening</gloss>. These should be described as abiding within the body of the yogini. Complete knowledge of these three is the <term>svabhavikakaya</term> <gloss>essential nature body</gloss>, which is the essence of knowing things in their state of equality. This is the meaning of the "wheel of great bliss." The form of the union of the three bodies exists as the wheel of great bliss.

<summary>This page explains the internal tantric anatomy where the deity Nairatmya and the letter A reside at the navel, while Hevajra and the letter Hum reside at the heart. It describes the union of these energies as the cause for achieving Mahamudra and the manifestation of the three Buddha bodies within the practitioner's own body.</summary>
<keywords>Nairatmya, Hevajra, Mahamudra, three bodies, dharmadhatu, navel chakra, secret absorption, yoga tantra</keywords>

text:
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the esoteric union and the transformation of the deity within the tantric practice, specifically focusing on the interactions between the yogini and the central figure.</meta>

Must be practiced! The phrase **"May the Mountain Hermitess <note>Sanskrit: Śabarī</note> accomplish the fruit"** means that I, Śabarī, should accomplish the intended purpose. Then, the **"Fierce Untouchable Woman"** <term>Caṇḍālī</term> <gloss>the inner heat or a specific yogini type</gloss> speaks of hosting the worldly guests. The phrase **"Chief of Joy"** means: "O, the primary leader of intense passion!"

**"Emptiness"** <note>Sanskrit: śūnyatā</note> refers to the state of having become melted <note>the dissolution of the essence in the central channel</note>. **"To reside"** means to remain. For what reason? The phrase **"I, Caṇḍālī, offer a prayer"** means: "I, Caṇḍālī, make a formal request." **"If you are absent, I do not seek that direction"** means: "If you do not remain, I do not seek the direction of acting to liberate sentient beings from suffering." Then, the **"Low-caste Woman"** <term>Ḍombī</term> says: **"O you who possess the power of illusion, please arise!"** This means: "O one possessing the optical illusion <note>Sanskrit: māyā</note>, stand up!"

If one asks, "What if I am not like an illusionist?" then the text says: **"I shall know your mind,"** which means: "I myself shall know your very mind." The phrase **"I, the Ḍombī woman, seek the skillful one"** means: "I, the one called Ḍombī, am the skillful woman; know that I do not belong to the ordinary city." **"Do not let the stream of compassion be cut off"** means: "Interrupting the stream of compassion; do not let it remain only in the nature of the vital fluid <term>śukra</term>."

Now, having arisen from the meditative absorption of the vital fluid, the Blessed One <term>Bhagavān</term> appears in a sixteen-armed form. To describe the hand-implements, the text mentions **"Elephant, horse, donkey,"** and so on. **"Śarabha"** <note>a mythical eight-legged creature</note> means a lion. **"Cat"** means a cat. **"Twice-drinker"** means an elephant and similar animals. **"Fire"** refers to the radiant one. **"The Ender"** refers to Yama <note>the Lord of Death</note>. **"Wealth-Giver"** refers to Vaiśravaṇa <note>the God of Wealth</note>. By the phrase **"Acting with charm,"** and so forth, the text describes the dance movements possessing the nine dramatic sentiments <term>navarasa</term> <gloss>the nine moods of classical Indian aesthetics</gloss>.

Now, following the exhortation, to show the arising from the meditative absorption of melting, the text says: **"By Oṃ and Hūṃ,"** and so on. Upon the disks of the Moon and Sun, which have arisen from the complete transformation of the meditative absorption of melting, the syllables **Oṃ** and **Hūṃ** completely...

<summary>This page provides a commentary on tantric verses involving figures like Caṇḍālī and Ḍombī, interpreting their dialogue as metaphors for the movement of inner energy and the transformation of the deity from a state of dissolution into a manifest sixteen-armed form.</summary>
<keywords>Caṇḍālī, Ḍombī, śūnyatā, compassion, śukra, sixteen-armed deity, navarasa, meditative absorption</keywords>

text:
Concerning the phrase, "then," and so forth: the phrase, "how it will be," means "what it is like." "Ink made from great honey smoke" refers to the ink of great honey <note>likely a reference to a specific alchemical or ritual preparation of incense soot</note>. The term "unfortunate" refers to those who have become hostile. "Without accomplishment" refers to the practitioner. "The other world" refers to other rebirths. The phrase, "endowed with the perfect gift," refers to those with superior devotion to <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>The Joyful Vajra, a major tantric deity</gloss>. "Only occasionally" means "taught at intervals." "The domain of the path" refers to the time of traveling upon the path. "Shown" means "what has been revealed." By the word "food," the rituals of the <term>elaborate conduct</term> <gloss>active tantric practice with external aids</gloss> and the <term>feast circle</term> <gloss>ganachakra</gloss> are also shown. "Where one has eaten" refers to when one performs the feast circle and the conduct. "All desired goals" refers to the accomplishment of <term>Mahamudra</term> <gloss>The Great Seal, the highest state of realization</gloss>.

To show the specific locations for conduct, the text says "charnel ground" and so forth. "Mountain bird-shelter" means a mountain cave. "And nine" means the number nine has been examined. "Commitments" <note>original: "samaya"</note> refers to <term>go, ku, da, ha, na</term> <gloss>code words for the five meats used in tantric ritual</gloss> and so forth. Regarding the phrase, "having eaten, again," and so forth: "Mothers" <note>original: "mamo"</note> refers to the constituent parts of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these must be definitively honored with dance, song, and proper offerings.

To show that very point, the text says, "Even if she is a sister," and so forth. By the words "mother" and so forth, the five sense faculties are actually being taught. These are to be satisfied by the five sensory qualities of form, sound, smell, and so on. This is the unsurpassed offering to those goddesses who reside in those sense locations. If one asks, "how could it be anything other than the eyes and so forth?", it is just as it was stated in the <term>Yogini Tantra</term> <gloss>class of tantras focused on feminine energy</gloss> called the <term>Buddhakapala</term> <gloss>The Buddha's Skull</gloss>:

Next, it shall be perfectly explained:
The impure mind must be purified.
The eye is the sister;
The ear is the sister's daughter;
The nose is the mother who gave birth;
Likewise, the tongue is the daughter;
The mind is the wife.
By these five supreme divine substances,
The Great Seal is perfectly bestowed.

Regarding the phrase, "having honored them well"...

<keywords>Hevajra, Mahamudra, feast circle, sense faculties, Buddhakapala Tantra, tantric conduct, symbolic language</keywords>

The syllable "Ba" is to be experienced continuously without interruption. Regarding the phrase "as a single part" and so forth, "the great skull" refers to the skull of a <term>twice-born</term> <gloss>a member of the higher social classes in Indian tradition, such as a Brahmin</gloss>. "Offer" refers to the beginning of the ritual. "Drink" refers to the subsequent action. The chapter that clarifies the consumption of food also speaks in this manner.

This concludes the commentary on the seventh chapter of the second part of the <term>Yogaratnamala</term> <gloss>The Precious Garland of Yoga</gloss>, which is a difficult points commentary on the <term>Hevajra Tantra</term> <gloss>The Tantra of Hevajra, a major deity in Vajrayana Buddhism</gloss>.

Regarding the phrase "after that" and so forth, "the Great Seal" <note>original: "Mahamudra"</note> is exactly as described previously. Now, concerning the practitioners who perform the ritual with elaborate activity, what is the nature of the partner through whom the Great Seal will be accomplished? Therefore, the text says, "of conventional conduct," meaning according to the conventions of the world. "Through conduct" refers to words of affection and so forth. "Form" refers to color, scent, and such qualities. "Navel of the deer" refers to musk. "Equal" means appearing similar. "Supreme power" refers to the <term>utpala</term> <gloss>blue lotus</gloss>. "Momentary" means occurring occasionally. "Arising" means arising everywhere. "Blood" refers to <term>turuska</term> <gloss>a type of incense or resin</gloss>. "Of that" refers to the body. "Black agarwood" refers to agarwood possessed of the supreme scent. "Charming woman" means one who makes the mind joyful.

Regarding "Reading the profound Dharma," this means reading the <term>Hevajra Tantra</term>. "Those who have become disciplined" refers to the disciples themselves. "Restoration and Purification" <note>original: "Sojong" or "Posadha"</note> refers to the period such as the full moon, lasting from before the sun rises until it has risen. "The bases of training" refers to the eight or fourteen precepts undertaken for as long as one lives; these are characterized by purifying the misdeeds of body, speech, and mind.

"Those who speak for the sake of being free from attachment" refers to the <term>Vaibhashika</term> <gloss>Great Exposition School, one of the four main tenet systems of Indian Buddhism</gloss>. That itself is the <term>Vaibhashika</term> system. Furthermore, that school's traditions include the <term>Hundred Accounts</term> <note>original: "Avadana-shataka"</note> of the Listener <note>original: "Shravaka"</note> vehicle and the <term>Garland of Three Staves</term> and so forth. "The Discourses" <note>original: "Sutras"</note> refers to the discourses that are not extremely profound, such as the <term>One Verse Discourse</term>, the <term>Four Verse Discourse</term>, the <term>Two Verse Incantation</term>, the <term>Six Gates</term>, the <term>Excellent Conduct</term> <note>original: "Bhadracarya"</note>, and the <term>Extensive Play</term> <note>original: "Lalitavistara"</note>.

<meta>continues from previous page: this text continues an analysis of the tantric deities and their correspondences to emotional states and subtle channels.</meta>

...is Vairochana <note>The Enlightened One, the central Buddha of the five families</note>. Slander is Ratnasambhava <note>The Jewel-Born Buddha</note>. Attachment is Amitabha <note>The Buddha of Boundless Light</note>. Jealousy is Amoghasiddhi <note>The Buddha of Unfailing Success</note>. Regarding the phrase "the <term>Pukkasi</term> <gloss>a low-caste female deity</gloss> and so forth": the <term>Pukkasi</term>, <term>Shavari</term>, <term>Chandali</term>, and <term>Dombini</term> <note>These four represent classes of yoginis or female spirits often associated with the outskirts of society</note> correspond to hatred, delusion, slander, and desire respectively.

Furthermore, <term>Gauri</term> <gloss>The White One</gloss> is the protectress. For <term>Gauri</term>, <term>Chauri</term>, <term>Vetali</term>, and <term>Ghasmari</term>, they correspond respectively to hatred, slander, delusion, and desire. Through delusion, one becomes a "Stalker of the Earth" <note>A class of female spirit or yogini active on the terrestrial plane</note>. Through desire, one becomes a "Stalker of the Heavens" <note>A celestial yogini or <term>Dakini</term></note>. The phrase "through desire" means having understood devotion.

To provide the answer to the third question, the text says "the <term>Ali</term> <gloss>the series of vowels in the Sanskrit alphabet</gloss> and so forth." The first <term>Ali</term> is the letter A. "Nairatmya" <gloss>The Lady of Selflessness</gloss> refers to the seed-syllable of the deity Nairatmya. To provide the answer to the fourth question, the text says "from the chapter on the families and so forth." The word "spoken" means it was taught.

"Two times sixteen" refers to the thirty-two <note>Thirty-two subtle channels or energy centers in the body</note>. For every two of these, there is one <term>Yogini</term> <gloss>female tantric practitioner or deity</gloss>. The phrase "in successive order" means following the proper sequence. The three channels starting with <term>Lalana</term> <gloss>the left subtle channel</gloss>, <term>Rasana</term> <gloss>the right subtle channel</gloss>, <note>The third is Avadhuti, the central channel</note> are described as the <term>Yogini</term> Nairatmya. This effectively demonstrates the fifteen <term>Yoginis</term>. The channels <term>Geha</term>, <term>Chandika</term>, and <term>Maradarika</term> are the celestial <term>Yoginis</term>.

If half of thirty-two is sixteen, one might ask: how do they become fifteen <term>Yoginis</term>? For this reason, the text says "strive to abandon the remainder of all and so forth." One should abandon the final part of all. This means that the last part is not of the same essence as the <term>Yoginis</term>. If one asks why, the text says "because the sixteenth has no part and so forth." By "not performing a function," it means it does not perform a meaningful action. For example, the fifteen days of the waxing moon perform the function of illustrating the increase of the moon's light. The sixteenth day does not, for it becomes the cause of the moon's waning. Therefore, one should strive to abandon it. If one asks what results from this: the Bodhichitta...

<summary>This page explains the symbolic correspondence between tantric deities, such as the five Buddhas and various Yoginis, and human emotions or subtle body channels. It specifically clarifies why fifteen Yoginis are counted instead of sixteen by using the metaphor of the lunar cycle.</summary>
<keywords>Vairochana, Amitabha, Yogini, Nairatmya, subtle channels, Lalana, Rasana, lunar days, Bodhichitta</keywords>

At that time, one should introduce a youth who is primarily characterized by whatever beauty can be found, because this way of the <term>Yogini</term> <gloss>female tantric practitioner</gloss> is the way of great passion. This provides a brief explanation of the characteristics of the student. 

Now, in order to briefly explain the secret initiation <note>original: "guhyabhisheka"</note>, it says "as long as," and so forth. The phrase "the face of the <term>mudra</term>" <gloss>consort or ritual seal</gloss> refers to the face of the student. The phrase "of the method" refers to the student. Regarding the phrase "should be done," and so forth, "to that very one" refers to <term>Prajna</term> <gloss>Wisdom</gloss>. "Equal taste" refers to the initiation of Wisdom. "The sphere of activity of the student" refers to the removal of the student's blindfold. 

If one asks what happens through these acts, it says "self-knowing," and so forth. By having the equal taste of suchness itself, it becomes the <term>jnana</term> <gloss>primordial wisdom</gloss> of self-knowing. If one asks what kind of special quality it has, it says "self and other," and so forth. It is free from the division of parts into self and other. "Equal to space" means it is equal to the sky because of its lack of any perceived appearance. It is "free from dust" because of the absence of afflictive emotions. It is "empty" because it has completely transcended conceptual elaboration. 

"Entities" are those things that arise. "Non-entities" are those things that cease. That which possesses the nature of both is called by that name. "Supreme" refers to the ultimate wisdom. The emptiness of method is wisdom. Method is great compassion, which is the complete experience of equality with oneself for all sentient beings. Their "union" means they appear as a single form. "Attachment" is supreme joy. "Freedom from attachment" is the joy of the absence of joy; it is the nature in which these two are unified. 

"Living beings" means sentient beings. They themselves are "life," for if they were not there, there would be no life. The "supreme syllable" is so called because it possesses the form of the <term>dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>sphere of reality</gloss>, which has no beginning or end. It is the "pervader" because the nature of all phenomena is that very thing. "All reside within the body" is said because consciousness resides within the bodies of living beings. From that itself, the wandering beings...

As for the phrase "there," it means while residing there. Regarding the phrase "he spoke," if one asks for whose benefit he spoke, it was for the benefit of those beings who were tormented by the desire to hear the teachings. 

If one asks what he spoke, it begins with the phrase "of all the <term>Tathāgatas</term> <gloss>Thus Gone Ones</gloss>." A <term>Tathāgata</term> is one who has gone as far as there is to travel; they have abandoned all obscurations along with their habitual tendencies. Alternatively, the word "gone" <note>original: "gatis"</note> has the meaning of "realization." Because they realize reality exactly as it is, as suchness, these are called <term>Tathāgatas</term>. They perfectly realize all that is to be known in every possible way. 

Alternatively, the syllables may be translated in the present tense: because he speaks exactly as things are to be demonstrated, he is a <term>Tathāgata</term>. He perfectly teaches the genuine <term>Dharma</term> <gloss>Buddha's teaching</gloss> in accordance with the intentions, dispositions, and needs of those to be trained, as well as the specific time. He is all of those things, and he is also the <term>Tathāgata</term>. 

The <term>Vajradhara</term> <gloss>Vajra Holder</gloss> is the very essence of their body, speech, and mind. The "heart" or "essence" refers to the most excellent. The term "Venerable" <note>original: "Bhagavan"</note> refers to the supreme deity. The essence of the body, speech, and mind of all the deities of secret mantra, who are the nature of non-conceptual primordial wisdom, is itself that which is most difficult to trust or comprehend. Their "great secret" is that which is even more secret than the secret itself. Because he is endowed with great intensity and is called <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>Vajra of Joy</gloss>, possessing the supreme intensity and great passion of body, speech, and mind, he is therefore the secret beyond the secret. The intention is that even faith in this is extremely difficult to find. 

The word "this" carries the meaning of "in this manner." For the retinue tormented by the desire to hear, three thoughts arise. The first thought is: "If this is indeed the secret beyond the secret, when and what kind of person would be fortunate enough to receive it? This must be explained." The second thought is: "Is it the established conclusion that there is no supreme being other than the <term>Vajradhara</term>?" Of that itself...

text:
Is this essence, or is it another more supreme one called Body, Speech, and Mind? This is the second <note>point of doubt or inquiry</note>. What is the name of this Venerable One? This is the third. To clarify these conceptions, the text says: "How wonderful!" <note>original: "E ma ho"</note> and so forth.

At the end of this phrase, one should take the word "this" from the previous sentence and apply it to understand its own meaning. "This too" means "even such as this." If the word "this" is absent in some versions, one should still understand the meaning in that way.

The phrase "How wonderful, Vajra Essence!" <note>original: "E ma ho rdo rje sྙing po"</note> means that all Bodhisattvas are the <term>Tathagatagarbha</term> <gloss>Essence of the One Gone to Bliss</gloss> and the <term>Tathagata-gotra</term> <gloss>Buddha Family or lineage</gloss>.

The five Buddha families are ignorance, hatred, pride, desire, and jealousy. In this context, that which is characterized by hatred is the <term>Vajra-garbha</term> <gloss>Vajra Essence</gloss>. The name of this Bodhisattva accords with its meaning. It is difficult to find a Bodhisattva lineage such as this. Because of the wonder felt at this, the text calls out: "How wonderful!"

Regarding the phrase "That Essence, Bodhisattva, Great Hero <note>original: "Mahasattva"</note>, excellent, excellent!": the intention to accomplish the benefit of others through methods such as supreme wrath is itself Great Compassion. Through that, the Awakening that accomplishes various purposes without a fixed time is Great Awakening. One who truly contemplates this is a Great Heroic Bodhisattva. One who possesses such an intention to benefit others and an intention to benefit themselves is the supreme of beings. For that reason, the word "excellent" is repeated twice.

The command "Listen!" is the engagement in hearing. This demonstrates that a holy being with such a lineage and such an intention is one who possesses the fortunate karmic connection. How is this lineage to be known? It is known through the specific signs of faith and desire for its qualities. As stated in the *Noble Descent into Lanka Sutra* <note>original: "Arya-Lankavatara-sutra"</note>:

By smoke, one knows there is fire;
By the water-crane, one knows there is water.

<summary>This page provides a commentary on the qualities of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, explaining the symbolic relationship between the five poisons and the five Buddha families. it defines the terms Mahasattva and Great Awakening in the context of altruistic intention.</summary>

<keywords>Vajragarbha, Tathagatagarbha, Buddha families, Mahasattva, Great Compassion, Lankavatara Sutra, Five Poisons</keywords>

text:
Consciousness <note>Tibetan: rnam shes</note> refers to being skilled in all the activities of the master. The phrase the deities <note>Tibetan: lha rnams</note> refers to the glorious Heruka together with his retinue, or alternatively, to Nairatmya <note>the female personification of egolessness</note>. The phrase how they arise <note>Tibetan: ji ltar 'byung ba</note> means how they are generated in a suitable manner. The phrase the other <note>Tibetan: cig shos</note> refers to the gazes, the rites of summoning, and so forth as they have been explained. Heruka is the result, Hevajra. Generation <note>Tibetan: bskyed pa</note> means attaining his level. Its cause is the meaning of the Method Tantra <note>Tibetan: thabs kyi rgyud</note>. Why is this mentioned first? Because this method of the generation stage <note>Tibetan: bskyed pa'i rim pa</note> through the forms of deities and so forth is the most excellent.

Furthermore, in this Great Vehicle, all phenomena are shown to be contained within consciousness alone. The Noble Ten Bhumis Scripture <note>Sanskrit: Dashabhumika Sutra</note> says: Thus, this triple world is mind only. The nature of that consciousness is clarity. If it were not of this nature, it would not be clear, as that would be a contradiction. Because blue, yellow, and so forth appear clearly, there are no external objects existing outside of consciousness.

What is the situation then? It is the mind itself, established by similar patterns of conceptual thought, which arises in various forms such as aspect, appearance, and experience, just like a dream. The Noble Descent into Lanka Scripture <note>Sanskrit: Lankavatara Sutra</note> says:

External objects do not exist
In the way the foolish imagine them.
The mind, stirred up by latent tendencies <note>Sanskrit: vasana</note>,
Appears as external objects.

Stirred up means afflicted. Furthermore, external objects like blue and so forth do not exist because they lack the nature of being either one or many. They are not one because they appear as distinct parts. They are also not many atoms because the concept of atoms is illogical. If an atom has parts, how can it be a minute atom? If it has no parts, then when atoms join together with their entire essence, they would be inseparable and occupy the same space. Thus, elephants, mountains, oceans, and the entire mass of the earth would be reduced to the size of a single minute atom.

<summary>This page explains the generation stage of the Heruka deity and provides a philosophical defense of the Mind Only view. It argues that external objects are mental projections and uses the logical refutation of atoms to prove that only consciousness exists.</summary>
<keywords>Heruka, Hevajra, generation stage, Mind Only, Yogacara, consciousness, Dashabhumika Sutra, Lankavatara Sutra, refutation of atoms</keywords>

text:
Thinking about this, the author stated: "The bondage of things" <note>original: "dngos po'i 'ching ba"</note> and so forth. Here, the term "things" refers to the five perfections <note>the perfections of generosity, discipline, patience, diligence, and concentration</note>, because these are the primary factors for remaining in the world and for attainment. The bondage of things itself is that which causes one to remain. Those who are liberated through being bound by these perfections remain for the benefit of all beings throughout the continuum of the three bodies <term>trikaya</term> <gloss>the three dimensions of a Buddha: the truth, enjoyment, and emanation bodies</gloss> until the very limits of space.

Thoroughly knowing the nature of these things is the knowledge of the ultimate truth, which is the perfection of wisdom <term>prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>transcendent wisdom</gloss> itself. Being liberated by this, one abandons all obscurations of habitual tendencies; this means completely exhausting all afflicted phenomena along with their seeds. This state is nirvana, specifically described as non-abiding nirvana <term>apratisthita-nirvana</term> <gloss>a state where a Buddha stays neither in the cycle of suffering nor in a state of solitary peace</gloss>, because one abides neither in cyclic existence nor in personal liberation.

Regarding the summary provided in the text starting with "things" and so forth: "things" refers to the virtue arising from the five perfections. "Should be meditated upon" means one should exert effort to generate these in the continuum of one's own mind and become endowed with them through the power of meditation.

"By thoroughly knowing the absence of things" means through the perfection of wisdom which thoroughly understands that things lack an inherent nature of subject and object. If one does not treat things as things <note>referring to engaging in the perfections</note>, one is liberated but falls into the enlightenment of a Hearer <term>shravaka</term> <gloss>one who seeks only personal liberation</gloss>. Yet, if one does not thoroughly know their nature, one remains in cyclic existence. Both paths are characterized by delusion.

The Bodhisattva who possesses wisdom does both <note>remains in the world through the perfections while knowing their empty nature</note>. For that reason, they are addressed as "The Wise One." This summarizes the conduct of the Great Vehicle <term>Mahayana</term> and establishes its system. Because the Great Vehicle is also contained within the Way of Secret Mantra, the <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>the "Joyful Vajra" tantra</gloss> is taught as the superior method. Thus it says, "In that way" and so forth. By mentioning the principal figure "Heruka" <gloss>a wrathful semi-nude male deity representing enlightened consciousness</gloss>, one also includes his attributes, his seat, and the celestial palace, just as one says "The King approaches" <note>implying his whole retinue and court are included in the statement</note>.

<summary>This page explains how a Bodhisattva uses the first five perfections to remain in the world for others while using the sixth perfection, wisdom, to avoid being trapped by worldly existence. It defines non-abiding nirvana as the balance between these two states and links this Mahayana path to the Hevajra Tantra.</summary>
<keywords>perfections, paramitas, non-abiding nirvana, Bodhisattva, Hevajra, Heruka, emptiness, Mahayana</keywords>
