text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
The purification of the hands is described. The reality of the sixteen hands is the sixteen types of emptiness. These are: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal and external emptiness, the emptiness of greatness, the emptiness of emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the emptiness of that which transcends limits, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, the emptiness of that which is not to be discarded, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-entities, and the emptiness of the essence of non-entities. These very things are represented as the hands.

The feet represent the purification that overcomes the <term>maras</term> <gloss>demonic obstructions or influencers</gloss>. These are the <term>mara</term> of the aggregates, the <term>mara</term> of afflictive emotions, the <term>mara</term> of the Lord of Death, and the <term>mara</term> of the son of a god.

The term "faces" refers to the literal faces of the deity. The term "three vajras" refers to the <term>vajra</term> body, <term>vajra</term> speech, and <term>vajra</term> mind. By the phrase "the earth is," and so forth, the purification of elements such as earth is shown; this refers to <term>Pukkasi</term> <gloss>a female deity representing the earth element</gloss> and the others. Regarding the phrase "by this," and so forth, "aggregates" refers to the five aggregates and the rest.

In that way, having briefly shown the purification from the perspective of the generation stage <note>Tibetan: bskyed rim; the yoga of visualizing oneself as a deity</note>, the text then presents the purification of the single taste of reality from the perspective of the completion stage <note>Tibetan: rdzogs rim; the yoga of internal energy and subtle channels</note>. It says, "by whichever and whichever," and so forth. Those very things such as form, by which the world is bound, are the very means by which one should liberate oneself. One should not even perform the meditation on the appearance of the deity <note>at this advanced stage of completion</note>.

If one asks: if liberation comes through those very things, then how is it that people in the world are bound by them? It is because worldly beings are deluded; they are ignorant of reality because they cling to these things as being true in themselves. They have not realized the unborn reality of these things. The phrase "abandoning that very thing" means being devoid of the meditation on the unborn. It is intended that "attainment," which is the state of the <term>Vajradhara</term> <gloss>the Holder of the Thunderbolt, representing supreme enlightenment</gloss>, will not be found <note>by those who cling to dualistic appearances</note>.

<summary>This page explains the symbolic purification of a deity's sixteen hands as the sixteen types of emptiness and the feet as the conquest of the four maras. It transitions from the symbolic generation stage to the completion stage, emphasizing that the same sensory objects that bind the ignorant can liberate the wise.</summary>
<keywords>sixteen types of emptiness, four maras, generation stage, completion stage, Vajradhara, purification, tantric symbolism</keywords>

If one asks: if liberation comes through those very things, then how is it that people in the world are bound by them? It is because worldly beings are deluded; they are ignorant of reality because they cling to these things as being true in themselves. They have not realized the unborn reality of these things. The phrase "abandoning that very thing" means being devoid of the meditation on the unborn. It is intended that "attainment," which is the state of the <term>Vajradhara</term> <gloss>the Holder of the Thunderbolt, representing supreme enlightenment</gloss>, will not be found <note>by those who cling to dualistic appearances</note>.

It transitions from the symbolic generation stage to the completion stage, emphasizing that the same sensory objects that bind the ignorant can liberate the wise.</summary>

The one called "Intoxicated" <note>original: <term>mada</term></note> is said to be the Moon. The one called "Blood" is explained as the Sun. The Moon and the Sun are widely explained as two channels <note>original: <term>nadi</term></note>.

Furthermore, it is stated in the *Union of the Bud* <note>original: <term>Samputa Tantra</term></note>:
The lotus situated in the center of the heart possesses eight petals at the navel. The channel situated in its center is clear, like a lamp flame. It hangs with its opening facing downward, like the flower of a plantain tree. The "Hero" <note>original: <term>vīra</term></note> situated in its center is the size of a mustard seed. The indestructible syllable <term>HUM</term> drips like a seed of frost. This which moves and comes stays perfectly within the entire body. What is widely known as the "Short One" <note>the short vowel A</note> stays at the navel in the form of the letter <term>A</term>. Possessing two curved strokes <note>referring to the vowel signs of the long vowels</note>, the long <term>HUM</term> stays in both <note>possibly referring to the heart or specific channels</note>. Possessing three curved strokes, the nature of <term>OM</term> stays at the throat. Along with the sound <note>original: <term>nada</term></note> and the drop <note>original: <term>bindu</term></note>, the indestructible <term>HAM</term> is in the forehead. It is the form of the glorious Vajrasattva, playing however he pleases. Also, on the four petals situated in the four directions, there are the channels of the four great elements, having the nature of a burning lamp.

If one asks how the presentation of the channels in these three Tantras is taught as one: the meaning is that if something is not taught here, it is established from other sources, and therefore that is the intention here. The <term>Lalana</term> <gloss>the left channel</gloss> and <term>Rasana</term> <gloss>the right channel</gloss> begin from the throat and extend as far as the interior of the navel. The channels on the left and right sides are called "Moon" and "Sun." The two channels of the birth-place <note>the secret organ</note> below the navel are those very same ones called <term>Lalana</term> and <term>Rasana</term>.

The five channels of the heart are:
1. The One Who Enters the Three <note>original: <term>Sumati</term></note>
2. The Lustful One <note>original: <term>Kamini</term></note>
3. The Housewife <note>original: <term>Geha</term></note>
4. The Fierce One <note>original: <term>Candika</term></note>
5. The Destroyer of Mara <note>original: <term>Maravajini</term></note>

If it is asked why the *Union of the Bud* speaks of one hundred and twenty channels: that is the division of the four chakras <gloss>energy centers</gloss>. Here, there are thirty-two supreme channels which are the nature of <term>Bodhicitta</term> <gloss>awakened mind/enlightenment-fluid</gloss>. Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever. text:
<meta>continues from previous page: ...the ten stages and so forth.</meta> The term <term>Yogachara</term> <gloss>Practitioner of Yoga</gloss> refers to the teaching that these various appearances are merely the mind. It is taught that when one is deluded regarding the nature of reality, which is not truly existent, things appear as objects; this is described as being like a dream. The term <term>Madhyamaka</term> <gloss>Middle Way</gloss> refers to the fact that all phenomena are without inherent birth.

The phrase "all vehicles of the secret mantra" refers to the five-fold division of <term>Kriya</term> <gloss>Action</gloss>, <term>Charya</term> <gloss>Performance</gloss>, <term>Yoga</term> <gloss>Union</gloss>, <term>Anuttara Yoga</term> <gloss>Unsurpassed Union</gloss>, and <term>Niruttara Yoga</term> <gloss>Absolute Union</gloss>. Regarding the systems of the <term>Vaibhashika</term> <gloss>Great Exposition School</gloss> and others, it is said that one should understand their general treatises only, but not all their substances, for they are beyond measure. The term "having taken up" means to act with devotion. "With devotion" means having devotion for this specific <term>tantra</term> <gloss>lineage text</gloss>.

This concludes the commentary on the eighth chapter of the second section from the <term>Yogaratnamala</term> <gloss>The Precious Garland of Yoga</gloss>, which is a difficult-point commentary on the <term>Hevajra Tantra</term>.

Regarding the phrase "after that" and so forth: <term>Samputa</term> <gloss>Union</gloss> refers to the union of consciousness and the body. "Differentiating" means making a distinction. The phrase "through meditative concentration" refers to what remains. "Siddhi" <gloss>Attainment</gloss> refers here to the attainment of wrathful activities. "Disturbed" means being extremely fierce. "Malevolent" refers to the intent to kill. "Meditation" refers to what was just explained. "That very thing" means that alone. Regarding the word "Buddha," it means that even if one is perfectly protected by the Buddhas and so forth. "Having seen" means having remembered. "In the form of" refers to the forms that will be explained. "Needle" refers to the <term>vajra</term> <gloss>adamantine</gloss> needle. "Possessing the form of fire" means becoming ablaze. "Seed of the fire-consumer" <gloss>Agni</gloss> refers to the intensely blazing syllable <term>Ram</term>. "Having visualized" means having meditated. The phrase "accomplished by reciting" means that the meaning of the words is true until completion. "Secret" refers to that which is not the sphere of experience for sentient beings who lack the fortunate connection. "Supreme" means achieving the desired result without hardship. "Non-conceptual" means without doubt. "Jewel" refers to the precious wish-fulfilling gem. If one asks what that jewel is, the text says "the body," referring to the primordial state.

<summary>This page defines key philosophical schools like Yogachara and Madhyamaka while classifying the five classes of Tantra. it concludes the eighth chapter of the Yogaratnamala commentary on the Hevajra Tantra and begins explaining ritual technicalities and wrathful attainments.</summary>
<keywords>Yogachara, Madhyamaka, Five Tantra Classes, Hevajra Tantra, Yogaratnamala, Siddhi, Agni, Vajra Needle</keywords>

text:
<meta>This page continues the commentary on tantric conduct and the classification of Buddha families within the Derge Tengyur collection.</meta>

And conduct is the ritual; it is the ritual of method and wisdom. The phrase "it should be offered through the desire for reality" means it is done for the purpose of perfectly realizing suchness. "With effort" means protecting the secret with diligence. That very effort is described as: "in a way that it does not become known."

"To be known" refers to being investigated by those with the power to know things other than themselves, or to the failure of the secret due to oneself or a confidant speaking of it to others out of pride, showing off, or anger, or through a servant. If the secret is not kept, the unseen faults, such as falling into hell and so forth, are extremely well known. The visible faults are also described by the phrase "if not kept secret" and so on. The phrase "snakes and so forth" should be connected to "causing suffering," meaning suffering caused by snakes, tigers, and such. "Those who move on the earth" refers to humans, <term>pishachas</term> <gloss>flesh-eating spirits</gloss>, and others who inflict punishment.

Regarding the term <term>mudra</term> <gloss>seal or hand gesture</gloss>: it is that which symbolizes these families such as the <term>vajra</term> <gloss>diamond-bolt</gloss> and the <term>padma</term> <gloss>lotus</gloss>. Regarding "He who has gone to suchness" <note>original: "Tathagata"</note>: it is to have gone into a single taste within the utterly pure suchness; it is to abide in the <term>dharmakaya</term> <gloss>truth body</gloss>. "Possessing glorious knowledge" means being the sovereign of the qualities of all Buddhas, which the <term>shravakas</term> <gloss>pious listeners</gloss> and others are not.

"Come forth" means from that very suchness. Coming forth from that is for the sake of the welfare of beings through the <term>sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>enjoyment body</gloss> and <term>nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>emanation body</gloss>, which are the natural results of that suchness. In this way, the term <term>Tathagata</term> captures this as a single entity, following the etymological explanation where letters are dropped, such as the hidden "ta" in <term>Tathagata</term>.

In that regard, all <term>Tathagatas</term> consist of the five families of those original wisdoms, such as the mirror-like wisdom and the rest. If all Buddhas possess the five wisdoms, how are they divided into families? The division of families is based on each wisdom like the mirror-like wisdom being similar in part or similar in many parts. Together with the <term>Sattva</term> <gloss>Heroic Being</gloss> family, there are six. Since they are established from beginningless time, these are the families of the <term>Bodhisattvas</term>. As it is said: "The families are explained as being of six types." "When condensed, there are five types" refers to...

<keywords>Tathagata, Secrecy, Buddha families, Five Wisdoms, Mudra, Bodhisattva, Dharmakaya</keywords>

text:
The nature of the <term>jnana</term> <gloss>wisdom</gloss> of great bliss is without conceptual elaboration, because all marks of delusion have subsided. This very authentic wisdom exhausts the afflictions along with their seeds. The stainless realm, which abandons the conceptualizations appearing as environment, body, and enjoyments, is also without conceptual elaboration. These three are the purified, space-like, infinite, and elaboration-free <term>dharmakaya</term> <gloss>truth body of a Buddha</gloss>. That ultimate truth exists as that very nature and essence. Therefore, the intention is to make that very nature manifest.

In that regard, that very essence is <term>Vairocana</term> <gloss>the Illuminator</gloss> by appearing as mere clarity. That same essence is <term>Akshobhya</term> <gloss>the Unshakeable</gloss> by the fact of non-appearance itself. That same essence is <term>Amoghasiddhi</term> <gloss>Unfailing Success</gloss> because it performs diverse purposes. That same essence is <term>Ratnasambhava</term> <gloss>the Jewel-Born</gloss> because all the qualities of a Buddha are obtained through it. That same essence is <term>Arolik</term> <note>a seed syllable associated with Amitabha and the Lotus family</note> because it perfectly practices the self-nature of these. Thus, the nature of the five wisdoms is the <term>sattva</term> <gloss>spiritual hero/being</gloss>, which is the meaning of the name <term>Vajrasattva</term> <gloss>Diamond Being</gloss>.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Brahma" and so forth: that very essence is described as Brahma and the rest. To explain why this is thought to be so, the text says: "He is called Brahma," and so on. Since that very nature of realizing perfect purity is the Buddha, he is the supreme Brahma. Thus, the phrase "Brahma is <term>nirvana</term> <gloss>extinction of suffering</gloss>" means the very nature of liberation. "Nirvana," "liberation," "peace," and "Brahma" are synonyms.

The term "entering" refers to entering into the identity of that. Into what? Into the profoundly deep <term>dharmakaya</term>. The phrase "always perfectly virtuous" is used because it is eternally virtuous and supremely virtuous. Regarding the passage beginning with "all": because it abides as that which makes known the <term>dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>sphere of reality</gloss> as the identity of all things, it is therefore called "all." "Supreme bliss" refers to the demonstration of the highest stainless bliss. The phrase "killed by the realization of bliss" <note>an idiomatic or esoteric reference to the destruction of ignorance through bliss</note> means realizing that very unsurpassable bliss. One who does not know that is like one who is asleep. Brahma...

<summary>This page explains the nature of the Dharmakaya as the integration of five wisdoms personified by the Five Buddha Families and Vajrasattva. It equates the realization of ultimate reality with the state of Brahma, defining it as synonymous with nirvana, liberation, and supreme bliss.</summary>
<keywords>Jnana, Dharmakaya, Five Buddhas, Vajrasattva, Nirvana, Brahma, Dharmadhatu, Supreme Bliss</keywords>

text:
Having explained the activities and other teachings, he states further: Regarding the phrase "the body" and so forth, the deity itself is produced from the body; this is the meaning. The term <term>dehasambhava</term> <gloss>arising from the body</gloss> means it originates from the body. In the previous syllable, the letter "ha" is made unmanifest, and in the following "sambha," it is also made unmanifest, meaning the deity itself arises from the body. Because this shows that it is easily found, its arising from the body makes it easily obtained. The phrase "to that Buddha" means "to Buddhahood itself." The one who desires <term>siddhi</term> <gloss>spiritual accomplishment</gloss> is defined as one who, through unremitting yoga and conduct, attains <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>The Joyful Vajra</gloss> in this very life. The meaning is that if such diligence exists—that is, if there is joy—one will attain buddhahood. This is how the text should be applied. The <term>vajra</term> girl is the most excellent among those of her family <note>lineage or class</note>, intended in the sense that she is not used by others. The phrase personal chosen deity means one should achieve the practice. The phrase born from another family refers to those arising from a lineage other than one's own <term>yidam</term> <gloss>meditational deity</gloss>. Purified means properly empowered. This should be applied to the act of taking hold of and engaging in the practice. Through joy refers to the joy arising from yoga. Possessing the <term>vajra</term> means that the <term>vajra</term> is the inseparability of the two truths; the meaning is the <term>vajra</term> song that expresses that inseparability. Through <term>vajra</term> steps refers to the hands, feet, facial expressions, and other <term>mudras</term> <gloss>symbolic hand gestures</gloss> that clarify reality. In the form of a wheel means exactly that: in the form of a wheel. On the hand refers to the bracelets on the forearms. Purified hatred refers to the form of <term>Hevajra</term>. The purity of mantra is the song regarded as mantra, which is performed as a song. Dance means the act of dancing. By the nature of meditation means regarding it as meditation itself. This should be connected to the instruction to always sing and always dance. Always means at all times. Even death refers to the experience of dying. Will be protected means obtaining protection. Arisen from <term>Hum</term> is <term>Akshobhya</term> <gloss>The Unshakeable Buddha</gloss>. The skull cup which has the nature of <term>Akshobhya</term> and the others is the <term>Buddhakapala</term> <gloss>Buddha-Skull</gloss>. The hair sash is a waistband made of hair. Ash refers to being smeared with ashes. The hair purifier is worn as an offering for the hair. Craving, delusion, and so forth are obstacles for the yogi and must be abandoned. Shame means the sense of embarrassment. Sleep is a great obstacle to yoga, and attachment to sustaining the body is also the root of a yogi's obstacles. Therefore, it is taught—

<keywords>Hevajra, siddhi, yidam, mudra, Akshobhya, Buddhakapala, yoga obstacles, tantric song</keywords>

text:
The term Lord means the Buddha as well. This refers to the fact that the Buddha is the sovereign of the eleventh stage <note>original: bhūmi</note>, and is thus described in this way. Regarding the thought, "How do these stages function?"—the phrase "by these" refers to the stages of the dwelling places and so forth. 

The <term>mudras</term> <gloss>ritual hand gestures or symbolic seals</gloss> of the stages of primordial wisdom—including the Stage of Practicing with Devotion <note>original: adhimukticaryā-bhūmi</note>, the Joyous Stage <note>original: pramuditā-bhūmi</note>, the Stainless Stage <note>original: vimalā-bhūmi</note>, and so forth up to the Radiance Stage <note>original: samantaprabhā-bhūmi</note>—are established in their respective dwelling places as appropriate. This is the intended meaning. 

The phrase "nothing else can be said" does not mean that the dwelling places and so forth are excluded; rather, it means that the <term>mudra</term> and that which is sealed by the <term>mudra</term> are inseparable. 

The city is Pataliputra. The distinction of Harikela refers to the Salt Ocean and so forth. The Land of Gold refers to <term>Suvarnadvipa</term> <gloss>the Golden Isle, likely Sumatra or the Malay Peninsula</gloss>. The "environs" are called such because they are near to that place. The "pond" is situated in a long, narrow shape. The phrase "the half-moon of the <term>pretas</term> <gloss>hungry ghosts</gloss>" refers to the latter half of the month. The "banner" refers to the graceful one. "Generating compassion" means contemplating the very suffering of those beings. "By the wise" refers to the learned ones. "The malicious" are those who feel hatred toward the <term>Mantrayana</term> <gloss>Vehicle of Secret Mantra</gloss>. "In order to lead them in" means to lead them into the Vehicle of Secret Mantra. "By that reason, all rituals" means all rituals are to be performed. "As the principal" means by making it the primary focus. 

After compassion was taught, wisdom <note>original: prajñā</note> was also taught with the phrase "in that" and so forth. "Should be viewed" means it should be contemplated. Those two times are <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>the "Joyful Vajra" deity</gloss> and his wisdom consort. Therefore, all actions gathered by that are virtuous. Other methods were taught in the phrase "nothing that should not be done" and so forth. 

"In this" refers to the divine pride of Hevajra. Just as one has great devotion for oneself, so it is for all sentient beings; therefore, to correctly gather them together, it says "oneself as well." "The supreme self" refers to this very Blessed Lord, meaning Hevajra. "Abiding in the state" is for the sake of making the divine pride firm.

<summary>This page provides a technical commentary on the stages of Buddhist realization and the symbolism of the deity Hevajra. It explains geographical locations, ritual mudras, and the integration of compassion and wisdom within the Secret Mantra tradition.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra, bhūmi, mudra, Pataliputra, Suvarnadvipa, Mantrayana, compassion, divine pride, prajna</keywords>

text:
{D1189} In the language of India: <term>Shri Hevajra Panjika Nama Muktika Avali</term> <gloss>The String of Pearls: A Commentary on the Difficult Points of the Glorious Hevajra</gloss>. In the language of Tibet: <term>Pal Gyepe Dorje Kah-drel Mutik Trengwa</term> <gloss>The String of Pearls: A Commentary on the Difficult Points of the Glorious Hevajra</gloss>.

I bow to the glorious <term>Vajra Dakini</term> <gloss>Diamond Sky-Goer</gloss>.

May you be protected by the dance of <term>Heruka</term> <gloss>The Blood-Drinker/Unconditioned Hero</gloss>, who is the essence of the essences of the Three Secrets of the Victors <note>the secrets of body, speech, and mind of a Buddha</note>. 
By placing his feet, he shatters the four earths. 
By his intense laughter, he topples the mountains. 
With the light of his eyes and the sound of his banners and bells, he destroys all wandering beings and then restores them to life. 
He holds the methods that show terrifying rites to utterly pacify those puffed up with pride.

Because it teaches the <term>Sutras</term> <gloss>Discourses</gloss> that follow the authentic standard, 
And because it is clear and exceptionally beautiful, 
This delightful commentary on the <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>The Joyous Diamond</gloss> 
Shall be composed like a string of pearls.

The word "principal" is meaningless to those without faith. 
It is a place of straying into being one with the deity. 
Because the Omniscient One <note>the Buddha</note> is the valid authority, 
One does not become omniscient through mere devotion. 
To say the Victor did not do what he did, 
Or to say he spoke what he did not speak, 
Are both equally mocking towards the <term>Sugata</term> <gloss>The One Gone to Bliss</gloss>, the supreme undeceiving guide of beings. 

The Victor spoke of many benefits, 
Which people take according to their own inclinations. 
Likewise, in this commentary, though the meaning is explained, 
One engages with it according to one's own desire. 
Without realization, there is no hearing. 
Without hearing, there is no contemplation. 
If both are impaired, there is no yoga. 
Without yoga, there will be no accomplishment. 
Thus, for those whose hearts have long been scorched by desire, 
Let this string of pearls, threaded within this Tantra, captivate them.

Regarding the introductory words "Thus have I heard" and so forth, some say that because it is an abridgment, it is actually a different Tantra. 
Others say that this "Second Part" was extracted from a Great Tantra <note>referring to the lost original version of the Hevajra Tantra said to consist of 500,000 stanzas</note>, and that it was summarized exactly as it was there and placed here together with the introductory words. 
Others say this has a different, supreme, and great secret meaning. 
That is correct, for it would be improper to state it at the beginning, as it will be explained later and relies upon the written syllables. Therefore, one applies a different meaning to the different meaning that is to be explained...

<summary>This page contains the title and opening verses of a commentary on the Hevajra Tantra, including an invocation to the deity Heruka and a philosophical justification for the text's structure and necessity.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra Tantra, Heruka, Vajra Dakini, Buddhist logic, yoga, commentary, string of pearls</keywords>

edits.old: It is a place of straying from being one with the deity.
edits.new: It is a place of straying into being one with the deity.
edits.why: The Tibetan 'gcig tu' means 'into one' or 'as one'; translating it as 'straying from' reverses the direction of the error (from separation to union).

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
and so forth. Regarding the phrase **even by a person of little merit**, this refers to those who did not accumulate merit in their previous lives. The statement **there is no doubt they will achieve success** refers to the fact that merit is accumulated through this very yoga. Regarding the term **eating**, it means while in the act of consuming food. The phrase **even while sleeping** refers to the fact that through constant training, one will likewise see <note>meaning the realization or deity</note> even in dreams. **Entering the stream** refers to the effortless arising of the <term>rasa</term> <gloss>essential taste or sapidity</gloss> through this yoga.

If one asks what should be done with this continuous practice, the text says **The Great Seal** <note>original: "Mahamudra"</note> and so forth, meaning it is intended for the sake of the <term>siddhi</term> <gloss>attainment</gloss> of the Great Seal. Through the treatise that expresses great devotion to such a yoga, the accumulation of merit is explained.

To explain the making of mental aspirations, the text says **In this way** and so forth. **All wandering beings** refers to both the sentient beings and the external vessel of the world. All of these are to be meditated upon as a single unity. Regarding the question of why one should hold this certain understanding, the text says **by the mind** and so forth. The **mind** is the consciousness that forms conceptual constructions; it is not through that conceptualizing mind that the truth is to be examined, yet it is with that mind that the certain understanding must be held. This is the meaning.

If one thinks, "If it is not to be examined conceptually, should it then not be meditated upon?" the text therefore says **all phenomena** and so forth. Meditation is the thorough knowledge of phenomena itself; it is not the conceptualization. This is the meaning. The intention is that conceptual thoughts are by their very nature delusive.

Regarding what that thorough knowledge is like at that time, the text says **examination and** and so forth. The word **and so forth** includes trees, mountains, oceans, and living beings. All of these are to be meditated upon as the supreme <term>tattva</term> <gloss>reality or suchness</gloss>. It is described as various within the reality of devoted interest, but it is not a variety of conceptual constructions. Furthermore, if one asks how that is the supreme reality, the text therefore says **by myself** and so forth. **Myself** refers to one's own mind. Its **entity** is that very thing, namely its own essential nature.

<summary>This page discusses the effectiveness of yoga for practitioners regardless of past merit and explains how to meditate on the unity of the world and mind as the Great Seal. It distinguishes between delusive conceptual thoughts and the non-conceptual thorough knowledge of reality.</summary>
<keywords>merit, Great Seal, Mahamudra, meditation, mind, reality, tattva, conceptualization</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
By that, it is accomplished; one should directly realize the <term>Sahaja</term> <gloss>Co-emergent or Innate joy</gloss>. text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>The abandonment of misdeeds is itself the changing of the three garments. In that regard, the act of bathing three times is the removal of the stains of the mental afflictions, discursive thoughts, and conceptual signs. The fire offering <term>homa</term> <gloss>burnt offering ritual</gloss> is itself the burning of discursive mental afflictions through the nature of the fire of non-elaborated primordial wisdom.

The <term>bodhicitta</term> <gloss>awakening mind</gloss> is itself <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>Joyful Vajra</gloss>, and it is the wheel of the <term>yogini</term> <gloss>female tantric practitioner</gloss> through its nature of transcendent wisdom. Therefore, it is the mandala. The support for these is the very cause of abiding in meditative concentration; since that is a quality of the mind, it is therefore the mandala.

In brief, with a single phrase, the meaning of the previously spoken verses is summarized. Regarding "in brief," through the reasoning explained, the practices such as mantra recitation are summarized and maintained, so that the mind becomes concentrated in nature; this is the remaining meaning of the text. The "mind" refers to the awakening mind as previously described. That itself is the "assembly," meaning the collection of all phenomena into a single taste. The one who possesses that nature is the <term>yogin</term> <gloss>tantric practitioner</gloss>, for apart from that nature, no self is observed. This is the supreme initiation, as it directly washes away the stains of mental afflictions and discursive thoughts. The chapter that clarifies the initiation is the Chapter on Initiation. This concludes the explanation of the tenth chapter from the *Pearl Garland* <note>original: "Mukhavali"</note>, a commentary on the difficult points of the *Hevajra Tantra*.

In order to lead sentient beings into the teaching, one should perform the four gazes: the gaze that causes to fall, the gaze of subjugation, the gaze of summoning, and the gaze of stiffening. The characteristics of these are shown in sequence by four half-verses. Regarding these, looking with a straight face and a wrathful expression while directing both pupils toward the forehead is the gaze that causes to fall. Looking toward the left while leaning to the left is the gaze of subjugation. Looking toward the right while leaning upward is the gaze of summoning. Looking straight ahead while focusing on the tip of the nose is the gaze of stiffening.

<summary>This page explains the symbolic meaning of tantric rituals as internal mental processes and concludes the tenth chapter of the Hevajra commentary. It then introduces the specific physical techniques for the four ritual gazes used to influence sentient beings.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra, bodhicitta, mandala, initiation, ritual gazes, mental afflictions, yoga, Pearl Garland commentary</keywords>

If you think that the <term>generation stage</term> <gloss>utpattikrama; the visualization phase of deity yoga</gloss> provides no path to liberation because it involves birth and death, this passage is spoken to clear that doubt. Regarding the words "birth and so forth": <term>method</term> <gloss>upaya</gloss> and <term>wisdom</term> <gloss>prajña</gloss> refer to the body of self-cognition and one’s own body. The phrase "not bound" means not being stained.

As for why this is, it is explained by the term "method." "Arising continuously" refers to manifestation. Through the power of the two accumulations <note>merit and wisdom</note>, the mind appears as the <term>kayas</term> <gloss>buddha bodies</gloss> for the benefit of beings. Because this continuity is never interrupted, it arises equal to the realm of space; this is "method." Therefore, why should the perfected fruit of meditation through method ever perish? 

"Perished" means non-observation <note>unfindability through analysis</note>. Since diverse appearances are {false, deceptive}, the manifestation of the body is shown to be like a moon in water or a star. That very perishing is "wisdom." Therefore, this is the "end of existence" <note>bhutakoti</note>; it brings to an end the cycle of existence rooted in grasping at objects as real. It brings that existence to its finality.

Because of that reason, since there is no perishing in this, there is also no birth, for there is no perishing. Furthermore, in the state of reality <note>tattva</note>, because there is no perishing, there is no birth. Because one knows that this body of <term>mahamudra</term> <gloss>the Great Seal; the ultimate nature of mind and reality</gloss> appears to itself as a {false, deceptive} appearance of what is {false, deceptive}, these appearances themselves arise as reality, and thus there is no birth.

If you then think that worldly beings themselves are just <term>samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of suffering</gloss>, it is explained by the words "perished" and so forth. Among those who have attained the <term>siddhi</term> <gloss>spiritual accomplishment</gloss> of <term>mahamudra</term>, if there is no one who clings to their own body as real, who is it that could be exhausted? There is no perishing. There are no <term>contaminations</term> <gloss>asravas; mental defilements</gloss>; it should be understood in this way. 

Furthermore, although beings like <term>Brahma</term> and others have no inherent existence in their bodies, because they possess clinging to them as real things, they have origins and they have destruction arising from those origins. The accomplishment of <term>mahamudra</term> is not like that, because there is no clinging to things as real. In that way, having transcended both cyclic existence and <term>nirvana</term> <gloss>suffering and the peace of cessation</gloss>, by the nature of non-abiding <term>nirvana</term>—

<summary>This page explains how the generation stage and Mahamudra practices transcend birth and death by viewing appearances as illusory like a moon in water. It distinguishes the enlightened state from worldly existence and worldly deities by the absence of clinging to the reality of the body.</summary>
<keywords>generation stage, method and wisdom, Mahamudra, non-abiding nirvana, two accumulations, siddhi, illusion</keywords>

text:
Furthermore, because the path is neither a functional entity nor a non-entity, the result, which is Buddhahood, is also not a functional entity. This is the definition of the exhaustion of all afflictions without exception. That itself is the Buddha. The phrase "nor is it the manner of non-existence" refers to the <term>dharmakaya</term> <gloss>truth body</gloss> itself, which is the nature of the utterly pure, single-taste wisdom. The phrase "the aspects of faces and hands" refers to the <term>sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>enjoyment body</gloss> and the <term>nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>emanation body</gloss>. From what does "formless" arise? It is called "supreme bliss." This means that the <term>dharmakaya</term> also enjoys the bliss of the <term>dharma</term> <gloss>reality</gloss>. Because of that, the result is neither a functional entity nor a non-entity. Therefore, all beings are the <term>sahaja</term> <gloss>co-emergent</gloss> joy. This co-emergence is connected to the co-emergence of Buddhahood itself. "All wandering beings" refers to all sentient beings.

In response to the thought "Why is it called the co-emergence of Buddhahood itself?", it is said, "Co-emergent," and so forth. "Nature" <note>original: "rang bzhin"</note> and "essence" <note>original: "ngo bo"</note> are synonyms for the word co-emergent. Buddhahood is primarily the <term>dharmakaya</term>. With respect to that, it is described as "utterly pure" and so forth. "Utterly pure" refers to the stainless nature, luminosity itself. The mind possesses that aspect. Because its nature is that essence, it is described in that way. Its very nature is <term>nirvana</term> <gloss>the state beyond suffering</gloss>. The utterly pure nature is that, and the mind is also that. Because it is pure in the ultimate sense and is <term>nirvana</term>, it has no functional existence. Because the mind itself is the utterly pure nature, it is also not a non-entity; this is the intended meaning. By this, it is said that because the mind is luminous by nature, the seed of Buddhahood is established from beginningless time.

One might ask: "In that case, the <term>sambhogakaya</term> would be without a seed, for the ordinary body belongs to that very [ordinary] body and is of a different type than that [Buddha body]." Therefore, it is said, "Of the deity," and so forth. Here too, the word "deity's form" refers to its very seed.

<summary>This text explains that Buddhahood and the nature of the mind are neither existing entities nor non-existent voids. It identifies the luminous nature of the mind as the beginningless seed of the three bodies of a Buddha.</summary>
<keywords>Buddha nature, dharmakaya, co-emergent joy, luminosity, nirvana, mind nature, three bodies, seed of awakening</keywords>

text:
<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on the relationship between the ordinary physical body and the divine body of a deity in the context of Vajrayana practice.</meta>

In that regard, embodied beings exist simply by being born. If one asks why, it is because of what is called "faces and hands" and so forth; this means that in general, they are similar in body. Just as the mind is naturally pure and is the seed that is free from adventitious stains, similarly, the ordinary body itself is considered the seed of the deity's body.

If that is the case, one might ask if meditating on the deity’s body and so forth is useless. It is said: "However," and so forth; the phrase "cause of the natural ordinary body" is an additional explanation. Therefore, it is intended that meditating on the deity’s body is not useless, because it is for the purpose of abandoning that <note>the ordinary body</note> and for the purpose of nourishing one's own seed <note>the potential for divinity</note>.

If one says it is difficult to endure this abandonment of the ordinary body simply by meditating on the <term>Kaya</term> <gloss>enlightened body</gloss>, then, in order to establish this through many examples, it is said: "That very thing," and so forth. If one asks how, it is like the phrase "Just as wind," and so forth. Just as wind unknowingly clears away urine, feces, and gas. 

"Examining the reverse as medicine" refers to being of a similar type; the "examination" of that is the <term>Vidhi</term> <gloss>ritual procedure</gloss>. "Existence" <note>Sanskrit: bhava</note> refers to <term>Samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of existence</gloss>. "To purify them" means they become exhausted. The phrase "by existence itself" refers to the mundane path.

How so? The four applications of mindfulness, the four right exertions, the four feet of miraculous power, the five faculties, and the five strengths—these twenty-two qualities constitute the mundane path. Without realizing these, the supramundane path cannot arise. Furthermore, without the fifteen qualities consisting of the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path, there is no exhaustion of existence. In that regard, embodied beings exist simply by being born. If one asks why, it is because of what is called "faces and hands" and so forth; this means that in general, they are similar in body. Just as the mind is naturally pure and is the seed that is free from adventitious stains, similarly, the ordinary body itself is considered the seed of the deity's body.

If that is the case, one might ask if meditating on the deity’s body and so forth is useless. It is said: "However," and so forth; the phrase "cause of the natural ordinary body" is an additional explanation. Therefore, it is intended that meditating on the deity’s body is not useless, because it is for the purpose of abandoning that <note>the ordinary body</note> and for the purpose of nourishing one's own seed <note>the potential for divinity</note>.

If one asks how, it is like the phrase "Just as wind," and so forth. Just as wind unknowingly clears away urine, feces, and gas.

text:
The conceptualization of entities refers to the conceptualization of the five <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates of experience</gloss> and so forth. The phrase by way of form refers to the forms of the eternal ones, the deities such as the Jewel Lords <note>referring to the Ratnasambhava buddha family</note> and others. Purification means to bring to exhaustion. Desire, namely the desire of the mental afflictions, is fire.

Burning by that means being tormented, which produces the suffering of the lower realms and so forth. The word passion refers to the passion for reality <note>original: "tattva"</note> itself. That very thing is the fire that burns the firewood of the mental afflictions. Through that, accomplishment will occur, which means to bring to complete ripening. Terrible deeds are those such as killing that arise from hatred. Method refers to the protection of the Buddha’s teaching through compassion and so forth. By desire means by the desire of the mental afflictions. By desire itself means by the passion for reality itself. Reversal refers to the use of opposing factors. These opposing factors appear similar <note>to the afflictions themselves</note>, yet that ultimate reality acts as the very antidote.

A Buddhist heretic <note>original: "mu stegs pa," typically meaning a non-Buddhist extremist, used here paradoxically</note> is a Buddhist outsider. In what way are they Buddhist? Because they have entered the teaching of the Buddha. In what way are they heretics? Because they harbor hatred toward the Vajrayana, which is the heart of the Buddha's teaching. By all these means, the meditation on the enjoyment of the Vajra Goddess is established. To establish this through the cause of the infinite families of this and that, it is said: "Everywhere" and so forth.

Everywhere <note>original: "kuntu ru"</note> means supreme joy, which arises from the lotus <note>the female reproductive organ in tantric metaphor</note> of the Vajra Goddess. Elements refers to the elements. Five refers to the five touches, which have the nature of the five elements. This means having the nature of the earth, water, fire, wind, and space realms. If one asks what these elements are, it is said: "The single one" and so forth. Great Joy is the supreme joy of the Vajra Holder <note>Vajradhara</note>. The fivefold nature refers to the nature of the five Buddha families. By division means by the division of the elements. The elements are reality itself.

<summary>This page provides a tantric commentary on transforming mundane desires and elements into spiritual realization. It defines "passion" as a tool for purifying mental afflictions and clarifies the distinction between worldly desire and the "passion for reality" used in the Vajrayana path.</summary>
<keywords>Vajrayana, five aggregates, mental afflictions, fire of desire, Vajra Goddess, five elements, Buddha families, Vajradhara, purification</keywords>

text:
The one who is pleased. Regarding that which, if practiced, results in the blessing of <term>Vajrasattva</term> <gloss>the Adamantine Being</gloss>, it is called receiving the blessing. To teach that is to make it clear. The offering itself is the <term>vajra</term> <gloss>indestructible reality</gloss>, for the sake of the teaching itself, through its power. The phrase with desire means with devotion. The phrase <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>Awakening Being</gloss> refers to one who appears as an illusion and so forth, or one who acts with a mind that does not perceive individual distinctions. That very point is stated: through the mind of non-dual primordial wisdom. Here, non-dual primordial wisdom is that which is without appearances. Mind refers to conceptual thought. The term impure refers to that which has not been purified through the form of the deity. Regarding those whose number is fixed at six, this is what is said. Thus, the intention is to say, please explain the purity of these. 

If one wonders from what the sensory faculties themselves are seen as pure, it is stated: the complete purity of all objects, and so forth. All objects refers to the purity of all objects of knowledge as deities, as was stated above. Therefore, the intended meaning is that this does not need to be explained here. The nature of the purity of the eyes and so forth is the essence of the support, such as <term>Moha-vajra</term> <gloss>Delusion-Vajra</gloss> and the others. Thus, the transformation of these is divided into three: the first, the sixth, and the seventh. 

The intention is the hidden meaning. To speak only of a portion is what is said; the meaning is that the hidden intention is spoken of as primary, whereas the literal words are not primary. The phrase great <term>samaya</term> <gloss>sacred commitment</gloss> refers to the secret symbolic language. The term unshakeable means that which cannot be illustrated. By this, the secret is spoken. Regarding that which is spoken of as the most secret, it says laughing and so forth. By the four refers to the <term>Kriya</term> <gloss>Action</gloss>, <term>Charya</term> <gloss>Conduct</gloss>, <term>Yoga</term>, and <term>Anuttarayoga</term> <gloss>Unsurpassed Yoga</gloss> tantras. It also symbolizes laughing, looking, embracing, and the union of the two. Thus, in the Action Tantras and so forth, where the deities of method and wisdom demonstrate their passion, it is shown through smiling, in some cases through looking at one another, in some through embracing, and in some through the union of the two.

<summary>This text explains the symbolic language and classifications of the four classes of Tantra. It emphasizes that the secret meaning or intention of the teachings takes precedence over literal interpretations.</summary>
<keywords>Vajrasattva, Bodhisattva, non-dual wisdom, sensory purity, four tantras, samaya, symbolic language</keywords>

text:
Why are these called awakening? It is said, "not knowing," and so forth. Fainting is the intoxication caused by eating poison. Not knowing refers to the lack of mental application <note>Sanskrit: manasikāra</note> intended to remove the poison, which here refers to the mind. Abandoning delusions means knowing the true nature <note>Sanskrit: tattva</note> of the poison. Because one possesses the mind that understands the reality that removes poison, that mind is connected to the phrase "whoever." "Completely cutting through that misery" means cutting through the miseries of those tormented by the suffering of having eaten poison; this is an analogy. To apply this to the actual meaning, it says, "likewise," and so forth.

Liberation is <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>the state beyond sorrow</gloss>. "Exerted" means having become very weary. Because it is not afflicted, "not knowing" refers to <term>Avidya</term> <gloss>ignorance</gloss>. The word "and so forth" includes stinginess, anger, laziness, and others. Delusion refers to the delusion of the mental afflictions <note>Sanskrit: kleśa</note>. The word "and so forth" refers to afflictions such as attachment and the like, which are themselves the bonds.

Another reasoning for the statement "sentient beings are the state of Buddhahood" is spoken: "not a Buddha," and so forth. "A single sentient being" means even one single being. "Perfect awakening" <note>Sanskrit: samyak-bodhi</note> means to correctly realize. "One's own" refers to the mind; it is the sixth <note>genitive</note> case of the agent. Mentioning the singular term "species" <note>Sanskrit: gotra</note> refers to the meaning of "all sentient beings." 

If one asks, "What is the correct realization of those beings?" it is "the perceived object itself." "Itself" is an emphatic term meaning "the very nature." Furthermore, that nature is the emptiness <note>Sanskrit: śūnyatā</note> of all phenomena from duality. To see that is to see emptiness itself. That itself is awakening, and thus all sentient beings are the state of Buddhahood. 

Merely seeing emptiness is not awakening. If one wonders what it is like at that time, it is "whatever is Great Bliss" <note>Sanskrit: mahāsukha</note>. If one thinks there is no bliss in the hells and so forth, it is said, "hell," and so forth. "Nature" means by the nature of equality; it means the mere seeing of emptiness without differentiation.

<summary>This page explains the nature of awakening and Buddhahood through analogies of poison and recovery. it argues that all sentient beings possess the potential for Buddhahood because their underlying nature is emptiness and great bliss.</summary>
<keywords>awakening, emptiness, Buddha-nature, Great Bliss, mental afflictions, ignorance, liberation</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
is clearly expressed. <term>Memari</term> and <term>Yid-zang-ma</term> <gloss>The One of Good Mind</gloss> are known as the two <term>Ghasmaris</term>. The two—<term>Juk-ma</term> <gloss>The Entering One</gloss> and <term>Dod-den-ma</term> <gloss>The Desirous One</gloss>—are the <term>Sa-chyö-ma</term> <gloss>Earth-bound Dakinis</gloss>, while the three—<term>Khyim-ma</term> <gloss>The House-holder</gloss>, <term>Tum-mo</term> <gloss>The Fierce One</gloss>, and <term>Dü-jom-ma</term> <gloss>The Subduer of Demons</gloss>—are the <term>Kha-chyö-ma</term> <gloss>Sky-goers</gloss>. Therefore, all the <term>nadis</term> <gloss>subtle energy channels</gloss> are condensed within these fifteen <term>yoginis</term>. 

This is also explained in the chapter on the summary of all mantras and mudras. Regarding the channels from the chapter on the Buddha-families:
The nature of sixteen multiplied by two is taught.
Each of the <term>yoginis</term> 
is claimed to govern two channels respectively.
There are <term>Lalana</term>, <term>Rasana</term>, 
<term>Avadhuti</term>, and <term>Nairatmya</term> <gloss>The Selfless One</gloss>.
And: 
The <term>bodhichitta</term> <gloss>enlightened essence/semen</gloss> becomes the Moon, 
consisting of fifteen phases.
The Great Bliss has the form of the <term>Ali</term> <gloss>vowels</gloss>, 
and the <term>yoginis</term> are its individual parts.

Just as the first yogini, <term>Nairatmya</term>, consists of three channels, the final yogini, the <term>Kha-chyö-ma</term> <gloss>Sky-goer</gloss>, also consists of three channels. This is taught implicitly, for otherwise, the claim that the yoginis condense the channels would not be established, especially since it is taught that the <term>bodhichitta</term> flows through thirty-two channels. 

According to the <term>Yogini-tantras</term>, the <term>bodhichitta</term> is divided into thirty-two parts, which reside in the <term>Chakra of Great Bliss</term> <gloss>located at the crown of the head</gloss>. From these thirty-two individual channels, the <term>bodhichitta</term> flows out from the <term>Chakra of Great Bliss</term>. Therefore, I shall explain the specific locations where they primarily reside and how they flow. The distinctions between these natures of the yoginis should be differentiated according to the specific Tantras, as not all causes are identical. One should understand how the minor branch channels circulate everywhere and interconnect based on the explanations of their locations and functions.

From the <term>Samputa Tantra</term> <gloss>The Tantra of the Union</gloss>:
In the center of the birth-place <gloss>the secret center</gloss> are two channels,
extending to the left and to the right.
Know that the white seed <gloss>semen</gloss> flows from the left,
and the blood <gloss>ovum/menstrual fluid</gloss> flows from the right.

Furthermore, it is taught in the <term>Samputa</term> and the <term>Vajradaka Tantra</term>:
Starting from the palate on the left side,
the channel is endowed with the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Enjoyment Body</gloss>.
Resting in the center of the navel,
looking downward, it is intoxicated...

<summary>This page explains the correlation between fifteen yoginis and the thirty-two subtle channels of the body, detailing how the enlightened essence flows from the crown chakra through these channels. It cites the Samputa Tantra to describe the binary nature of the channels in relation to the male and female essences.</summary>
<keywords>yoginis, nadis, channels, bodhichitta, Great Bliss, Samputa Tantra, Vajradaka Tantra, Nairatmya, lunar phases</keywords>

Furthermore, it is taught in the <term>Samputa</term> and the <term>Vajradaka Tantra</term>:
Starting from the palate on the left side,
the channel is endowed with the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Enjoyment Body</gloss>.
Resting in the center of the navel,
looking downward, it is intoxicated...

Regarding the phrase "from then on" and so forth: <term>Samvara</term> <gloss>vow/commitment</gloss> refers to the union <note>the stabilization of energy and mind</note> and so on. <term>Carya</term> <gloss>conduct</gloss> refers to joyful speech and so forth. "Form" refers to color, shape, scent, and so on. The "navel of the deer" refers to musk. A "vessel similar to that" means appearing in the same likeness. <term>Utpala</term> <gloss>blue lotus</gloss> refers to the blue lotus itself, and the word "such" is also applied here. The word "cause" refers to the elements and is connected to the word "scent." "Fragrant scent" means an agreeable or pleasant odor. "Crow's beak" refers to black <term>agaru</term> <gloss>aloe wood</gloss>. The phrase "in birth after birth" means in all successive lifetimes. "May it become" means may it be obtained.

"Discipline" <note>Sanskrit: Vinaya</note> refers to that which is to be tamed. <term>Upavasa</term> <gloss>fasting/restoration</gloss> refers to abiding by the eight basic precepts from dawn to dawn during the full moon and other specific dates. The "ten basic precepts" refers to the commitment to refrain from the seven wrong actions of body and speech for as long as one lives, and the refraining from the three wrong actions of the mind.

The phrase "speaking of being free from passion" refers to the <term>Vaibhashika</term> <gloss>Great Exposition School</gloss>; that very person is a follower of the <term>Vaibhashika</term>. This belongs to the <term>Sravakayana</term> <gloss>Vehicle of Hearers</gloss>, following the traditions of the "One Hundred Instructions" and the "Series of Three Mixed Works" and so forth.

"Sutras" refers to the Mahayana sutras that are not extremely profound, such as the "One Verse Sutra," the "Four Verse Sutra," the "Incantation of Two Verses," the "Sutra of the Six Doors," the "Conduct of Excellence" <note>Sanskrit: Bhadracarya</note>, the "Four Dharmas," the "Detailed Play" <note>Sanskrit: Lalitavistara</note>, and the "Ten Bhumis Sutra" and others.

<term>Yogacara</term> <gloss>Yoga Practice School</gloss> refers to the view that these various appearances are "Mind Only." Objects that appear are not real; rather, mind itself arises in that way through the power of habitual tendencies, just like a dream.

Regarding the "Middle Way" <note>Sanskrit: Madhyamaka</note>: the Middle Way is the path. This means that mind does not exist by way of a dualistic nature, nor is it non-existent by way of an nature empty of those two.

"Taught" means it should be taught gradually in that manner. Regarding "by all tantras" and so forth, this should be connected to what follows. "All" refers to the five classes: <term>Kriya</term> <gloss>Action</gloss>, <term>Carya</term> <gloss>Performance</gloss>, <term>Yoga</term> <gloss>Union</gloss>, and <term>Anuttarayoga</term> <gloss>Highest Union</gloss>...

The path that removes the thorns of existence
I have shown to you.
The <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>One Gone Thus; the Buddha</gloss> is the teacher;
You must strive for it yourselves.

One might ask: "If the <term>Sahaja-ananda</term> <gloss>innate joy</gloss> of this world is already direct experience for those who engage in desire, then instruction is unnecessary, let alone meditation. What use is another's instruction for something that is already a direct object of experience?" To this, the text says: "Virtue," and so forth.

This is the intention: here, the innate joy of the world is not what is to be accomplished. It is already established, it is inferior to the bliss of higher realms such as the god realms, and because it possesses <term>asrava</term> <gloss>defilements or taints</gloss>, it is the very root of the faults of those in <term>samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of suffering</gloss>. 

If one asks: "Then what is the nature of it?" Here, that which is to be accomplished is the <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body</gloss> which is the individual pristine awareness of the <term>Tathagatas</term>, innate like space, and the exceptionally sublime, utterly pure, and definitive characteristic of innate bliss that arises as the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Enjoyment Body</gloss>, which is its natural expression.

Furthermore, since this cannot be realized by other means, one understands it for oneself by manifesting the perfection of meditation. This is achieved through the power of devoted interest, following the instructions exactly as they pertain to the world's own innate joy. This does not happen from the very beginning. Therefore, in this context, listening <note>to the teachings</note>, contemplating, and meditating are not without purpose.

"Method" refers to the path. "Relying upon it" refers to authentic meditation. "The lineage of many of these" refers to many different types <note>of methods</note>. "Obtained from the Guru" refers to the Guru's timing; the Guru should bestow this in accordance with the ritual to a student who is a suitable vessel for the lineage. This is the meaning of "bestowing the instructions." Regarding that which is to be realized <unclear>...</unclear>

<summary>This page explains that while worldly pleasure is innate, it is a source of suffering and differs from the innate bliss of a Buddha. Realization of the Truth Body and Enjoyment Body requires systematic meditation, contemplation, and authentic instruction from a Guru.</summary>
<keywords>innate joy, Sahaja, Dharmakaya, Sambhogakaya, meditation, Guru, lineage, Tathagata, desire, purification</keywords>

text:
This refers only to the number itself; it is not an explanation of numbers based on lotus petals. There is no explanation given regarding numbers fixed to petals, as it is also said, the channel in the center of the lotus of the heart. Regarding that, the movement of <term>Akshobhya</term> <gloss>The Unshakable One; here representing the stable aspect of consciousness</gloss> is the <term>lalana</term> <gloss>the left channel, associated with lunar energy and wisdom</gloss> itself. From the <term>rasana</term> <gloss>the right channel, associated with solar energy and method</gloss> itself, blood primarily flows. This is what was said in the passage starting with, among those.

That which is of the nature of wisdom <note>Sanskrit: prajna</note> refers to the primary movement of the moon. That which is of method <note>Sanskrit: upaya</note> refers to the essence of method, which is the movement of blood. The phrase <term>avadhuti</term> <gloss>the central channel</gloss> which has abandoned the grasped and the grasper means that through the letting go of conceptual thought, the <term>avadhuti</term> flows as the simple non-dual <term>bodhichitta</term> <gloss>the mind of awakening; here referring to vital essence</gloss>, and thus it has abandoned the grasped and the grasper.

As for the phrase in the central region, it should be connected to the phrase is perfectly situated. If one asks where the central region is: it is in the center of the head, the throat, the heart, the navel, and the secret place <note>the genital region</note>. Here, the three primary channels are the <term>Nairatmya</term> <gloss>Selfless One</gloss> yoginis. The three such as the <term>Khimama</term> of the end are the <term>Khechari</term> <gloss>Sky-goers</gloss>. The remaining thirteen pairs of channels are the yoginis such as <term>Gauri</term> and the rest.

Regarding those, as to which channel arises and increases from which, or how they proceed appropriately, they flow from this and that:
The <term>Abhedya</term> <gloss>Indivisible One</gloss> resides in the head; from her, the nails and teeth arise.
The <term>Sukshmarupa</term> <gloss>Fine-Formed One</gloss> resides at the crown of the head; from her, the head hair and body hair arise.
The <term>Subhaga</term> <gloss>Fortunate One</gloss> resides in the right ear; from her, the skin and impurities arise.
The <term>Vama</term> <gloss>Left-hand One</gloss> resides in the back; from her, the flesh arises.
The <term>Vamana</term> <gloss>Dwarf One</gloss> is in the left ear; from her, the nerves and sinews arise.
The <term>Kurmapala</term> <gloss>Tortoise-born One</gloss> resides between the eyebrows; from her, the vertebrae arise.
The <term>Jvalani</term> <gloss>Meditating One</gloss> is in the two eyes; from her, the kidneys arise.
The <term>Abhishekani</term> <gloss>Empowering One</gloss> is at the shoulders; from her, the heart arises.
The <term>Vikalpa</term> <gloss>Fault-possessing One</gloss> is in the two armpits; from her, the two eyes arise.
The <term>Vikasita</term> <gloss>Well-situated One</gloss> is in the two breasts; from her, the bile arises.
The <term>Mamo</term> <gloss>Mamo Spirit</gloss> is at the navel; from her, the lungs arise.
The <term>Shabari</term> <gloss>Mountain-dweller One</gloss> is at the tip of the nose; from her, the coils of the intestines arise.
The <term>Shitala</term> <gloss>Cooling-giver One</gloss> is at the kidneys <note>alternatively: the waist</note>; from her, the membrane of the ribs arises.
The <term>Ushma</term> <gloss>Warm One</gloss> is at the neck; from her, the stomach arises.
The <term>Lalana</term>, <term>Avadhuti</term>, and <term>Rasana</term>—these three were explained previously.
The <term>Pravaravana</term> <gloss>Excellent Forest One</gloss> is at the heart;

The qualities conducive to enlightenment, such as the <term>applications of mindfulness</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: smṛtyupasthāna; focusing the mind on the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena</gloss> and the <term>correct exertions</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: samyakprahāṇa</gloss>, as well as the qualities of a Buddha, such as the <term>ten powers</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: daśabala</gloss> and the <term>fearlessnesses</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: vaiśāradya</gloss>, and the qualities obtained through the fruits of the path, such as <term>stream-entry</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: srotāpanna; the first stage of enlightenment</gloss> and so forth.

The thorough analysis of these includes their characteristics, functions, causes, effects, and number. It also includes their gratification, drawbacks, and emergence; their afflictions and purification; and their full understanding, abandonment, realization, and cultivation.

Furthermore, there are external phenomena regarding how this world system arises and how it is destroyed. It describes how it perishes and how it forms: how long it remains destroyed, how long it takes to form, and how long it endures. These include the hell beings, the animal realm, the <term>hungry ghosts</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: preta</gloss>, and humans. These include the <term>desire realm</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: kāmadhātu</gloss>, the <term>form realm</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: rūpadhātu</gloss>, and the <term>formless realm</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: ārūpyadhātu</gloss>.

The quantity of atoms of earth is this much. The quantity for water is this much; for fire, this much; and for wind, this much. The measurements of the thickness, width, height, and depth of the <term>rim of the world</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: cakravāḍa; the mountain range encircling the universe</gloss> and so forth are this much. The extent of the four continents is this much. A <term>thousand-fold world system</term> is this much; a <term>two-thousand-fold world system</term> is this much; and a <term>great third-order thousand-fold world system</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu; a universe comprising one billion worlds</gloss> is this much.

In the same way, the thoughts of all beings, their <term>latent tendencies</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: anuśaya</gloss>, their behaviors, their inclinations, and their faculties are analyzed. This includes those with few faults and those with many faults; those with the <term>spiritual disposition</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: gotra</gloss> and those without the disposition; those who are certain and those who are uncertain; those who have entered the path and those who have not entered; those who are matured and those who are not matured; and those who are liberated and those who are not liberated. Such is the manner of—

A <term>thousand-fold world system</term> is this much; a <term>two-thousand-fold world system</term> is this much; and a <term>great third-order thousand-fold world system</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu; a universe comprising one billion worlds</gloss> is this much.

In the same way, the thoughts of all beings, their <term>latent tendencies</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: anuśaya</gloss>, their behaviors, their inclinations, and their faculties are analyzed. This includes those with few faults and those with many faults; those with the <term>spiritual disposition</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: gotra</gloss> and those without the disposition; those who are certain and those who are uncertain; those who have entered the path and those who have not entered; those who are matured and those who are not matured; and those who are liberated and those who are not liberated. Regarding the phrase **with the natural light**, if one asks what the difference is between **light** <term>prabhā</term> and **radiance** <term>raśmi</term>, it is as follows. That which arises from within is called **radiance**. That which arises from the outer skin is called **light**. Alternatively, that which arises from the radiation of primordial wisdom <term>jñāna</term> is called **radiance**, while that which arises from the radiation of color is called **light**. Even in the scriptures <term>śāstra</term>, it is said: The radiances of the Buddha emerged at the time of perfectly realizing the Dharma at the seat of enlightenment <term>bodhimaṇḍa</term>. It is explained in the Sutras that when the Buddha Bhagavans teach the Dharma, generally, as soon as they intend to explain a particular teaching, radiances will emerge. Therefore, one should understand that since the illumination of primordial wisdom arises from within, radiance also emerges.

One should also know that the activity of the natural light has two aspects. The miracle of making illumination with the tongue is shown as a preliminary sign for the sake of teaching the Dharma. The emergence of radiances from the faculty of the tongue is also a sign of teaching the Dharma. The fact that lotuses emerged from those radiances is a definite sign that the Bodhisattvas are entering into faultlessness. The emergence of Buddhas from those lotuses and their teaching of the Dharma is a sign that all those Bodhisattva lotuses, having blossomed through the opening of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, will teach such Dharma in every direction.

By the phrase **having entered meditatively into the concentration called the Lion’s Play** <term>siṃhavikrīḍita</term> and so forth, two miracles of meditative concentration <term>samādhi</term> are shown. These miracles are shown in two ways: the cleansing of the vessel-world <note>the physical environment or universe</note> and the benefiting of the world of sentient beings. The cleansing of the vessel-world is for the sake of making offerings to the explanation. That cleansing is shown through five aspects: shaking, trembling, quaking, rising, and falling. Regarding those, shaking refers to when the bodies of humans, though otherwise unmoving, have their feet and hands <unclear>not transcribed</unclear>

Due to causes, many sufferings appear among sentient beings in hell, animals, <term>pretas</term> <gloss>hungry ghosts</gloss>, the ranks of <term>asuras</term> <gloss>demigods</gloss>, and humans. In most Buddha-fields, this is not the case. The <term>kalpa</term> <gloss>aeon</gloss> is also of a degenerate nature. By the power of the intermediate aeon of famine, the unbearable suffering of hunger arises intermittently in the world. By the power of the intermediate aeon of illness, many diseases arise. By the power of the intermediate aeon of weapons, much mutual harm occurs.

Many defects of time arise: by the power of destruction by water, the afflictions of the realm of existence become dominant; by the power of destruction by fire, the side of hatred becomes dominant; and by the power of destruction by wind, the side of ignorance becomes dominant.

Regarding the dregs of lifespan, the life of sentient beings is uncertain. At some times the lifespan is immeasurable, while at other times the lifespan becomes ten years, and even that is not fixed. Some die in the very womb. Some die immediately after birth, or in childhood, or in youth, or in the prime of life, or in maturity, or when half of life is spent, or in old age. Because there is no certainty regarding death, there are many instances of grief, lamentation, suffering, and mental unhappiness in the world.

As for the dregs of views, there are sixty-two distinct types of very evil views that destroy all virtue. Regarding those who have definitely entered into such wrong views, even a thousand Buddhas cannot heal them. Furthermore, all <term>tirthikas</term> <gloss>non-Buddhist extremists</gloss> are by nature prone to disparaging others, lack faith, do not join the assembly, are highly contemptible, and are naturally unfit vessels. The continuum of their minds has mostly become like salty, barren soil; the continuum of their minds has mostly become like garlic, such that the sublime Dharma cannot enter their minds.

<summary>This page describes the various sufferings and degenerations of the current age, focusing on the three intermediate aeons of destruction and the uncertainty of human lifespan. It also addresses the corruption of views and the spiritual unsuitability of those who hold extremist non-Buddhist beliefs.</summary>
<keywords>sufferings, six realms, aeons of destruction, famine, illness, weapons, lifespan uncertainty, sixty-two wrong views, tirthikas, spiritual degeneration</keywords>

Those are the prophecies made by observing their lineages.

The Buddha was then asked: Blessed One, since those <term>Sravakas</term> <gloss>Hearers</gloss> who are without <term>asravas</term> <gloss>mental impurities or taints</gloss> and who have severed the fetters of all existence do indeed possess a lineage, how is it that they will achieve the manifest and complete awakening of unsurpassable, true, and perfect <term>bodhi</term> <gloss>enlightenment</gloss>?

The Blessed One replied: Noble son, therefore, listen as I provide an analogy. Noble son, it is like this. For example, a king of the <term>Kshatriya</term> <gloss>warrior or ruling</gloss> caste, who has been consecrated upon his crown, has a son. That son studies all the fields of craftsmanship, yet because his faculties are dull and not sharp, he studies later what should have been studied earlier, and studies earlier what should have been studied later. Noble son, what do you think? Because of that reason, should it be said that he is not the king’s son?

The reply was given: Blessed One, that is not so. <term>Sugata</term> <gloss>One Gone to Bliss</gloss>, that is not the case. Blessed One, he is indeed to be called the king's son.

The Buddha continued: Noble son, in the same way, there are Bodhisattvas belonging to the lineage of dull faculties who first exhaust their afflictions through the path of meditation and only later achieve the manifest and complete awakening of unsurpassable, true, and perfect enlightenment. Noble son, what do you think? Because of that reason, should it be said that they have not achieved manifest and complete Buddhahood?

The reply was: Blessed One, that is not so. Sugata, that is not the case, and so forth. 

Furthermore, as it has been said: Maitreya, there is a certain type of lineage where one initially seeks the lower distinction, attains that lower state, and having recognized it as lower, does not remain satisfied with just that. Instead, by seeking the higher, excellent distinction above it, one comes to attain excellence itself.

When this was spoken, the Bodhisattva Maitreya said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One...

<summary>The Buddha uses the analogy of a king's son with dull faculties to explain how those who initially follow a lower spiritual path can still reach full Buddhahood. The text emphasizes that the sequence of attainment does not disqualify one from their inherent noble lineage or ultimate enlightenment.</summary>
<keywords>Bodhisattva, Sravaka, enlightenment, lineage, Maitreya, analogy, spiritual faculties, Buddha nature</keywords>

text:
It is free from what is to be expressed and the mode of expression. It is free from the appearance of the inexpressible. This nature of the thoroughly established <term>pariniṣpanna</term> <gloss>the perfected or absolute nature of reality</gloss>, which is known by individual self-awareness, is called the eye of reality <note>original: "dharma-cakṣu"</note>.

Regarding the phrase, the eye is empty of the eye:
The term eye refers to the eye of the actual nature of reality <term>dharmatā</term> <gloss>the intrinsic nature of phenomena</gloss>.
The phrase by the eye refers to the imagined <term>parikalpita</term> <gloss>constructed by the mind</gloss> and the conceptualized <term>vikalpita</term> <gloss>discriminated or fabricated</gloss> eye.
The term empty is a synonym for being free from.
The same logic should be applied to the phrase the ear is empty of the ear and so forth.

One might object: If the inexpressible ultimate truth is not the nature of the eye, then it is correct. However, if it is the nature of the eye, it would then become expressible. Why then is it called the eye of the actual nature of reality?

That is true. Nevertheless, whatever conditioned phenomena exist—such as the eye, forms, sounds, and so on—there is no differentiation in their aspect of being thoroughly established through the process of transformation. Although they are of a single aspect, when one wishes to explain them for the sake of instruction, there is no other method. Therefore, they are merely distinguished and taught using terms such as the suchness of form, the suchness of sound, the suchness of smell, and so forth. However, that suchness <term>tathatā</term> <gloss>the way things truly are, beyond conceptual labels</gloss> does not possess their specific aspects, nor is it expressed as them.

In that way, because those things like the eye of the actual nature of reality are free from the essence of internal sense bases such as the eye, it is called internal emptiness <term>adhyātma-śūnyatā</term>.

Thus, having reversed the apprehension of the internal entity as an enjoyer <note>the subjective "eater" or experiencer</note>, the emptiness of the external <term>bahirdhā-śūnyatā</term> is established to reverse the apprehension of external entities as the enjoyed <note>the objective "food" or objects of experience</note>. Regarding the apprehension of the enjoyed, outsiders <note>non-Buddhists</note> apprehend forms and such as being mine. Those of this tradition <note>Buddhists</note> apprehend them as objects through conceptualization. To reverse the former, it is said: form is empty of self and what belongs to self, and sound is empty of self and what belongs to self <unclear>2-3 syllables</unclear>

<summary>This text explains the concept of emptiness by distinguishing between the absolute nature of reality and conceptual fabrications. It defines internal and external emptiness as methods to remove the false attachment to a subjective experiencer and objective entities.</summary>
<keywords>emptiness, suchness, internal emptiness, external emptiness, dharmata, parinispanna, sense bases</keywords>
