text:
This is what is called <term>dependent origination</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: pratityasamutpada</gloss>. For those things such as an illusory elephant and the consciousnesses that perceive them, their dependent origination cannot possibly exist in an ultimate sense. Likewise, all ordinary beings whose vision is deceived by ignorance will see things such as illusory elephants that are conceptually constructed by the craftsmanship of karma. Those conceptually constructed objects also serve as the conditions for the arising of the consciousnesses in which they appear, and those consciousnesses in turn perceive those objects. Thus, the way in which conceptually constructed objects of perception and the subjects that perceive them function as causes and effects is called dependent origination. Because the dependent origination of these subjects and objects cannot possibly exist in an ultimate sense, all phenomena are said to lack intrinsic nature.

If phenomena possessed some kind of inherent essence that was not artificial and was natural to them, they would not arise in dependence on others through the power of causes and conditions; rather, they would arise of their own accord. However, phenomena arise through the power of other conditions in a state of dependency. They do not arise through a natural, non-artificial essence of their own. Therefore, one should understand that their own inherent existence does not exist. Because they lack such inherent existence, they are said to be without <term>intrinsic nature</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: svabhava</gloss>. Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are <term>emptiness</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: shunyata</gloss>.

Therefore, the meaning of lacking intrinsic nature is the meaning of dependent origination. The meaning of emptiness is the meaning of dependent origination. When the vision of seeing things exactly as they are arises and the power of the mantra of ignorance is completely destroyed, then the conceptually constructed phenomena which are like illusory elephants, and the consciousnesses that grasp them, <note>text continues to next page</note>

<summary>This page explains the fundamental Mahayana Buddhist equivalence between dependent origination, the lack of intrinsic nature, and emptiness. It uses the analogy of an illusory elephant to show how subjects and objects arise interdependently but lack ultimate reality.</summary>
<keywords>dependent origination, emptiness, intrinsic nature, illusion, karma, subject and object, Mahayana philosophy</keywords>

The abandonment for the purpose of making the field nonexistent is called the five aggregates <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>the five components of individual existence: form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness</gloss>. In the scriptures of the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>Thus Gone One</gloss> Kashyapa, this was designated by the name abandonment of the aggregates. Even now, it is spoken of as one existence to be abandoned or five existences to be abandoned.

The term non-abandonment refers to the nonexistence of the entity of abandonment.
### Where the aggregates cease
That is called non-abandonment, and thinking that this is cessation, the Bodhisattva settles the matter in this way: It is not reasonable for any phenomenon called non-abandonment to exist. Rather, the absence of the aggregates is what is called non-abandonment. That absence of the aggregates is the <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>passing beyond suffering</gloss> without a remainder of the aggregates, characterized by the absence of all entities. Therefore, it cannot be established as any other phenomenon in its own nature.

For that reason, the expression nonexistence of entities is described through synonyms such as Nirvana, cessation, the pacification of all conditioned things, and non-abandonment. If Nirvana did not exist, why would conditioned things <term>samskaras</term> <gloss>mental formations or volitional factors</gloss> not arise? Therefore, if one asks whether Nirvana is the phenomenon that serves as the antidote to the future arising of conditioned things, that is also not correct. It is not possible in any way for conditioned things to undergo Nirvana. 

If conditioned things were to pass into Nirvana, would something permanent or something impermanent pass into Nirvana? If one says that something permanent passes into Nirvana, #that is also not correct because what is permanent is unchanging at all times and has no need for Nirvana. If one says that #something impermanent passes into Nirvana#, because it is impermanent, it does not arise again after perishing. For that which is of the nature of non-arising, there is #nothing to be done# by passing into Nirvana. If one argues that it acts as the antidote to other conditioned things arising from #its causes#, that too does not exist. In the world...

<summary>This page discusses the Buddhist concept of abandonment in relation to the five aggregates and defines Nirvana as the cessation of conditioned existence. It argues that Nirvana is not a produced entity but rather the absence of the aggregates and the pacification of all conditioned things.</summary>
<keywords>aggregates, skandhas, Nirvana, cessation, conditioned things, samskaras, abandonment, permanence, impermanence</keywords>

text:
If you recite the mantra twenty thousand times and smear that powder on your forehead, you will become invisible to your enemies. <term>Om mama huyati</term>. If you smear that powder on your hands and touch anyone, they will come under your power. If you smear that powder on your feet, you can travel hundreds of thousands of <term>yojanas</term> <gloss>a traditional unit of distance, roughly 5 to 9 miles</gloss> and return.

If you smear that powder on the side of an enemy's door and recite the mantra eight thousand times at the entrance of the house, the enemy will be expelled. If you mix that powder with cemetery soil and bury it at the enemy's doorstep, the enemy's entire family line will be destroyed.

Alternatively, if you wish to expel an enemy's family, take the skin of a <term>chuchundara</term> <gloss>a musk shrew or mole-like rodent</gloss>, recite the mantra eight thousand times, and fill the skin with earth from a place where the enemy has urinated. Bind it with a blue thread and hang it in the air. This will cause the enemy's urine to be blocked. If you untie it, they will be released.

Grind the skin of a <term>chuchundara</term> into powder and recite the mantra eight thousand times before an image of the Great God <note>Mahadeva, often referring to Shiva</note>. Offer perfumes, flowers, incense, and <term>tormas</term> <gloss>ritual cakes made of flour and butter</gloss>, then recite the mantra another eight thousand times to achieve accomplishment. 

If you smear that powder on the tip of your nose, all living beings will be drawn to you. If you place it on your head, you will be able to answer the challenge of any enemy. If you smear that powder on your own heart and show yourself to an enemy, their heart will turn bad.

If you make a figurine from <term>shalu</term> <gloss>a type of fine rice</gloss> and smear it with the powder, the enemy will become paralyzed. If you make a figurine from <term>shalu</term> rice and smear it with the powder, they will be afflicted by leprosy. If you mix the powder with ashes from a cemetery and scatter it over a host of enemies, whoever steps on it or sees it will be afflicted by disease.

If you recite the mantra one thousand times over the powder and pour it on someone's head, they will come under your power. If you place that powder together with a skull at a doorway, the enemy's household will be divided. If you smear that powder on a woman's hand, that woman will die. If you hide the powder at anyone's door, they will be driven away. If you mix that powder with <term>great flesh</term> <gloss>a tantric euphemism for human flesh</gloss> and give it to someone to drink, they will die in seven days. If you mix those powders with excrement and give it to an enemy, the enemy will suffer hunger.

<summary>This page details various magical applications of a consecrated powder, including invisibility, travel, subjugation, and causing harm or illness to enemies. It specifies rituals involving animal skins, figurines, and cemetery materials combined with mantra recitation.</summary>
<keywords>mantra, powder, invisibility, subjugation, chuchundara, shalu rice, cemetery ash, ritual figurines, expulsion</keywords>

text:
Because it aims at what is produced <note>the arising of sensory or mental objects</note>, it is desire. Because it aims at the <term>Sahaja-ananda</term> <gloss>co-emergent joy</gloss> that arises immediately after the cessation of that desire, it is freedom from desire. Because the first joy is even lower than those, it is called the "middle" <note>here meaning mediocre or intermediate</note>. Clarity is called the "medium" just as one might speak of a medium-sized body or a medium-sized <term>chillon</term> <gloss>a type of garment or measurement</gloss>. That which is none of those three is the ultimate.

The phrase "the end of the first supreme joy" refers to making the immediately preceding state perfectly clear. The phrase "this is supreme great bliss" means this is the very highest form of great bliss, which is the meaning of co-emergent joy. To explain the certainty of that very moment, it is said: "There is no self and no other." In that very state, the appearance of "another" as the perceived object and the appearance of "self" as the perceiver do not exist. This is the meaning of "natural joy" <note>original: "prakriti-ananda"</note>, which is perfectly clear because it is infinite, non-dual, and beyond conceptual observation, being nothing but the most excellent bliss.

As it is said in the *Chapter on Union*:
Joy is a slight bliss;
Supreme joy increases from that.
Special joy becomes free from desire;
The remaining one is co-emergent joy.
The first is the desire for touch;
The second is the desire for bliss.
The third is the exhaustion of bliss;
Therefore, the fourth is what should be meditated upon.
Supreme joy is described as craving;
Nirvana is the absence of joy.
The middle is merely joy;
Co-emergent joy abandons all of these.

And from the *Chapter on Student Empowerment*:
Neither without desire nor possessing desire,
Not even observed in the middle;
Because the three are separated,
It is called the perfectly awakened nature.

And also:
Either it is the nature of everything,
Or it is completely abandoned.
The first distinction to be made
Is the abandoning of the three joys.

That which is to be meditated upon in this way is the fourth joy. Also, from the *Chapter on Student Empowerment*:
The first is merely joy;
Supreme joy is the second in number.
The third is explained as special joy;
The fourth is called the co-emergent.

While this identifies special joy as the third, how is the fourth described as the "nature"? After counting the three joys that are to be abandoned, then the co-emergent joy which is to be adopted <insert>is established</insert>.

<summary>This page analyzes the four joys of the tantric path, distinguishing between ordinary joys based on desire and the fourth joy, co-emergent bliss, which transcends the subject-object duality. It cites scriptural authority to define the progression from sensory joy to the realization of natural, non-dual awakening.</summary>
<keywords>four joys, co-emergent joy, Sahaja, bliss, non-duality, tantric empowerment, meditation, Tengyur</keywords>

text:
By stating "devoid of intrinsic nature," it is shown that things lack inherent existence. A Bodhisattva <note>an awakened being who seeks enlightenment for the benefit of all</note> is said to discern things as being like an illusion. This is demonstrated by the fact that when a Bodhisattva, a Great Being, practices the Perfection of Wisdom <term>Prajnaparamita</term> in such a manner, they do not truly perceive the arising of any phenomena.

Regarding this, the "imagined nature" <term>parikalpita</term> <gloss>the purely conceptualized aspect of reality</gloss> lacks both arising and ceasing; it is merely a matter of appearing or not appearing. The "dependent nature" <term>paratantra</term> <gloss>the aspect of reality arising from causes and conditions</gloss> lacks both increase and decrease; it is merely a construction of the imagined. The "thoroughly established nature" <term>parinispanna</term> <gloss>the ultimate, unchanging nature of reality</gloss> lacks both affliction and purification; it is simply primordial purity by its very nature.

Although all phenomena are thus shown to be without intrinsic nature, in order to clear away further doubts, the text asks: "Why is this?" It then states: "In this way, names are artificial." The names and signs for the aggregates <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>the five components of a person</gloss> such as form, sensation, and perception are artificial fabrications. They do not exist by way of their own intrinsic nature. Therefore, one should understand that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, because an intrinsic nature is not something that is fabricated.

That which is fabricated is explained by the statement: "Those phenomena that are dependently originated are conceptualized." This means that those phenomena which depend on conceptualized causes and conceptualized conditions are termed "dependently originated" <term>pratityasamutpada</term> <gloss>the principle that all things arise in dependence upon causes</gloss> because they are conceptualized in various ways.

This demonstrates the following: if a thing depends on something else, it arises through the power of another and not through its own power. How, then, could it possess an intrinsic nature? Therefore, since it lacks its own entity and exists as the entity of another, it is established that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Thus, the meaning of "lacking intrinsic nature" is the meaning of "dependent origination." Following that, the conventional use of names arises from the causes of imagined names.

<summary>This page explains the lack of intrinsic nature in all phenomena through the lens of the three natures: imagined, dependent, and thoroughly established. It argues that because things are dependently originated and conceptually named, they cannot possess an independent, inherent essence.</summary>
<keywords>intrinsic nature, dependent origination, three natures, Bodhisattva, Perfection of Wisdom, emptiness, conceptualization</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>then, in order to show what the characteristics of those who apply diligence are, it is said: Then, the Blessed One was asked, "In what way should a bodhisattva mahasattva apply diligence in the perfection of wisdom to be called diligent?" Thereupon, all phenomena—the aggregates <term>skandhas</term>, elements <term>dhatus</term>, sense bases <term>ayatanas</term>, the noble truths, dependent origination, and all conditioned and unconditioned things—are summarized into seven groups. When one practices the emptiness of these seven groups, that alone does not complete the task of diligence, so for the time being, it is not called diligence. Furthermore, because the work of diligence has begun, it should not be said that there is no diligence. Therefore, to demonstrate this, it was said: "One does not say 'diligent' or 'not diligent.'"

If one wonders, "Then how is it diligence?" the phrase "Why is that?" was spoken to address the doubt. Having said that, it is shown that diligence consists in practicing through four aspects of emptiness: the non-apprehension <note>the inability to find a truly existent essence</note> of the individual nature of form and the rest; the non-apprehension of the nature of their collection; the non-apprehension of their own defining characteristics; and the non-apprehension of all phenomena. This is taught in detail, starting from the statement, "In this regard, he does not correctly perceive form as something subject to arising or something subject to ceasing," up to the conclusion, "he does not correctly perceive his own enlightenment, the Buddha, or awakening." 

In this context, the phrase "form as something subject to arising or something subject to ceasing" refers to the essence of arising or the essence of ceasing. If form were an essence of arising, it could not be an essence of ceasing. If it were an essence of ceasing, it could not be an essence of arising, because it is completely contradictory for a single thing to have two natures. If form possessed a property called arising...

<summary>This page explains the true nature of diligence in the Perfection of Wisdom, defining it through the non-apprehension of the inherent existence of phenomena. It argues that because arising and ceasing are contradictory natures, form cannot possess both as a fixed essence.</summary>
<keywords>perfection of wisdom, diligence, non-apprehension, emptiness, aggregates, arising and ceasing, bodhisattva</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
In the state of total affliction, it is designated as such. In the state of complete purification, it is simply designated as purified because the adventitious afflictions are absent; however, it is incorrect to view the <term>dharmata</term> <gloss>intrinsic nature</gloss> of form and other phenomena in this way. Therefore, it is said that one does not truly perceive form as having the nature of total affliction, nor as having the nature of purification.

Having thus shown the absence of an essential nature in form and the other aggregates, the text now states that one does not truly perceive form as being truly assembled together with feeling, and so forth. This demonstrates that an assembly lacks the defining characteristics of an <term>skandha</term> <gloss>aggregate</gloss>. The term aggregate means a heap or collection. If a true assembly or gathering of a heap existed, it could possibly exist as a real entity; however, as there is no true assembly among phenomena, it is shown that the defining characteristic of an aggregate is also absent.

Furthermore, if phenomena were to truly assemble together, they would either have to be confused or share a single defining characteristic. However, form is not confused with feeling and the other aggregates, and their defining characteristics are distinct. Likewise, it is incorrect for feeling and the other aggregates to be truly assembled with form. Similarly, the defining characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are each distinct. How could these things, which have such entirely distinct characteristics, truly assemble into a single essential nature of an aggregate?

Furthermore, whatever identity form, feeling, and the others may have as distinct from one another, those are merely <term>parikalpita</term> <gloss>conceptually imputed</gloss>; they are like an illusion and are empty by their very nature. Just as the objects of an illusion, such as horses or elephants, do not truly assemble as one in an ultimate sense, so too the conceptually imputed form and other aggregates do not assemble as one. Whatever identity is the <term>tathata</term> <gloss>suchness</gloss> of form and the others is also nothing but emptiness by its very nature. Thus, by stating "because of being empty by nature," it shows how—

<summary>This page explains that the five aggregates lack a truly existent collective nature because their individual characteristics are distinct and their assembly is merely a conceptual imputation. It emphasizes that both affliction and purification are adventitious designations rather than intrinsic properties of the natural state.</summary>
<keywords>aggregates, skandha, emptiness, nature, tathata, purification, affliction, conceptual imputation, parikalpita</keywords>

text:
Having entered into meditative equipoise in all the <term>paramitas</term> <gloss>perfections</gloss>, they take birth from one Buddha field to another in order to completely purify the Buddha fields. Those of the fourteenth stage abide in the <term>prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>perfection of wisdom</gloss> which is free from conceptual construction; they remain absorbed in the meditative equipoise of <term>thod rgal</term> <gloss>the leap-over or direct crossing</gloss>. Those of the fifteenth stage possess the qualities that harmonize with enlightenment and the qualities of a Buddha. text:
Bound with a waistband made of a flayed skin, holding a spear and a sword in her hands, she is intoxicated by the wine of blood. Her eyes are bloodshot, and she wanders the charnel grounds at night, visible to the great assembly of <term>bhuta</term> <gloss>spirits or elementals</gloss>. Wearing a garment made of a large, freshly torn-open hide, she is half-clothed and half-wrapped in a coarse hair-blanket. The moon of her face is adorned with the tubes of fresh human entrails, and she rings a bell against her cheek. Her body is freshly anointed with grease and marked with spots of blood, fat, and other substances. May the skull-bearer, who crunches and tears at human flesh with her teeth, protect me.

You are the fierce god and goddess, the unbearable one with human flesh in your mouth. Seeing you, such as has never appeared before, even the <term>mamo</term> <gloss>wrathful maternal goddesses</gloss> are terrified and agitated; gasping for breath and with staring eyes, they bow to you. Noble Black Lady, your body color is pitch black and difficult to endure; even Indra and the other gods offer praises to you every single day. Even Yama, the Lord of Death, constantly trembles and bows before you.

For all humans and living beings without exception, you have subdued their pride. On one ear, a serpent with a thousand hoods serves as an ornament from behind. On the other ear, she holds a peerless lion and tramples the entire earth surrounded by the ocean. The sun that moves above, possessing a thousand rays, is positioned at the level of your navel.

You are the fire blazing from the depths of the ocean, capable of drying up the waters. For the sake of pacifying all women, you are placed as half of the body of the Great God <note>This refers to the Ardhanarishvara form, where the goddess makes up half of Shiva's body.</note>. Great Black One, the Fortress and the Dispeller of Difficulties, you are worshipped by gods and anti-gods alike. Whatever human diseases exist, you know them; pray, make us free from fear.

I praise the Sister of Yama, the Mother of Mara, the Powerful Goddess of the Desire Realm.

The Eightfold Praise to the Great Goddess Palden Lhamo <note>The Glorious Goddess</note>, the mistress of all diseases, composed by the supreme Brahmin Vararuci <note>original: "mchog sred"</note>, is hereby completed.

# In the Indian language: <term>Sri Mahakala-ashtaman-tra-stotra-nama</term> <gloss>The Eight-Line Praise to the Glorious Mahakala</gloss>
# In the Tibetan language: <term>dpal nag po chen po'i bstod pa rkang pa brgyad pa zhes bya ba</term> <gloss>The Praise to the Glorious Great Black One in Eight Lines</gloss>

Do you think that form is the <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>Heroic Seeker of Enlightenment</gloss>? Do you think that feeling is the Bodhisattva? Do you think that perception is the Bodhisattva? Such was the speech of the Buddha.

Secondly, considering the perspective of distinctness, he asked: Do you think that the Bodhisattva is something other than form? Do you think that the Bodhisattva is something other than feeling?

Furthermore, in the second perspective, by examining the entity in terms of its foundation and its abiding, he asked: Do you think the Bodhisattva exists in form? Do you think form exists in the Bodhisattva? Do you think the Bodhisattva exists in feeling? Do you think feeling exists in the Bodhisattva?

By these statements, he teaches that form, feeling, and the other <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates of experience</gloss> have no connection to the Bodhisattva in any way whatsoever. The meaning is that the Bodhisattva is entirely separate from those things.

Taking up the third perspective, he asked: Do you think that the absence of form is the Bodhisattva? Do you think that the absence of feeling is the Bodhisattva? 

Thus, if one analytically examines this Bodhisattva, it cannot be sustained as being identical to, distinct from, possessing a foundation or abiding within, or even as being the absence of these entities. Thinking that the Bodhisattva itself does not truly exist, he said: Blessed One, that is not so.

Among those who profess a belief in a self <note>original: "atman"</note>, some hold the view that the perceiver is all-encompassing. Because of this, they conceive of "sentient beings" as being the very nature of the sense organs such as the eyes. Thinking of the nature of form as being a "sentient being," they believe the seer is the self. For that reason, the Buddha asked: Do you think that form is the Bodhisattva?

Similarly, like a cowherd or similar person, they imagine the "sentient being" is the one who consumes or experiences, and regarding feeling...

It addresses misconceptions that equate the self with physical form, sensory experience, or the act of perceiving.</summary>

text:
Shariputra, the bodhisattva thinks in this way <note>original: "shā ri'i bu byang chub sems dpa' ni 'di snyam du sems te"</note>, continuing until the passage where it is said: he thinks he will lead all sentient beings to pass completely beyond suffering <note>original: "yongs su mya ngan las bzla'o"</note>. This is what the text teaches. Following that, the examples of <term>shravakas</term> <gloss>hearers</gloss> and <term>pratyekabuddhas</term> <gloss>solitary realizers</gloss> are shown through the analogy of a firefly. Then, the example of a bodhisattva is shown through the analogy of the rising sun. Since the meaning of these two sets of analogies has been clearly explained, there is no need to explain the meaning further.

Then, following that, in order to clear away the doubts of the assembly, the Elder asked: "Blessed One, how is one called a bodhisattva mahasattva?" and so forth. He inquired about three stages: the stage of transcending the levels of the <term>shravakas</term> and <term>pratyekabuddhas</term>, the stage of attaining the level of non-retrogression, and the stage of completely purifying the path to enlightenment.

Following that, the Blessed One taught that after the first incalculable <term>kalpa</term> <gloss>aeon</gloss> has passed, beginning from the first production of the spirit of enlightenment called the Joyous <note>the first bodhisattva bhumi or level</note>, one transcends the levels of <term>shravakas</term> and <term>pratyekabuddhas</term> by means of realizing that the characteristics of all phenomena are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Having transcended those, one becomes non-retrogressive at the eighth level. It is taught that one completely purifies the path to enlightenment through the perfections of ripening.

Furthermore, the Elder became hesitant, wondering: "Do they become worthy of offerings immediately upon transcending the levels of the <term>shravakas</term> and <term>pratyekabuddhas</term>, or does it happen at another time?" He then asked: "Blessed One, in what do they abide?" and so forth.

Then, the Blessed One taught with the words, "from the first production of the spirit of enlightenment" and so forth, that they become worthy of offerings immediately upon attaining the Joyous level. The reason for this is taught with the words: "Shariputra, it is because all virtuous qualities arise in the world by depending upon the bodhisattva mahasattva."

<summary>This page explains the stages of a bodhisattva's progress, specifically how they transcend the levels of hearers and solitary realizers to reach the first level of joy. It clarifies that bodhisattvas become worthy of offerings as soon as they reach this stage because they are the source of all worldly virtue.</summary>
<keywords>Shariputra, Bodhisattva, Shravaka, Pratyekabuddha, Joyous Level, Emptiness, Non-retrogression, Offerings, Path to Enlightenment</keywords>

Thinking that there might be <note>categories for those who have entered the path</note>, it is necessary to teach the specific divisions of exertion. From this point onward, the six practices of <term>definite emergence</term> <gloss>the attainment of liberation or higher realization</gloss> are taught.

The six practices of definite emergence are:
1. Practice free from the two extremes.
2. Practice that is non-abiding.
3. Practice without grasping.
4. Practice of thorough investigation.
5. Practice of skillful means.
6. Practice of swiftly and perfectly awakening into enlightenment.

The Bhagavan <note>the Buddha</note> himself taught that these are indeed definite emergence in the concluding summary by stating: "This Bodhisattva Mahasattva <gloss>Great Hero of Awakening</gloss> abides by the manner of not abiding on the stage of non-retrogression <note>the level from which one no longer falls back into cyclic existence</note>. He emerges definitely into omniscience itself and draws near to omniscience," and so forth. Those six practices will be taught sequentially in their respective places below.

Now, in order to open the opportunity for those six practices, the Elder Subhuti said: "Bhagavan, since I do not find, do not perceive, and do not truly see the Bodhisattva or the Perfection of Wisdom <note>Prajnaparamita</note>, which Bodhisattva should I instruct and advise in which Perfection of Wisdom?" and so forth.

By this, four aspects are shown. Regarding the Bodhisattva and the Perfection of Wisdom, because they are shown through direct perception, inference, and philosophical determination, they are not perceived by the three <term>pramanas</term> <gloss>valid means of cognition</gloss>. Having not truly seen the person worthy of instruction or the suitable Perfection of Wisdom for instruction, Subhuti wonders how to apply them to a person. Thus he petitioned with the text ending in: "In which Perfection of Wisdom should I instruct and advise?"

Furthermore, because any entity suitable for instruction is not perceived by the three valid means of cognition, I would feel regret <note>feel it to be an error</note> if a thing without intrinsic nature were to be instructed in a thing without intrinsic nature. Perceived phenomena...

<summary>This page introduces the six practices of definite emergence in the Prajnaparamita literature. It frames Subhuti's inquiry regarding the ultimate non-perception of the practitioner, the teaching, and the act of instruction itself.</summary>
<keywords>definite emergence, Subhuti, six practices, non-abiding, omniscience, three pramanas, valid cognition, non-perception</keywords>

text:
It is shown that one should train in nominal designations, conventional designations, instructional designations, and dharmic <gloss>phenomenal</gloss> designations. In order to abandon the extremes of reification <note>original: "sgro btags pa", superimposition of qualities that do not exist</note> and nihilism <note>original: "skur pa 'debs pa", denial of qualities that do exist</note>, nominal and conventional designations were mentioned first.

In order to mature sentient beings by teaching the Dharma while relying on those designations, the instructional designations are mentioned later. After that, it is stated that through both of these, phenomena are designated conventionally; thus, they are described as conceptually imputed phenomena <note>original: "kun brtags pa'i chos", imputed natures</note>.

Then, to demonstrate the qualities of those three types of designations, it is said: "Subhuti, when a Bodhisattva Mahasattva practices the Perfection of Wisdom in this way, he does not truly perceive that 'form is impermanent'," and so forth. It is shown that the abandonment of all conceptual elaborations is the fruit of training in the understanding that things are merely designations.

### Fascicle Eight

Regarding the conceptualizations of Disciples <term>Sravakas</term> and Solitary Realizers <term>Pratyekabuddhas</term>, there are three types: the objective domain of insight <term>vipasyana</term>, the objective domain of the gates of liberation, and the objective domain of the correct individual investigation of phenomena as they truly are.

Among these, the objective domain of insight consists of four types of conceptualizations regarding the summary of the Dharma, which serve as the foundation for the Four Noble Truths. These involve the dark and white sides according to the power of what is to be accepted and what is to be rejected. They are:
1. Conceptualizations of impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and peace.
2. Conceptualizations of their opposing sides: permanence, pleasure, the existence of a self, and lack of peace.

The objective domain of the gates of liberation consists of:
1. Conceptualizations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
2. Conceptualizations of what is to be abandoned: non-emptiness, signs, and wishes.

The correct individual investigation of phenomena as they truly are consists of the remaining categories: conditioned things, birth, and lack of solitude <note>entanglement with the world</note>; as well as non-virtue and those things that are faulty <note>original: "kha na ma tho ba", misdeeds or transgressive actions</note>.

### Fascicle Eight

Regarding the conceptualizations of Disciples <term>Sravakas</term> and Solitary Realizers <term>Pratyekabuddhas</term>, there are three types: the objective domain of insight <term>vipasyana</term>, the objective domain of the gates of liberation, and the objective domain of the correct individual investigation of phenomena as they truly are.

Among these, the objective domain of insight consists of four types of conceptualizations regarding the summary of the Dharma, which serve as the foundation for the Four Noble Truths. These involve the dark and white sides according to the power of what is to be accepted and what is to be rejected. They are:
1. Conceptualizations of impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and peace.
2. Conceptualizations of their opposing sides: permanence, pleasure, the existence of a self, and lack of peace.

The objective domain of the gates of liberation consists of:
1. Conceptualizations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
2. Conceptualizations of what is to be abandoned: non-emptiness, signs, and wishes.

The correct individual investigation of phenomena as they truly are consists of the remaining categories: conditioned things, birth, and lack of solitude <note>entanglement with the world</note>; as well as non-virtue and those things that are faulty <note>original: "kha na ma tho ba", misdeeds or transgressive actions</note>.

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
There is none. When they do not appear, there is also no cessation. Even when becoming one, there is no decrease, and even when becoming many, there is no increase. Within these, there is not even a slight amount <gloss>alternative reading: a small amount</gloss> of affliction or purification. In that same way, because the nature of the thoroughly imagined <term>parikalpita</term> <gloss>the conceptualized or imagined nature of reality</gloss> is utterly non-existent, there is no arising and no cessation. There is no increase, no decrease, no affliction, and no purification.

Enlightenment is the thoroughly established nature <term>pariniṣpanna</term> <gloss>the ultimate, perfected nature of reality</gloss>. Because that too is utterly secluded, transcending all conceptualization, and is like space, there is no arising and no cessation. There is neither increase nor decrease. Because of its utter purity, there is no affliction. Because it is pure by its very nature, there is no purification. 

Why is this so? It is shown through the statement that form is like an illusion, and feeling is like an illusion, and so forth. This is shown in two ways: through the absence of the illusion and through the absence of the consciousness that grasps at the illusion. 

An illusion is merely a name; it does not abide in an object. It does not abide in a direction. By this, it is shown that because the illusion is thoroughly imagined, it does not exist. Seeing an illusion is a reversal <gloss>an error</gloss>; by saying it does not exist, it shows that consciousness does not exist. 

In this context, the phrase does not abide in an object shows that the illusion does not have the characteristics of matter <term>rūpa</term> <gloss>physical form or substance</gloss>. This is because material phenomena do not abide in an object. The phrase does not abide in a direction shows that it does not have the characteristics of the formless. Although phenomena with formless characteristics, such as consciousness, do not abide in an object, they are designated as abiding in a direction because they abide in the direction of the eyes and so forth. The term reversal shows that it is not true. The phrase it does not exist shows the characteristic of being without entity.

<summary>This page discusses the three natures of reality, focusing on how enlightenment and illusory phenomena lack inherent arising, cessation, or change. It explains that illusions are merely nominal and do not possess the characteristics of material or immaterial substances.</summary>
<keywords>three natures, parikalpita, pariniṣpanna, illusion, emptiness, purification, affliction, formless, consciousness</keywords>

text:
After explaining that one will attain that state, it is concluded that a student who practices in this way, through the manner of non-observation <note>original: "mi dmigs pa," the meditative state where one does not perceive phenomena as having inherent existence</note>, will certainly emerge and attain it. In that same way, because those five aggregates <note>original: "phung po lnga," the components of a person: form, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness</note> are by nature without substantial entity, they are like dreams, echoes, optical illusions <note>original: "mig yor," specifically the appearance of floating spots or hair-like shapes in the vision</note>, reflections, emanations, and mirages. Since the six sense bases <note>original: "skye mched drug," eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind</note> are also like that, there is no such thing as a "Bodhisattva" <gloss>Hero of Awakening</gloss> because they are empty of substantial entity and so forth.

After teaching this training in seeing things as like illusions and so on, in order to categorize the practice of skillful means <term>upaya-kaushalya</term>, the text states: "O Blessed One, will a Bodhisattva who has newly entered the vehicle not be terrified, frightened, and awestruck upon hearing this teaching?" It is then explained that one who lacks skillful means and has not come under the guidance of a spiritual friend <term>kalyanamitra</term> <gloss>virtuous teacher</gloss> will indeed be terrified and frightened in that way. Conversely, one who possesses skillful means will not be terrified or frightened. This is followed by the question: "O Blessed One, by what skillful means does a Bodhisattva Mahasattva <gloss>Great Hero of Awakening</gloss> hear this teaching and not feel terrified, frightened, or awestruck?" through which skillful means is taught.

The meanings of terror, fright, and so on have already been explained previously. Those skillful means are taught in four aspects:

1. Skillful means in the analytical investigation of all phenomena.
2. Skillful means in the complete perfection of the six perfections <term>paramitas</term>.
3. Skillful means in relying upon a spiritual friend.
4. Skillful means in avoiding a spiritual friend who is a negative influence <note>original: "sdig pa'i grogs po," literally a sinful or non-virtuous friend</note>.

Regarding these, beginning from the passage: "One analytically investigates form as impermanent, yet even that is not observed," up until the passage: "This should be understood as the skillful means of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva practicing the Perfection of Wisdom <term>Prajnaparamita</term>."

<summary>This page discusses how Bodhisattvas avoid fear when facing the doctrine of emptiness by employing four types of skillful means. It compares the aggregates and sense bases to illusions and emphasizes the necessity of a spiritual teacher.</summary>
<keywords>skillful means, emptiness, five aggregates, six sense bases, spiritual friend, Perfection of Wisdom, fearlessness</keywords>

text:
<meta>This page continues the analytical commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom sutras within the Tengyur, specifically focusing on the ontological status of a Bodhisattva.</meta>

Regarding the statement that form and the other aggregates <note>the five skandhas: form, sensation, perception, formation, and consciousness</note> do not exist, and the question of why these elements are not counted among things that are non-dual: these twenty-eight questions, along with the subsequent detailed questions and answers provided by the two elders <note>likely referring to Subhuti and Sariputra</note> in sections, should be understood as the definitive establishment <note>original: གཏན་ལ་དབབ་པ་, Sanskrit: viniscaya</note> of the teaching up until the chapter where Kausika <note>an epithet for Indra</note> asks his questions.

In that context, Subhuti, the meaning of the term <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>enlightenment-hero</gloss> is the "meaning of having no foundation." Regarding this, there are four aspects to the meaning of Bodhisattva:
1. Enlightenment <note>bodhi</note>
2. The Hero <note>sattva</note>
3. The conventional Bodhisattva consisting of the nature of the aggregates
4. The ultimate Bodhisattva

Because all four of these are of the nature of non-existence, the meaning of the word Bodhisattva is the meaning of lacking a foundation. Lacking a foundation means having no localized existence. If the so-called Bodhisattva possessed any kind of substantial nature, the meaning of that term would have a foundation and a localized existence. However, in this way, enlightenment does not exist, the hero does not exist, and even the union of the two as "Bodhisattva" does not exist. Therefore, the foundation for the meaning of the word Bodhisattva does not exist; this is the meaning of the phrase "without localized existence."

To categorize this very point: it is because enlightenment is unproduced and the hero is also unproduced. Subhuti, regarding enlightenment and the hero, birth and existence itself do not exist and are not observed. In this regard, enlightenment is unproduced because it is unconditioned <note>asamskrta</note>. The hero is unproduced because they do not truly exist. Therefore, Subhuti, the phrases "enlightenment is unproduced" and "existence is not observed in the hero" should be applied respectively. Following that, in order to explain the sound of the meaning of the words, it is said: "Subhuti, enlightenment has no foundation, and the hero also has no foundation."

<summary>This text provides a linguistic and philosophical analysis of the term Bodhisattva, arguing that neither enlightenment nor the individual being possesses a foundational reality or inherent existence.</summary>
<keywords>Bodhisattva, foundation, unproduced, non-existence, aggregates, Subhuti, ultimate truth, conventional truth</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
Birth does not occur <note>independently</note>, but rather it arises through the power of causes and conditions. For example, when a seed produces a sprout, it is not produced by its own power alone. Just as it is produced through the combined power of earth, water, and other factors, likewise all phenomena arise through the power of the collection of causes and conditions.

Because they do not arise through their own power alone, they are exclusively <term>pratityasamutpada</term> <gloss>dependent origination</gloss>. Those phenomena which arise depending upon other phenomena may possess the nature of being suitable as form, or the nature of experiencing <note>referring to the five aggregates of form and feeling</note>, yet because they arise precisely from the collection of causes and conditions, they are called "arisen from aggregation" <note>original: "saṃskṛta" or conditioned</note>.

How can that which arises from aggregation be called its own intrinsic nature? Therefore, because all phenomena arise through the entity of another, they lack their own entity and thus are without intrinsic nature. Because they lack their own entity, they are called "the intrinsic nature of non-entities." Therefore, it is said: "Subhuti, conditioned phenomena have no intrinsic nature because they arise dependently." This itself is the "intrinsic nature of non-entities" of all phenomena, and this "emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-entities" is so named.

The other explanation is as follows: "Entities are empty of entities. Non-entities are empty of non-entities." In this context, entity and intrinsic nature are synonyms. Non-entity and the absence of intrinsic nature are also synonyms. In this conceptual analysis, the term "non-entity" is understood as the non-existence of an entity; thus both "entity" and "non-entity" are apprehended. By the term "lacking intrinsic nature," one understands that it is not one's own entity; thus both "the entity of another" and "one's own entity" are apprehended. These four types of emptiness are called the "emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-entities."

Because it arises from those <note>causes</note>, it is called an entity. The term "entity" refers to conditioned phenomena. For that reason, it is said that "entities are empty of entities." By the term "non-entity"...

<summary>This page explains the philosophical concept of dependent origination and the lack of intrinsic nature in conditioned phenomena. It argues that because things arise from causes and conditions rather than self-power, they are empty of a permanent, independent essence.</summary>
<keywords>dependent origination, intrinsic nature, emptiness, conditioned phenomena, causes and conditions, Subhuti, entities, non-entities</keywords>

### Teaching the faults of abiding
After thus showing the practice of not abiding, the following was taught to show the faults of abiding:

O Blessed One, furthermore, when a <term>bodhisattva mahasattva</term> <gloss>great heroic being dedicated to awakening</gloss> practices the <term>prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>perfection of wisdom</gloss>, if through a lack of skillful means they abide in form with a mind fallen into grasping at a self or grasping at "mine," then they are practicing the conditioning of form. They are not practicing the perfection of wisdom.

This means that if, through a lack of <term>upaya</term> <gloss>skillful means</gloss>, one grasps at things incorrectly and fails to understand that phenomena are characterized by a nature of non-substantiality, one might think, "I am the essence of form," or "this form is me," or "this is the defining characteristic suitable to be form." If one abides in form in this way, one is conditioning form. This is to practice the phenomena of conditioning that follow the conceptual construction of form. It is not practicing the perfection of wisdom, which follows the defining characteristic of emptiness.

To show the faults of practicing such conditioning, it is said:

To practice the manifestation of conditioning is not the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

Why is it that if one practices conditioning by falling into grasping at a self or "mine" through a lack of skillful means, one will fail to practice the perfection of wisdom, fail to enter the yoga of non-grasping, and fail to attain the deliverances of complete perfection? Regarding this, it was said:

O Blessed One, in this way, form is without any grasping.

This is called the practice of non-grasping. This practice is also shown through three aspects: not grasping at phenomena, <unclear>one line of text regarding the remaining two aspects</unclear>

<summary>This page discusses the distinction between practicing the perfection of wisdom and the mistaken practice of conditioning form through ego-grasping. It emphasizes that true wisdom requires non-grasping and an understanding of the empty nature of phenomena.</summary>
<keywords>perfection of wisdom, prajnaparamita, skillful means, upaya, conditioning, ego-grasping, emptiness, non-grasping, bodhisattva</keywords>

text:
Because mindfulness is not perceived <note>original: "dran pa mi dmigs pa"</note>, it means that suchness <term>tathatā</term> <gloss>the true nature of reality</gloss> is not an object of the knowledge that performs mindfulness. Because calling out <note>original: "bod pa," referring to naming or addressing</note> is not perceived, it is not an object of names. A name is a calling out. Because enthusiasm for phenomena is not perceived, it means all phenomena are without movement or agitation.

Because thickness <note>original: "stug po," often referring to the density of material or conceptual obscuration</note> is not perceived, it means the conceptualization of thickness has been reversed. Because accomplishment <note>original: "rnam par bsgrub pa"</note> is not perceived, it refers to the arrangement of conditioned factors <term>saṃskāra</term> <gloss>formative forces or mental constructions</gloss> as accomplishment; since that arrangement is absent, it is not perceived.

Because there is no affliction <term>kleśa</term> <gloss>disturbing emotions or mental poisons</gloss>, it means one is free from the affliction of the afflictions themselves and from the affliction of conceptualization. Because the result is not perceived, it means the aspect of a result is not perceived within the phenomena that constitute the result. Because the aggregates <term>skandha</term> <gloss>the five heaps of physical and mental components</gloss> are not perceived, it means the aggregates of afflictions, karma, and ripening results are absent.

Because aging is not perceived, it means there is no aging characterized by the change of a state into something else. Because conduct is not perceived, it means the conduct of coming and going is not perceived. Because sin <note>original: "sdig pa"</note> is not perceived, it means there is no harmfulness. Because the "I-grasping" <term>ahaṃkāra</term> <gloss>the ego-sense or self-identification</gloss> is not perceived, it means there is no "I-grasping" consisting of the nature of views or the nature of pride.

That which establishes conventions, that which expresses, and that which teaches: these are the phenomena of the speaker. That which conceptualizes and that which sees: these are the phenomena of the listener. Regarding the phrase "that which establishes conventions," this refers to what is seen, heard, distinguished, and cognized by the noble ones and those who are not noble ones. This is expressed through the power of the sixteen conventions, which include what is seen and not seen, heard and not heard, distinguished and not distinguished, and cognized and not cognized.

<keywords>emptiness, non-perception, aggregates, mindfulness, conventions, speech, listening, ego-grasping, suchness</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>explained. Then, following the series of statements spoken by the Elder <note>referring to Subhuti</note>, the Blessed One expressed his great delight. Through the sequence previously explained, he showed that the qualities such as the <term>paramitas</term> <gloss>perfections</gloss> possess the nature of full maturation. He demonstrated that these are contained within the <term>dharmakaya</term> <gloss>truth body</gloss> and constitute the <term>mahayana</term> <gloss>great vehicle</gloss> itself.

Having thus shown the Great Vehicle by means of the six perfections and so forth, the Elder then addressed the Blessed One with five specific statements: that this vehicle emerges having surpassed the world of gods, humans, and <term>asuras</term> <gloss>demigods</gloss>; that this vehicle is equal to space; that just as space provides room for immeasurable, infinite, and limitless sentient beings; that neither coming nor going is perceived; and that neither a prior limit nor a posterior limit is perceived. 

The Blessed One then took up each of these statements individually, starting with: Subhuti, as for what you said, that this vehicle will emerge having surpassed the world of gods, humans, and demigods; and he explained them extensively. 

If one asks how the teaching is presented in the passage beginning with: Subhuti, if the desire realm were suchness, unerring and so forth: if all phenomena such as the desire realm were not conceptually constructed and unreal, but were instead the truly established nature of reality itself, then this Great Vehicle would not emerge from them and would not abandon them. However, since all these phenomena are conceptually constructed and unreal, it is taught that this Great Vehicle completely abandons them. 

Subhuti, if the desire realm were suchness, unerring and not otherwise <unclear>...</unclear>

text:
Since that itself is <term>imputational</term> <gloss>conceptual construction</gloss>, it does not exist. The meaning of the phrase "form exists within emptiness" refers to the transformation within form. After teaching that phenomena such as the <term>paramita</term> <gloss>perfection</gloss> of generosity are not observed within the equality of the three times, one might ask: what is the intention behind saying "if equality itself is not observed within equality"? On the ultimate stage of the <term>Mahayana</term> <gloss>Great Vehicle</gloss>, all phenomena such as the perfections become the nature of complete maturation. They follow the essence of emptiness itself. Therefore, within that state, there is no such thing as the "equality of the three times," nor are there perfections like generosity that belong to the three times. For this reason, it is said: "How could one observe the perfection of generosity of the past, future, or present within equality?" The same should be applied to all things.

The systematic sequences <note>the repetitive structures or "wheels" of the argument</note> should be understood as:
* The sequence of examining the equality of the three times.
* The sequence of examining all phenomena through the gate of duality.
* The sequence of examining the phenomena of the five <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates</gloss> in the three times.
* The sequence of examining the phenomena of the five aggregates belonging to the three times within emptiness.
* The sequence of examining the six perfections within the equality of the three times.
* The sequence of examining emptiness within those perfections.
* The sequence of examining everything from the <term>applications of mindfulness</term> <gloss>smrtyupasthana</gloss> up to the ultimate <term>unmixed qualities</term> <gloss>avenika-dharma</gloss> within those.
* The sequence of examining <term>ordinary beings</term> <gloss>prthagjana</gloss>.
* The sequences of examining <term>Hearers</term> <gloss>Sravakas</gloss>, <term>Solitary Realizers</term> <gloss>Pratyekabuddhas</gloss>, <term>Bodhisattvas</term>, and <term>Tathagatas</term> <gloss>Buddhas</gloss>.

Therefore, the statement "this is called the Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattva Mahasattvas" is an explanation using a definitive term: it is called the Great Vehicle because it is the vehicle of the Great Beings. Then, the Elder Subhuti addressed the Blessed One, saying "This <term>Prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss>..."

<summary>This page discusses the non-conceptual nature of the Great Vehicle, explaining how phenomena and the three times are not found within the state of ultimate equality and emptiness. It lists the systematic sequences of Buddhist categories used to analyze reality and defines the Mahayana as the vehicle of great beings.</summary>
<keywords>Emptiness, Three Times, Equality, Mahayana, Perfections, Skandhas, Subhuti, Prajnaparamita</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>and signs, designations, and examinations are the indications. The definitions and the conduct are the characteristics. Regarding the statement: Venerable Shariputra, that which is called the Perfection of Wisdom has gone far; because the wisdom that has gone to the far shore of all phenomena is far removed from all those phenomena, it is called the <term>Prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss>. Realizing through method and reasoning is thorough realization.

Following that, the second section is shown by the passage: Venerable Subhuti, why do you say that the non-arising of form is not form? and so forth. The statement: Venerable Sharadvatiputra <note>another name for Shariputra</note>, form is empty of form; the meaning of this is that the imagined form does not exist as a substantial entity of form. Regarding the statement: Whatever is the emptiness of form, that is not form and is unproduced; this means that whatever is the emptiness of the nature of form—the true nature of things—is not the essence of form, nor is it the essence of arising. Venerable Sharadvatiputra, by that explanation, whatever is the non-arising of form is not form; in this way, imagined form is without arising and does not have the essence of arising. Therefore, non-arising is not form; such is the established meaning.

After that, the occasion of the third section is shown by: Venerable Subhuti, why do you say that the decrease of form is not form? and so forth. The statement: Whatever is form and whatever is decrease, both of these are neither joined nor disjoined; this means that according to the previously explained method, form is imagined and decrease is also imagined. Therefore, both are without defining characteristics. Regarding the fourth section: The unproduced is not one thing and form another; the unproduced itself is form. Form itself is the unproduced; this means that what is called form, according to the previously explained method, is...

does not enter <note>referring to a state of mental non-engagement or distraction</note>. This is the fifth of the eighteen unmixed qualities <note>original: "ma 'dres pa'i chos"; these are qualities unique to a Buddha</note>.

Regarding the statement "there is no equanimity that is not based on discernment" <note>original: "so sor ma brtags pa'i btang sྙoms"</note>, it means that just as <term>Arhats</term> <gloss>worthy ones who have attained liberation for themselves</gloss> might neglect the welfare of sentient beings without careful discernment, a <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>Thus-Gone One; a Buddha</gloss> does not act in such a way. A Buddha remains indifferent only after discerning whether the time is right or wrong, whether a being is fortunate or unfortunate, and whether it is meaningful or meaningless to act. He never acts otherwise. This is the sixth quality.

There is no decline in aspiration. There is no decline in diligence. There is no decline in mindfulness. There is no decline in meditative concentration. There is no decline in wisdom. There is no decline in total liberation. There is no decline in the wisdom-vision of total liberation. 

Regarding these points, due to the influence of their limited spheres of activity, <term>Arhats</term> do not naturally develop an aspiration for the level of a Buddha or for the natural activities of a Buddha. Instead, they possess aspirations only for the deeds of a <term>Shravaka</term> <gloss>Hearer; a disciple on a path toward personal liberation</gloss>. Similarly, the diligence, mindfulness, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and wisdom-vision of liberation belonging to the level of a Buddha are absent in Hearers. Therefore, they are said to have a "decline" in these seven qualities, such as aspiration, because they have failed to attain them.

Buddhas, however, never fail to possess these distinguished qualities. Because they have fully realized all phenomena, they do not experience even the slightest decline. Thus, the aspiration of Buddhas to work for the benefit of sentient beings arises continuously at all times. Their aspiration for qualities such as great love and great compassion, for teaching the Dharma, for maturing sentient beings, and for maintaining the continuity of the <term>Three Jewels</term> <gloss>the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha</gloss> after having committed to the <term>Bodhicitta</term> <gloss>the mind of enlightenment</gloss>, arises without interruption. Likewise, the <term>Tathagata</term> possesses diligence—

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
Because this is realized through one’s own individual awareness <term>svasamvedana</term> <gloss>self-cognizing awareness</gloss>, it transcends the path of conceptual thought. For this reason, it is inconceivable and is not of the nature of the ordinary mind. 

Koushika, when it is said, "This is the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva, the great being," it is a term that refers to the <term>nirvikalpa-prajna</term> <gloss>non-conceptual wisdom</gloss>. In this context, that which is called "discerning all phenomena" refers to the relative truth <term>samvrti-satya</term> <gloss>conventional reality</gloss>. The statement "not being attached to any phenomenon and not perceiving them" refers to the ultimate truth <term>paramartha-satya</term> <gloss>absolute reality</gloss>.

What is shown by the phrase, "I shall act to repay kindness, and I shall not act without repaying kindness"? It means that previously, when our Blessed One was a bodhisattva, he was in the retinue of the former Tathagatas <gloss>Buddhas</gloss>. There, through the instructions and advice of the great disciples <term>shravakas</term> <gloss>hearers</gloss>, he was correctly taught and led to perfectly uphold the teachings. Having been placed in the correct practice, he practiced according to the stages of their teaching and attained manifest, complete enlightenment. Therefore, I too, in this assembly, shall place these bodhisattvas into the correct practice through instruction and advice. 

By practicing according to the stages of the teachings given by those of the past, they will attain manifest, complete enlightenment. Thus, it shows that "I should acknowledge the deeds performed by the disciples of the past." 

What distinction is there between the terms "instructing" and "advising" and so forth? In this regard, there are three stages: the beginning, the middle, and the end.
*   In the beginning, one should instruct and advise.
*   In the middle is the practice.
*   In the end is the fruit <gloss>the result or realization</gloss>.

Regarding the beginning stage: turning someone away from what is improper by saying "do not do these things" is instruction. Engaging them in the application by saying "do these things" is advice.

In the middle stage, there are four states: 
1.  Non-practice
2.  Wrong practice
3.  Partial practice
4.  Correct practice

Among these, to lead one who does not practice due to ignorance into practice <unclear>one line of text continued on next page</unclear>

Therefore, I too, in this assembly, shall place these bodhisattvas into the correct practice through instruction and advice. 

By practicing according to the stages of the teachings given by those of the past, they will attain manifest, complete enlightenment. Thus, it shows that "I should acknowledge the deeds performed by the disciples of the past." 

What distinction is there between the terms "instructing" and "advising" and so forth? In this regard, there are three stages: the beginning, the middle, and the end.
*   In the beginning, one should instruct and advise.
*   In the middle is the practice.
*   In the end is the fruit <gloss>the result or realization</gloss>.

Regarding the beginning stage: turning someone away from what is improper by saying "do not do these things" is instruction. Engaging them in the application by saying "do these things" is advice.

In the middle stage, there are four states: 
1.  Non-practice
2.  Wrong practice
3.  Partial practice
4.  Correct practice

Among these, to lead one who does not practice due to ignorance into practice <unclear>one line of text continued on next page</unclear>

Because it is conceptualized that there is something else, the Buddha asked, "Do you think that a non-form is a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>a being striving for awakening</gloss>? Do you think that a non-feeling is a Bodhisattva?" and so forth. Thinking that all those conceptualizations are inconsistent with logic, the Buddha addressed the five <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates</gloss>, the six <term>dhatus</term> <gloss>elements</gloss>, the twelve <term>ayatanas</term> <gloss>sense fields</gloss>, the eighteen elements, and the twelve links of <term>dependent origination</term> <gloss>the chain of causes leading to rebirth</gloss>. He questioned each of these individually, and the Elder Subhuti replied, "No, Blessed One, that is not so," thus negating them.

Then the Blessed One considered: if this Bodhisattva were something that became a different phenomenon, would it be <term>conditioned</term> <gloss>produced by causes</gloss> or <term>unconditioned</term> <gloss>existing beyond cause and effect</gloss>? If it were conditioned, it would have to be observed within these five aggregates and so forth, yet it is not observed. Even if one claims it is unconditioned, to clear that doubt, the Buddha again took up the <term>tathata</term> <gloss>suchness or true nature</gloss> of the aggregates and so forth. He asked, "Subhuti, what do you think? Is the suchness of form itself the Bodhisattva?" and so on.

Then the Elder Subhuti considered the distinct suchness of the aggregates, elements, sense fields, and dependent origination. If these were collected and existed within a Bodhisattva, then a single Bodhisattva would possess an infinite and immeasurable number of intrinsic natures. Thinking that such a logic is also impossible, he negated this as well, saying, "No, Blessed One, that is not so."

Afterward, the Blessed One asked for the reason, saying, "Subhuti, do you say that because you have grasped the underlying meaning?" Subhuti replied with the reason: "Blessed One, since a Bodhisattva is utterly non-existent and unobservable, how could form possibly be a Bodhisattva?" and so forth. This is like the examples of a rabbit's horns or the son of a barren woman, where qualities such as long or short, or white <unclear>...</unclear>

<summary>The Buddha and Subhuti engage in a dialectical inquiry to demonstrate that a Bodhisattva cannot be identified with the aggregates, elements, or even their ultimate suchness. The passage concludes that since the Bodhisattva lacks inherent existence, it cannot possess any physical or mental characteristics.</summary>
<keywords>Bodhisattva, Subhuti, five aggregates, suchness, tathata, dependent origination, emptiness, non-existence</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>Whatever is the complete purity of <note>purity implies the essential nature or emptiness of a phenomenon</note> is the complete purity of form. Whatever is the complete purity of form is the complete purity of omniscience itself. In this way, the complete purity of the perfection of wisdom, the complete purity of form, and the complete purity of omniscience itself are non-dual. They cannot be divided into two; they are not separate; they are not distinct.

This same logic should be applied to feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness, up to the perfection of wisdom. Whatever is the complete purity of the feelings conditioned by mental contact <note>the sixth sense consciousness and its interaction with mental objects</note>, that is the complete purity of omniscience itself. In this way, the complete purity of the perfection of wisdom, the complete purity of feelings conditioned by mental contact, and the complete purity of omniscience itself are non-dual. This should be applied to all such categories.

Furthermore, the complete purity of the perfection of meditative concentration <note>term: Dhyana-paramita</note>, the complete purity of all phenomena starting from the aggregates <note>term: Skandhas</note> up to the end of feelings, and the complete purity of omniscience itself are shown to be non-dual.

Similarly, the complete purity of all perfections <note>term: Paramitas</note> and all aspects of emptiness <note>term: Shunyata</note>, the complete purity of all phenomena up to the end of feelings, and the complete purity of omniscience itself are shown to be non-dual.

Likewise, it should be explained in a unified way that the phenomena ranging from the applications of mindfulness <note>term: Smrityupasthana</note> up to omniscience itself, and the phenomena ranging from form to the six collections of feelings, and the complete purity of omniscience itself, are all one. Furthermore, the sections on the complete purity of the conditioned and the unconditioned <note>referring to phenomena that arise from causes and those that do not, such as nirvana</note>, and the three times <note>past, present, and future</note>...

<summary>This page explains the non-duality of the perfection of wisdom, omniscience, and the various components of existence like form and feelings. It asserts that the essential purity of all these categories is identical and inseparable.</summary>
<keywords>non-duality, complete purity, omniscience, perfection of wisdom, aggregates, mental contact, emptiness</keywords>

text:
Regarding the question of what constitutes the "other shore," it is said: that which does not grasp at form and so forth. Because there is no grasping at form and the other aggregates, it is called the other shore. The phrase, he does not pass into <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>the state beyond suffering</gloss> in the intermediate state, refers to the fact that because this <term>Parivrajaka</term> <gloss>wandering mendicant</gloss> belongs to the lineage of the Buddha, he does not attain final liberation during the intermediate state between lives. 

The inclusion of the word "until" refers to the passage: those aspirations are not aspirations; those powers are not powers; those fearlessnesses are not fearlessnesses; those specific perfect realizations are not specific perfect realizations—extending until—even those qualities of a Buddha are not the qualities of a Buddha. By using this word "until," the text demonstrates the other shore.

In this way, after the practice of non-grasping is fully established, the practice of thorough examination is then undertaken. It is explained through the phrase: Furthermore, Blessed One, when a <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term> <gloss>great heroic being focused on enlightenment</gloss> practices the <term>Prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss>, they should perform a thorough examination in this manner.

This practice of thorough examination is shown in four aspects: 
1. What is this? 
2. Whose is this? 
3. Why is this? 
4. Where is this? 

From the phrase, when they examine in such a way and think in such a way, until the phrase, if one practices the Perfection of Wisdom in this way, one is not separated from <term>Sarvajna</term> <gloss>omniscience</gloss>, the text explains the aspect of "What is this?"

From the phrase, Venerable Shariputra, form is devoid of the intrinsic nature of form, until the phrase, the ultimate reality is devoid of the intrinsic nature of ultimate reality, it likewise explains "What is this?"

Furthermore, Venerable Shariputra, from the phrase, form lacks the defining characteristics of form, until the phrase, whoever trains in this training will definitely emerge into omniscience, it explains the same point.

<summary>This page explains the philosophical meaning of the other shore as a state of non-grasping and details the fourfold method of thorough examination used by a Bodhisattva to maintain connection with omniscience.</summary>
<keywords>Prajnaparamita, Perfection of Wisdom, non-grasping, fourfold examination, omniscience, Shariputra, Nirvana, Buddhist philosophy</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta> and since there is not the slightest attachment to the notion that this is the truth as a self-entity of truth, and because one does not perceive any engagement with the objects of the white or black sides <note>referring to virtuous and non-virtuous actions or phenomena</note>, there is neither grasping nor rejecting. At that time, because one abides in the essence of <term>Sarvajna</term> <gloss>all-knowingness or omniscience</gloss>, it is said that one attains omniscience. It is also said that one attains nothing at all.

### The Great Wonder of Wisdom

When it is said, "Blessed One, this Perfection of Wisdom is a great wonder," it refers to the fact that because all phenomena do not exist, they do not arise, they do not cease, they are not composed, they are not observed, and they do not perish. Therefore, in that state, they are described by terms such as "non-arising" and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "The Perfection of Wisdom brings about the attainment of all phenomena; the Perfection of Wisdom does not bring about the attainment of all phenomena," if one were to have such a perception, it is said that this is because of conceptualizing both existence and non-existence.

The phrase "one will not have conviction in form" means that one has reached conviction and internal understanding that form has the characteristic of non-existence. The same should be applied to the other <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates</gloss> as well.

### Conviction Through Non-Observation

Subhuti, because one does not observe form, one will have conviction in the Perfection of Wisdom. This means that by understanding all phenomena, such as form, to be non-existent by their very nature, one gains conviction in the Perfection of Wisdom and will manifest it directly.

When it says, "It does not make form large and it does not make form small," it means that it does not make the form of the <term>dharmata</term> <gloss>intrinsic nature</gloss>, which is thoroughly established, large; nor does it make the <term>parikalpita</term> <gloss>imagined or imputed</gloss> form small. This should be applied to all things in the same way.

Blessed One, a <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term> <gloss>Great Hero of Awakening</gloss> who has such a perception regarding the Perfection of Wisdom...

<summary>This page discusses the non-conceptual nature of the Perfection of Wisdom, explaining that true omniscience involves neither grasping nor rejecting phenomena. It clarifies that understanding the non-existence of form and other aggregates leads to direct realization of ultimate reality.</summary>
<keywords>omniscience, Perfection of Wisdom, non-arising, form, aggregates, Subhuti, intrinsic nature, non-existence</keywords>

"Called so" is the forty-sixth. 
"O Blessed One, that which is called awakening, awakening" <note>the term used is <term>bodhi</term> <gloss>awakening/enlightenment</gloss></note> is the forty-seventh. 
"O Blessed One, whichever Bodhisattva, Great Being <note><term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term> dwells in this awakening" is the forty-eighth. 

"O Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva, Great Being practices the Perfection of Wisdom, then that which is called awakening" is the forty-ninth.

"O Blessed One, how is it that for the sake of the roots of virtue of a Bodhisattva, Great Being" is the fifty-first. 
"O Blessed One, just as those who have not rendered service to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones" is the fifty-second. 

"O Blessed One, will the Bodhisattva, Great Being not attain omniscience?" <note><term>sarvajñatā</term> <gloss>all-knowingness or the state of a Buddha</gloss></note> is the fifty-third. 
"O Blessed One, for what reason does a Bodhisattva, Great Being render service to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones?" is the fifty-fourth. 
"O Blessed One, by being endowed with which skillful means?" <note><term>upaya-kaushalya</term> <gloss>effective methods used by Buddhas to teach</gloss></note> is the fifty-fifth. 
"O Blessed One, is it not possible for non-existent things to achieve manifest, complete Buddhahood through non-existent things?" is the fifty-sixth. 

At this point, there are four intermediate questions. 

"O Blessed One, what is the conceptual elaboration of the Bodhisattva, Great Being?" <note><term>prapañca</term> <gloss>mental proliferation or the tendency of the mind to fabricate reality through language</gloss></note> is the fifty-seventh. 
"O Blessed One, if no phenomenon whatsoever is perceived to have an intrinsic nature" <note><term>svabhāva</term> <gloss>inherent existence or self-nature</gloss></note> is the fifty-eighth. 
"O Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva, Great Being has completely perfected all the paths" is the fifty-ninth. 
"O Blessed One, how can my Bodhisattva, Great Being attain omniscience without having generated these paths?"
