<meta>This text is a series of numbered questions or topical outlines from a commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom literature in the Tengyur. It continues the enumeration of points of inquiry addressed to the Buddha.</meta>

...to act is the sixtieth. 

O Blessed One <note>original: "bcom ldan 'das", often translated as Lord or Bhagavan</note>, what is the path of the knowledge of the aspects of the path of the Bodhisattva? This is the sixty-first. 

O Blessed One, what are the qualities that are factors of enlightenment <note>original: "byang chub kyi phyogs kྱི་ chos", refers to the thirty-seven factors of awakening</note> and what is enlightenment? This is the sixty-second. 

O Blessed One, what are the qualities <note>original: "chos", translates the Sanskrit "dharma" in the sense of phenomena or constituent factors</note> which the Bodhisattva Mahasattva <gloss>Great Being</gloss> should understand, realize, and train in through seeing? This is the sixty-third. 

O Blessed One, in the Noble Discipline <note>original: " 'phags pa'i chos 'dul ba", referring to the Vinaya or the spiritual training</note>... This is the sixty-fourth. 

O Blessed One, then should one not train in the characteristics of form? This is the sixty-fifth. 

O Blessed One, if one should not train in the characteristics of these phenomena, how then does the Bodhisattva Mahasattva <gloss>Great Being</gloss>... This is the sixty-sixth. 

O Blessed One, if all phenomena lack characteristics... This is the sixty-seventh. 

O Blessed One, how can there be meditation on that which lacks characteristics, and how can there be meditation on the Perfection of Wisdom? This is the sixty-eighth. 

O Blessed One, how is meditation on form the destruction of form, and how is it meditation on the Perfection of Wisdom? This is the sixty-ninth. 

O Blessed One, is there no concordant patience <note>original: "mthun pa'i bzod pa", a specific stage of realization on the path</note> for one who possesses the perception of things as real entities? This is the seventieth. 

O Blessed One, what is it like when a Bodhisattva Mahasattva practices the Perfection of Wisdom? This is the seventy-first. 

O Blessed One, what is that which is called a real entity <note>original: "dngos po", Sanskrit: "bhava"</note> and what is that which is called the absence of a real entity? This is the seventy-second. 

O Blessed One, what is duality and what is non-duality? This is the seventy-third. 

O Blessed One, if all phenomena are of the nature of the absence of real entities...

It focuses on the definitions of reality, non-duality, and the methods of meditative training.</summary>

text:
The <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term> <gloss>Great Heroic Being of Awakening</gloss> does not abide in other phenomena, but abides solely in the <term>Prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss>; this is the forty-fourth section.

Blessed One, if the Perfection of Wisdom is empty by its own nature; this is the forty-fifth section.

Blessed One, how is one called a <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term>; this is the forty-sixth section.

Blessed One, what is the path by which one will manifest the complete awakening of unsurpassable, true, and perfect enlightenment; this is the forty-seventh section.

If all phenomena are empty of their own defining characteristics; this is the forty-eighth section.

Blessed One, what is it that after the Blessed One manifested the complete awakening of unsurpassable, true, and perfect enlightenment; this is the forty-ninth section.

Blessed One, does the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>Thus Gone One</gloss> perceive phenomena as black or white <note>referring to non-virtuous or virtuous actions and qualities</note>; this is the fiftieth section.

Blessed One, if all phenomena are empty of their own defining characteristics, how then; this is the fifty-first section.

Blessed One, is it through the knowledge of suffering; this is the fifty-second section.

Blessed One, how does a <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term> practice the Perfection of Wisdom; this is the fifty-third section.

Blessed One, what is the true nature of all phenomena exactly as it is; this is the fifty-fourth section.

Blessed One, if that is so, and awakening has no substantial entity; this is the fifty-fifth section.

Blessed One, if all phenomena are of the nature of having no substantial entity, and they were not created even by the Buddha; this is the fifty-sixth section.

Blessed One, the substantial entity that ordinary childish beings are attached to, regarding it as a real thing, its unerring reality; this is the fifty-seventh section.

Blessed One, regarding the vision of reality...

text:
Having shown that everything from <note>the first stages of the path</note> up to the state of an omniscient buddha is without birth, the text concludes: Venerable <term>Sharadvatiputra</term> <gloss>Sariputra</gloss>, in this enumeration, what is expressed is without birth. The eloquence is without birth, and the phenomena are without birth. Those phenomena which serve as the basis for eloquence are also without birth.

Venerable <term>Sharadvatiputra</term>, the statement that form is empty by its very nature refers to the form of the <term>dharmata</term> <gloss>intrinsic nature of reality</gloss>. Therefore, it does not abide within, it does not abide without, and it is not observed as something existing apart from both. If it were to abide somewhere, it would have to abide within, without, or in some third place other than those two. However, in the ultimate sense, it does not exist in any of those three. Therefore, it is non-abiding.

Having shown this, the text extensively expands on the definition of abiding and non-abiding to teach the method for practicing the path to enlightenment. This includes the distinction between what is worldly and what is transcendent. The phrase "not moving, not rising above, and not passing beyond the world" means "from what is mentally constructed". There are three types based on the levels of small, medium, and great patience. The meaning of the remaining parts is clear.

Regarding the seven phrases beginning with "those by which it becomes a world," the term "world" is applied in several ways. In some contexts, it refers to the five <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates</gloss>. In others, it refers to the world of sentient beings, the container world <note>the physical universe</note>, the world of ordinary beings, <term>samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of existence</gloss>, mentally constructed phenomena, or the five objects of sensory desire. "Those by which it becomes a world" refers to the world of the aggregates. "Those which establish the world" refers to the container world. "Those which are equal to the world" refers to being equal to mentally constructed phenomena. "Those through which gifts are given for the sake of the world" refers to the five objects of sensory desire given for the sake of the world.

<summary>This page explains the emptiness and non-abiding nature of form and eloquence while defining the various technical applications of the term world in Buddhist philosophy. It clarifies that reality is neither internal nor external but transcends mental construction.</summary>
<keywords>Sariputra, emptiness, non-abiding, dharmata, world, aggregates, five sensory desires, transcendence, mental construction</keywords>

text:
That which is called "the <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>enlightenment being</gloss> will fall away from the <term>Prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss>" refers to the attachment caused by the fault of perceiving signs <note>referring to the error of viewing phenomena as having inherent, concrete characteristics</note>. 

That which is called "not grasping all phenomena" means that very lack of attachment to the Perfection of Wisdom is itself "not grasping." The wisdom of a Bodhisattva is not attached to anything at all, nor does it grasp anything. 

In this way, that which is called "the Perfection of Wisdom is not separated from the Perfection of Wisdom" means that the Perfection of Wisdom is, at all times, not separated from the essential nature of the Perfection of Wisdom. This is the intended meaning. 

If all phenomena are never separated from their respective essential natures in such a manner, then the question "How should the Perfection of Wisdom be accomplished?" asks: if all phenomena are never separated from their essential nature, then how can they be apprehended through the roots of virtue and so forth? 

The phrase "there is no clinging to form; one does not cling by thinking 'this is form, this is form'" and so on, demonstrates the following: phenomena do not accomplish phenomena, because there is no clinging to any phenomena. 

By not seeing things as real entities, one realizes the reality of phenomena just as they are, in accordance with their abiding nature. This realization itself is called "accomplishment," and it is not accomplished in any other way. This is what is being shown. 

This should also be understood through the examples of the <term>Chakravartin</term> <gloss>Universal Monarch</gloss> and the chariot driver. 

"O Blessed One, if the Perfection of Wisdom does not produce any phenomenon and does not cease any phenomenon," and so forth, asks the following: if the wisdom of a Bodhisattva does not produce any phenomenon at all, and does not even cease "black phenomena" <note>unwholesome or negative states of being</note>, then what is the purpose of the six perfections? How are the six perfections to be brought to completion? 

Subhuti, regarding the state of omniscience...

<summary>This page discusses the non-attachment and non-grasping central to the Perfection of Wisdom, explaining that realization consists of seeing phenomena as they are without clinging to their signs. It addresses the paradoxical nature of spiritual accomplishment where no phenomena are produced or destroyed.</summary>
<keywords>Perfection of Wisdom, Prajnaparamita, Bodhisattva, non-attachment, emptiness, essential nature, Subhuti, six perfections, omniscience</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
"Is it unconditioned?" <note>original: "’dus ma bgyis"</note> This was asked because the nature of cessation is exactly that. Since cessation is merely the exhaustion of abandonment, changes in body and speech do indeed occur. "These do not cause harm to childish ordinary beings" <note>original: "byis pa so so'i skye bo"</note> refers to actions like looking in a mirror or #jumping and moving about#. It is like when the monk <term>Pilindavatsa</term> spoke to a low-caste woman using harsh words; such actions do not cause harm to either childish ordinary beings or to noble beings.

"Does one abide in the path or abide in what is not the path?" and so forth. Regarding such conceptualizations, the Blessed One replied: because the path is of the nature of non-entity <note>original: "dngos po med pa'i ngo bo nyid"</note>, it is not suitable as a place to abide. 

"Blessed One, if the path is a non-entity and <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>extinction of suffering</gloss> is also a non-entity, then for what purpose is it said: 'This is a Stream-Enterer' or 'This is a Once-Returner'?" and so forth. By this, the speaker asks about the noble individuals and the Buddha. If they are described by virtue of the path or described by the attainment of <term>Nirvana</term>, yet if both path and <term>Nirvana</term> are non-existent, how can the noble individuals be established?

"Subhuti, all of them are distinguished by the unconditioned," the Buddha replied. This means that although the path and <term>Nirvana</term> do not exist as entities, they are distinguished by <term>Tathata</term> <gloss>Suchness</gloss>, which is the nature of the absence of the conditioned.

"Blessed One, does that which is unconditioned distinguish and say, 'This is a Stream-Enterer'?" By asking this, Subhuti is thinking that if they are distinguished by the unconditioned, does the unconditioned itself categorize or produce those individuals? 

"Subhuti, while the unconditioned does not categorize," the Buddha replied, meaning that while the unconditioned does not produce anything, nevertheless...

<summary>The text discusses the ontological status of the path and Nirvana as non-entities and explains how noble individuals are categorized through the unconditioned nature of reality.</summary>
<keywords>unconditioned, Nirvana, path, noble individuals, Subhuti, Pilindavatsa, Suchness, non-entity</keywords>

"Blessed One, if the path is a non-entity and <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>extinction of suffering</gloss> is also a non-entity, then for what purpose is it said: 'This is a Stream-Enterer' or 'This is a Once-Returner'?" and so forth. By this, the speaker asks about the noble individuals and the Buddha. If they are described by virtue of the path or described by the attainment of <term>Nirvana</term>, yet if both path and <term>Nirvana</term> are non-existent, how can the noble individuals be established?

"Subhuti, all of them are distinguished by the unconditioned," the Buddha replied. This means that although the path and <term>Nirvana</term> do not exist as entities, they are distinguished by <term>Tathata</term> <gloss>Suchness</gloss>, which is the nature of the absence of the conditioned.

"Blessed One, does that which is unconditioned distinguish and say, 'This is a Stream-Enterer'?" By asking this, Subhuti is thinking that if they are distinguished by the unconditioned, does the unconditioned itself categorize or produce those individuals? 

"Subhuti, while the unconditioned does not categorize," the Buddha replied, meaning that while the unconditioned does not produce anything, nevertheless...

<summary>The text discusses the ontological status of the path and Nirvana as non-entities and explains how noble individuals are categorized through the unconditioned nature of reality.</summary>
<keywords>unconditioned, Nirvana, path, noble individuals, Subhuti, Pilindavatsa, Suchness, non-entity</keywords>

This phrase refers to the seventy-fifth chapter. The phrase, "The Blessed One spoke thus," refers to the seventy-sixth chapter. The phrase, "Blessed One, if a beginner <note>literally: a person of the first action</note> seeks to fully investigate emptiness by its very essence, how should they be instructed and taught?" refers to the seventy-seventh chapter.

It should be understood that all these questions were asked for the benefit of the non-returning <term>bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>those awakened beings who will not fall back into cyclic existence</gloss> sitting in that assembly, and for the sake of helping future generations.

### Fascicle Twenty-Three

Regarding the statement, "Subhuti, form is profound":
In this context, the <term>tathata</term> <gloss>suchness or true nature</gloss> of form is expressed using the word "form." Therefore, when asked how it is profound, the answer is given: "Subhuti, just as the suchness of form is, so form is profound." This shows that it is indeed suchness itself. The meaning is that form is profound through the same manner in which suchness is profound.

When the question was asked, "Blessed One, what is the suchness of form like?", what was the underlying intent? Suchness is without any characteristics. It is neither the characteristic of things like form, nor is it dependent on form and so on. The question asks how one can use words like form to say "the suchness of form" or "the suchness of feeling."

The reply, "Subhuti, in that suchness of form, form does not exist, nor is there suchness apart from form; such is the suchness of form," means that the <term>parikalpita</term> <gloss>imagined or constructed nature</gloss> has been abandoned. That <term>parinispanna</term> <gloss>perfected nature</gloss> of suchness, which exists apart from the imagined, is free from all characteristics. It is improper to express it using terms like "form." For ordinary childish beings, that defiled suchness, which cannot be said to be the same as or different from the imagined "form" and so on, is metaphorically designated by terms such as "form" in order to point toward its state.

<summary>This page concludes the seventy-seventh chapter and begins fascicle twenty-three with a commentary on the profundity of form and its relationship to suchness. It explains that while the ultimate nature of reality is beyond verbal description, terms like form are used metaphorically to guide practitioners toward understanding.</summary>

<keywords>Tengyur, Subhuti, suchness, tathata, emptiness, form, bodhisattva, perfected nature, imagined nature</keywords>

text:
That criticism should be applied in the same way. It is like the analogy of following the tracks of an ox <note>This refers to a seeker trying to find the source through secondary signs</note>, or a carpenter who wishes to build the **Palace of Victory** <note>original: "Vaijayanta," the celestial palace of Indra</note> by searching for the mandala of the sun and moon's celestial mansions, and saying, "The Palace of Victory is exactly this large."

Subhuti, the statement that "the Perfection of Wisdom has no inspired eloquence" is because it is non-conceptual. The statement that "it is inconceivable" is because it completely transcends the domain of logic <note>original: "tarka"</note>. The statement that "it is without birth and without cessation" is because it is established as the unchanging, perfected nature <term>parinispanna</term> <gloss>the thoroughly established nature of reality</gloss>.

The statement that "it is without affliction and without purification" is because it is pure by nature. The statement that "it is without agitation" is because it is always in a state of meditative equipoise. It is "ineffable" because it is known by personal self-awareness <term>svasamvedana</term>. It is "unspeakable" because it completely transcends sound. It is "utterly inexpressible" because it completely transcends conceptual thought and analytical examination. It is "unobservable" because it is free from all observations of entities as things.

The statement "if one perceives this profound Perfection of Wisdom as a non-entity, that too is the work of Mara <gloss>the Tempter or personification of obstacles</gloss>" refers to the fault of failing to show respect when the Perfection of Wisdom is explained, due to an obsession with the notion of nothingness. The statement "this Perfection of Wisdom is without letters" is because it cannot be spoken or heard. The remaining works of Mara are easy to understand through their respective signs.

Subhuti, when it is said that "this Perfection of Wisdom generates the ten powers of a Tathagata <gloss>One Thus Gone; a Buddha</gloss>," and so forth, it demonstrates that the ultimate Tathagata is generated because the qualities of a Buddha are generated.

Regarding the term **Teacher of the World**, it is explained that the world is shown in eleven ways: showing the world of the aggregates <term>skandha</term> <gloss>the five components of individual existence</gloss>, and the lack of observing a self-nature in any phenomena <unclear>...</unclear>

<summary>This page explains the metaphysical attributes of the Perfection of Wisdom, emphasizing its transcendence of logic, language, and conceptual thought. it defines the Perfection of Wisdom as the source of a Buddha's powers while warning against the nihilistic misconception of reality as a mere non-entity.</summary>
<keywords>Perfection of Wisdom, Prajnaparamita, non-conceptual, Mara, Tathagata, ten powers, emptiness, ineffability, Buddhist logic</keywords>

text:
Entering into the intention, having no doubt regarding one’s own <term>bhūmi</term> <gloss>spiritual level or stage</gloss>, sacrificing even one’s life for the sake of completely upholding the <term>Dharma</term> <gloss>Buddha’s teachings</gloss>, and doing so so that the grasped teachings do not go to waste. Regarding this, the phrase there is no doubt that <term>tathatā</term> <gloss>suchness or reality as it is</gloss> is neither one nor both shows that because of the suchness of all individuals, the <term>Tathāgata</term> <gloss>the Thus-Gone One; the Buddha</gloss> is shown to be singular. The meaning is that whatever is the essence, or the essence of both, is not the essence of suchness.

All phenomena are without aspects, without signs, and without characteristics because suchness has no aspects. Regarding the phrase O Blessed One, if all phenomena lack aspects <note>original: "bhagavan yadi sarvadharmā nirākārāḥ"</note> and so forth, it demonstrates the following: if there are no aspects and no signs, how can the aspects and signs of <term>avaivartika</term> <gloss>the state of non-retrogression or never falling back</gloss> be explained? This is the meaning of the question.

The phrase O Subhūti, a <term>bodhisattva mahāsattva</term> <gloss>great heroic being striving for enlightenment</gloss> who turns back from form <note>original: "rūpād vinivartate"</note> and so forth shows that the very knowledge of the absence of aspects is the sign. This is called turning back from the aspects of form and the signs of form. To know what is to be known means to know the object of knowledge. To see what is to be viewed means to see the view.

The phrase does not regard purity through wonders and auspicious signs refers to the auspiciousness of wonders and miracles created merely by thought. This includes rituals such as bathing, fasting, spiritual engagements, the practices of <term>tīrthika</term> <gloss>non-Buddhist extremists</gloss>, and sacrificial offerings.

All the signs of non-retrogression are easy to understand through conventional terms. Although one becomes non-retrogressive simply by attaining the first <term>bhūmi</term> <gloss>spiritual stage</gloss>, a second type of retrogression pertaining to the eighth stage is also taught. Regarding the terms retrogression and non-retrogression: one is retrogressive because of turning back from the levels of the <term>śrāvaka</term> <gloss>pious hearer</gloss> and <term>pratyekabuddha</term> <gloss>solitary realizer</gloss>. One is non-retrogressive because of not turning back from the level of a Buddha.

<summary>This page explains the signs of a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva, emphasizing that true reality or suchness lacks formal aspects and that spiritual progress involves turning away from mundane rituals and lower spiritual paths.</summary>
<keywords>non-retrogression, suchness, tathatā, bhūmi, signs, Subhūti, Bodhisattva, emptiness of aspects</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
Transforming things just as one wishes is the mastery of action <note>original: "las la dbang ba," Sanskrit: "karmavashitā"</note>. Taking birth in any place of birth, wherever one wishes and exactly as one desires, is the mastery of birth <note>original: "skye ba la dbang ba," Sanskrit: "janmavashitā"</note>. When whatever things one resolves upon are accomplished exactly as intended, this is the mastery of resolve <note>original: "mos pa la dbang ba," Sanskrit: "adhimuktivashitā"</note>. 

When all of one's prayers are fulfilled exactly as desired, this is the mastery of prayer <note>original: "smon lam la dbang ba," Sanskrit: "pranidhānavashitā"</note>. When all necessary miraculous feats are accomplished exactly as one wishes, this is the mastery of miracles <note>original: "rdzu 'phrul la dbang ba," Sanskrit: "riddhivashitā"</note>. Regarding any profound object of knowledge, the ability to understand it instantly whenever one wishes to know it is the mastery of primordial wisdom <note>original: "ye shes la dbang ba," Sanskrit: "jñānavashitā"</note>. Attaining collections of names, collections of phrases, and collections of syllables just as one wishes, and being skilled in correctly arranging all phenomena, is the mastery of dharma <note>original: "chos la dbang ba," Sanskrit: "dharmavashitā"</note>.

Regarding the question, "What are the three ways in which a Thus-Gone One <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>an epithet of the Buddha</gloss> is beyond the need for protection?", these three are easily understood from the main text itself. The three applications of mindfulness, characterized by the absence of attachment and the absence of aversion, are also easily understood. 

The quality of having no forgetfulness <note>original: "bsnyel ba mi mngat ba'i chos nyid"</note> means that whenever and however he acts for the benefit of sentient beings, the Thus-Gone One accomplishes it precisely in that way; this is the quality of never forgetting. 

As for the thirty-two marks of a great man <note>original: "skyes bu chen po'i mtshan," Sanskrit: "mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa"</note>, these are displayed in order to inspire faith in those individuals who take physical form as their standard of measurement. Because of the greatness of their lineage, intention, resolve, prayer, exertion, engagement, perfect accomplishment, wisdom, skillful means, and so forth, the great Bodhisattvas and Buddhas are called "Great Beings." Since they are Great Beings, these marks which express and distinguish them are the marks of a Great Being. Now, through these...

<summary>This page explains the various masteries of a Bodhisattva, such as the masteries of action, birth, and wisdom. It also discusses the Buddha's lack of forgetfulness and the purpose of the thirty-two marks of a Great Being.</summary>
<keywords>ten masteries, vashitā, Tathagata, mindfulness, thirty-two marks, Great Being, mahapurusha</keywords>

text:
<meta>The text discusses the thirty-two major marks of a Great Being, specifically focusing on the Thousand-Spoked Wheel mark found on the palms and soles.</meta>

Regarding the limbs and appendages that manifest on a Great Being: if there were no distinction among them at all, it would be inappropriate to say there are exactly this many, and the number thirty-two would become meaningless. While that is true, based on what has been heard and remembered, the fixed number is taught accordingly, and here as well, it is presented by this very number. 

These marks are presented through four aspects: the brief summary, the explanation, the cause, and the result. 
First is the brief summary. 
Following that, the commentary on those marks is the explanation. 
The mention of past actions <term>karma</term> <gloss>intentional actions from previous lives</gloss> is the cause. 
The mention of the signs is the result.

Regarding the statement "having the mark of a wheel on the palms and soles," there are two types of wheels in the world: the wheel as a weapon, and the wheel that facilitates movement, such as the wheel of a chariot. These appear on both the hands and the feet. 

The past actions <note>original: "sngon gyi las"</note> that cause this are also of two types:
One type is included within the <term>Paramita</term> <gloss>Perfection</gloss> of Ethics, involving the practice of escorting and welcoming one's teachers <term>Guru</term> <gloss>spiritual preceptors</gloss>. As a result of this, the wheel that facilitates movement appears on the soles of the feet. 

The other type is included within the Perfection of Generosity, involving listening to the Dharma, stringing garlands, visiting temples and <term>stupa</term> <gloss>relic monuments</gloss>, and providing attendants. As a result of this, the marks appear on the two palms of the hands. 

Regarding the description "a wheel with a thousand spokes, a rim, and a hub": at the time when these three components are not fully complete, one becomes a Universal Monarch <term>Chakravartin</term> <gloss>wheel-turning king</gloss> through those marks and then enters the religious life. At that time, one does not attain complete awakening. This is exemplified by figures such as King Shankha. However, when all these components are fully complete in every aspect, one attains complete and perfect Buddhahood.

<summary>This page explains the symbolic and karmic origins of the Buddha's thirty-two major marks, specifically the wheel marks on the hands and feet. It distinguishes between the physical marks of a Universal Monarch and those of a fully awakened Buddha.</summary>
<keywords>Thirty-two marks, Great Being, Karma, Paramita, Chakravartin, Thousand-spoked wheel, King Shankha, Buddhahood</keywords>

Regarding the description "a wheel with a thousand spokes, a rim, and a hub": at the time when these three components are not fully complete, one becomes a Universal Monarch <term>Chakravartin</term> <gloss>wheel-turning king</gloss> through those marks and then enters the religious life. At that time, one does not attain complete awakening. This is exemplified by figures such as King Shankha. However, when all these components are fully complete in every aspect, one attains complete and perfect Buddhahood.

<summary>This page explains the symbolic and karmic origins of the Buddha's thirty-two major marks, specifically the wheel marks on the hands and feet. It distinguishes between the physical marks of a Universal Monarch and those of a fully awakened Buddha.</summary>
<keywords>Thirty-two marks, Great Being, Karma, Paramita, Chakravartin, Thousand-spoked wheel, King Shankha, Buddhahood</keywords>

The phrase "incapable" is explained immediately below as being due to the power of objective perception <note>referring to the cognitive tendency to grasp at objects as having inherent existence</note> and therefore lacking in skillful means. The question "How can the Perfection of Generosity be fully embraced?" was asked with the thought that if one gives a gift while focusing on enlightenment, it becomes designated as the "Perfection of Generosity." The statement "one does not practice the Perfection of Generosity through the mode of duality" means that one does not practice by conceptually imagining the duality of the thing to be aimed for—thinking "this is for the sake of enlightenment"—and the person who is aiming.

The question, "Blessed One, if one does not practice the Perfection of Generosity through the mode of duality," asks how roots of virtue can increase if one does not dedicate them for the sake of enlightenment through that dualistic mode. 

The reply, "Subhūti, those who practice within duality <note>The text here clarifies the Buddha's intent</note> cause their virtuous qualities to increase," demonstrates that practicing non-dually is itself the cause for the increase of roots of virtue, whereas practicing with duality is not. This is what is called the "Perfection of Wisdom that practices without duality." 

Furthermore, the practice of the six perfections through skillful means, the practice of the factors of enlightenment, the practice of the qualities of a Buddha, and the remaining unshakable from the essential nature of a Bodhisattva's praise, are easily understood from the main text itself.

Regarding the four conceptualizations, beginning with "Is one able to realize perfectly complete enlightenment through the non-existence of entities?", there is no teacher for this because such conceptualizations are not suitable to be applied to perfectly complete enlightenment. To see equality in such a way that it is neither an entity nor a non-entity is called "clear realization." This is like an illusion; that which is conceptually constructed <term>parikalpita</term> <gloss>the imagined nature</gloss> is not the form of an actual entity, yet it is not absolutely non-existent like a rabbit's horns <unclear>one line of text regarding the nature of existence and non-existence</unclear>

text:
The action is truly singular, which means that worldly beings do not understand reality exactly as it is. Because they lack this understanding, they develop a strong attachment to things and accumulate karma, thereby grasping at and clinging to the karmic maturation of form <term>rupa</term> and the other aggregates.

Due to the cause of clinging, they continue to exist within the cycle of becoming <term>bhava</term>. This is the meaning of the statement that they will not be liberated from suffering. The nature of emptiness does not cause form to be disturbed by thinking of it as either empty or not empty. This means that form is not disturbed by the perception of duality because emptiness and form are non-dual. Among these things, there is no such nature that creates a disturbance by thinking, "This is form" and "This is emptiness." This refers to the absence of an inherent essence or self-nature in any thing or entity.

The statement that a <term>bodhisattva mahasattva</term> <gloss>great heroic being of awakening</gloss> does not practice by making a dual distinction between awakening <term>bodhi</term> and form means that they do not treat awakening as a dualistic concept while practicing with regard to form. The phrase means that when it is said a bodhisattva practices toward awakening, they do not treat the bodhisattva and the awakening as two separate things while practicing with regard to form.

Subhuti, the statement that a bodhisattva mahasattva does not think "I am practicing toward awakening and form" means they do not practice with regard to form by creating a duality through the thought "I am practicing toward awakening." The phrase "practicing with grasping" means practicing with signs <term>nimitta</term> <gloss>mental constructs or conceptual characteristics</gloss>.

The phrase "abiding in the nature of form" means abiding in the emptiness of form. Furthermore, the statement "by relying on the designations of worldly conventions" demonstrates that even unexcelled, perfect awakening does not exist from the perspective of ultimate truth <term>paramartha</term>. The phrase "practices those very phenomena" means that although the act of giving <term>dana</term> and the giver and so forth are not observed as having independent existence, the bodhisattva still practices those very acts of giving and so on.

Worldly Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahasattva practice the perfection of wisdom <term>prajnaparamita</term>? <note>The text breaks here mid-question.</note>

<summary>This page explains the non-duality of form and emptiness, emphasizing that bodhisattvas avoid conceptual grasping and dualistic distinctions during their practice. It clarifies that while phenomena like awakening and giving are designated conventionally, they lack inherent existence in ultimate truth.</summary>
<keywords>non-duality, emptiness, bodhisattva, form, grasping, conventional truth, ultimate truth, Subhuti, perfection of wisdom</keywords>

text:
One does not attain realization through duality. Nor does one attain realization through non-duality. This means that if one were to perceive any entity, whether <term>conditioned</term> <gloss>products of causes and conditions</gloss> or <term>unconditioned</term> <gloss>phenomena like space or nirvana that do not arise from causes</gloss>, then realization would occur through duality. If things were utterly non-existent, like the horns of a rabbit, then realization would occur through non-duality. Therefore, reversing those two modes is the thorough realization of <term>equanimity</term> <gloss>the essential sameness of all things</gloss>; this is what is shown to be realization.

The phrase "inexpressible" refers to that which is neither an object of verbal expression nor a subject of thorough description, yet Subhuti, it is spoken of in the terms of worldly convention. The statement "The Tathagata <gloss>One Gone Thus; the Buddha</gloss> has perfectly awakened to the Dharma" refers to the ultimate transformation of the basis. Because one dwells in equanimity, having abandoned all conceptual construction and <term>proliferated thought</term> <gloss>the tendency of the mind to elaborate on perceptions</gloss>, there is nothing even to be known. Since no object to be known is seen, what is there to be perfectly awakened to? This is what is being shown.

The question "Blessed One, what is this called 'equanimity' regarding phenomena that are non-existent by nature?" reflects the thought that if phenomena existed, then equanimity would also exist. The reply, "Subhuti, herein that itself is equanimity," means that the equanimity of phenomena that are non-existent by nature is itself their non-existent nature. This is because even the conceptualization of them as entities has been abandoned.

The phrase "Subhuti, the equanimity of phenomena is not even the sphere of the Tathagata" means that the equanimity of phenomena does not become the sphere of anyone at all. Even the Tathagata does not perceive the essence of the equanimity of phenomena as an object. Regarding the phrase "In the equanimity of phenomena, ordinary childish beings..." and so on, the equanimity of the Dharma is the same for ordinary childish beings, for all noble ones, and for the Tathagata. It does not waver from the equanimity of phenomena, yet the arrangement of phenomena <unclear>one line of text not transcribed</unclear>

text:
By eliminating the perception of objects and cultivating a perception that is naturally and completely pure, one attains perfect awakening through the contemplation of space itself. Furthermore, through the subsequent primordial wisdom <term>jnana</term> <gloss>highest cognitive faculty</gloss> attained after that awakening, one perfectly realizes the four noble truths. Having manifested the qualities of a Buddha, one then uses conventional contemplation <note>relative or mundane mental engagement</note> to provide prophecies regarding the three categories <note>or "lineages"</note> of sentient beings. Therefore, because one practices and awakens precisely through non-apprehension <note>the state of not grasping at inherent existence</note>, there is no fault or error. This is the essential meaning.

When the text asks: How does the Blessed One, the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>Thus Gone One</gloss>, the Arhat, the perfectly completed Buddha, and so forth, develop meditations and clairvoyance if sentient beings possess the nature of non-existence? And how are these beings then given prophecies? This was the question asked by the Elder <note>referring to Subhuti</note>. 

In response, the Blessed One said: Subhuti, if desires and sinful, unwholesome states, and so forth, exist as they do, it is because everything is established through the nature of non-existence, and not otherwise. Thus, because desires and unwholesome states have the nature of non-existence, prophecies can be given. Meditations can be generated. 

Regarding the terms "existence," "non-existence," "self-existence," or "other-existence": these do not refer to the nature of objects as they are mentally constructed. Nor do they refer to a state of absolute non-existence like the horns of a rabbit. They do not exist in any sense of an inherent self-nature, nor do they exist as some "other" nature. This is what is being taught. 

Regarding the question: How is it that there is a gradual practice, a gradual training, and a gradual application? This refers to the following:

<summary>This page explains how spiritual attainment and the guidance of beings are possible only because all phenomena lack inherent existence. It clarifies that emptiness is not total nothingness but the very basis that allows for meditation and awakening.</summary>
<keywords>non-apprehension, four noble truths, emptiness, non-existence, gradual practice, Subhuti, Buddha nature</keywords>

text:
At that time, the state of remaining in the essence of the <term>unutterable</term> <gloss>indescribable by words</gloss> and the <term>non-conceptual</term> <gloss>free from discursive thought</gloss> is called the form of the nature of phenomena <note>original: "chos nyid kyi gzug" / dharmatā-rūpa</note>. Regarding the phrase lack of nature <note>original: "ngo bo nyid med pa" / niḥsvabhāvatā</note>, this refers to the lack of nature of the <term>imagined</term> <gloss>the mentally constructed or conceptualized nature</gloss>. The selflessness of phenomena means the absence of an inherent essence within phenomena.

<term>Suchness</term> <gloss>tathatā</gloss> refers to the aspect that is unerring and non-distorted. The <term>ultimate reality</term> <gloss>bhūtakoṭi</gloss> refers to reaching the limit of that very aspect. The same logic should be applied to feelings and the other aggregates <note>the five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness</note>.

Maitreya, the statement that imagined form should be viewed as non-substantial is because it is utterly non-existent. Regarding the statement that the <term>dependent form</term> <gloss>paratantra-rūpa</gloss> should be viewed as existing substantially because conceptualization exists substantially, this means it exists in a relative or conventional sense. It is considered a substance because it undergoes destruction in the manner of conditioned things and possesses the qualities of form. Therefore, it is explained as having a conceptual existence and being a substance.

The statement that it does not function independently is said because its nature is dependent on other factors. That which is the form of the nature of phenomena is neither substantially non-existent nor substantially existent. The phrase distinguished by the ultimate refers to the form of the nature of phenomena. Because it exists as an unutterable essence, it is incorrect to say it does not exist; therefore, it is not substantially non-existent. However, because it does not exist in the manner of a conceptually constructed thing, it is incorrect to say it exists; therefore, it is not substantially existent. Thus, by abandoning the two extremes <note>the extremes of eternalism/existence and nihilism/non-existence</note>, the Middle Way is shown.

The phrase distinguished by the ultimate is a synonym for the ultimate nature. The word distinguished conveys the meaning of essence. This same application should be made up to the final qualities of a Buddha.

After mentioning the three characteristics according to the three natures in this way, the Noble Maitreya spoke to introduce the section on the characteristic of non-duality. In this context of establishing the summary of the Perfection of Wisdom, twenty-eight questions were presented as follows:

<keywords>Three Natures, Middle Way, emptiness, suchness, Maitreya, non-duality, ultimate reality, dependent nature, imagined nature</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>completing and attaining the meditative concentration <term>samadhi</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss> that accomplishes omniscience. One also manifests the accomplishment of acting for the benefit of all sentient beings, as far as the world extends.

The Commentary on the Noble Dhāranī of the Six Gates <note>original: "Arya-ṣaṇmukhi-dhāraṇī-vyākhyāna"</note>, composed by the Master Vasubandhu <note>a prominent 4th-century Indian Buddhist scholar and philosopher</note>, is complete.

# The Commentary on the Noble Four Dharmas
<note>original: "Arya-caturdharma-vyākhyāna"</note>

Homage to Mañjuśrī in youthful form.

Why was this sūtra composed, which states: "A Bodhisattva, a great being, should not give up these four dharmas <gloss>qualities or principles</gloss> even for the sake of his life, for as long as he lives"?

It was composed to correctly teach those who are confused about the methods for attaining unexcelled enlightenment after having correctly entered the Great Vehicle <term>Mahāyāna</term>. It is also to cause the heedless to correctly hold these principles, to correctly encourage those who are discouraged, and to correctly delight those who have entered the path.

The number four is mentioned to avoid the concern that the teachings are too extensive, which might cause some to be unwilling to listen. By stating the number, they can be easily remembered. Furthermore, because patience and gentleness, which appear below, have the same purpose, they are not differentiated.

Although there are many categories for those who have correctly entered the Great Vehicle, two names <note>Bodhisattva and Mahāsattva</note> are mentioned for three reasons: through aspiration, through application, and through realization.

How is it through aspiration? One is called a Bodhisattva because of aspiration toward profound objects of knowledge. One is called a Great Being <term>Mahāsattva</term> because of aspiration toward great power.

How is it through application? Because of striving for the sake of one's own unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and for the sake of completely protecting all sentient beings from suffering.

How is it through realization? Because enlightenment is realized through two strengths. What are these two? The strength of intelligence and the strength of diligence. One cannot realize enlightenment through ignorance or through minor diligence. For as long as one lives...

<summary>This page concludes Vasubandhu's commentary on the Six Gates and begins his commentary on the Four Dharmas Sūtra. It explains the purpose of the text and provides etymological reasons for the titles Bodhisattva and Mahāsattva.</summary>
<keywords>Vasubandhu, Four Dharmas, Bodhisattva, Mahāsattva, Mahayana, diligence, enlightenment</keywords>

The Commentary on the Noble Dhāranī of the Six Gates <note>original: "Arya-ṣaṇmukhi-dhāraṇī-vyākhyāna"</note>, composed by the Master Vasubandhu <note>a prominent 4th-century Indian Buddhist scholar and philosopher</note>, is complete.

# The Commentary on the Noble Four Dharmas
<note>original: "Arya-caturdharma-vyākhyāna"</note>

Homage to Mañjuśrī in youthful form.

Why was this sūtra composed, which states: "A Bodhisattva, a great being, should not give up these four dharmas <gloss>qualities or principles</gloss> even for the sake of his life, for as long as he lives"?

It was composed to correctly teach those who are confused about the methods for attaining unexcelled enlightenment after having correctly entered the Great Vehicle <term>Mahāyāna</term>. It is also to cause the heedless to correctly hold these principles, to correctly encourage those who are discouraged, and to correctly delight those who have entered the path.

The number four is mentioned to avoid the concern that the teachings are too extensive, which might cause some to be unwilling to listen. By stating the number, they can be easily remembered. Furthermore, because patience and gentleness, which appear below, have the same purpose, they are not differentiated.

Although there are many categories for those who have correctly entered the Great Vehicle, two names <note>Bodhisattva and Mahāsattva</note> are mentioned for three reasons: through aspiration, through application, and through realization.

How is it through aspiration? One is called a Bodhisattva because of aspiration toward profound objects of knowledge. One is called a Great Being <term>Mahāsattva</term> because of aspiration toward great power.

How is it through application? Because of striving for the sake of one's own unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and for the sake of completely protecting all sentient beings from suffering.

How is it through realization? Because enlightenment is realized through two strengths. What are these two? The strength of intelligence and the strength of diligence. One cannot realize enlightenment through ignorance or through minor diligence. For as long as one lives...

<summary>This page concludes Vasubandhu's commentary on the Six Gates and begins his commentary on the Four Dharmas Sūtra. It explains the purpose of the text and provides etymological reasons for the titles Bodhisattva and Mahāsattva.</summary>
<keywords>Vasubandhu, Four Dharmas, Bodhisattva, Mahāsattva, Mahayana, diligence, enlightenment</keywords>

text:
The phrase "never to give them up in the meantime" indicates that one should engage in these practices continuously. The phrase "even at the cost of one's life" indicates that they should be performed with great devotion.

One might ask: why are there four qualities? Why are they neither fewer nor more? 

There are four qualities that create obstacles to the accumulations of <term>bodhi</term> <gloss>enlightenment</gloss>. Thus, there are four qualities as their remedies. 

What are the four qualities that create obstacles? They are: 
1. Lacking the aspiration for the goal.
2. Not knowing the methods.
3. Not being oriented toward sentient beings.
4. Being oriented toward worldly objects.

Alternatively, there are another four:
1. Not undertaking the work.
2. Undertaking the work incorrectly.
3. Abandoning the work once started.
4. Being distracted while working.

Furthermore, there are four qualities that are conducive to the accumulations of enlightenment. There are four because they serve as the basis for those accumulations. What are the four qualities conducive to the accumulations of enlightenment? They are:
1. Desiring instruction and advice.
2. Obtaining those instructions.
3. Being a fit vessel for them.
4. Accomplishing them.

Again, there are four:
1. Having the aspiration for the goal.
2. Knowing the methods.
3. Practice <note>The text explains that practice is twofold: ripening sentient beings and ripening the qualities of a Buddha</note>.

There are yet another four:
1. Not abandoning <term>samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of existence</gloss>.
2. Remaining untainted by afflictions while within it.
3. Gathering sentient beings.
4. Purifying one's diligence.

Furthermore, through four causes one crosses the path that is difficult to travel. These are:
1. The desire to go.
2. Knowing the path.
3. Not being discouraged by hardships.
4. Acting with conscientiousness.

In this way, one crosses the path of cyclic existence. There are four because they serve as the basis for that crossing.

Why is someone who strives for the enlightenment of a <term>shravaka</term> <gloss>pious hearer</gloss> or a <term>pratyekabuddha</term> <gloss>solitary realizer</gloss> not called a <term>bodhisattva</term> <gloss>enlightenment being</gloss>? Because the name is established for that which has nothing superior to it, just as with the sun <note>original: "snang byed", the bringer of light</note>.

To summarize the meaning: in this <term>sutra</term> <gloss>scripture</gloss>, the Blessed One has fully shown the appropriate actions for those who have correctly entered the Great Vehicle <note>Mahayana</note>, and how their results will not be lost.

The Explanation of the Noble Four Qualities composed by the Master Vasubandhu is complete.

<summary>This page concludes Vasubandhu’s commentary on the Four Qualities Sutra by categorizing the spiritual obstacles and remedies into groups of four. It emphasizes the unique status of the Bodhisattva path compared to other Buddhist paths and confirms that correct practice leads to certain results.</summary>
<keywords>Vasubandhu, Four Qualities, Bodhisattva, Samsara, Accumulations of Enlightenment, Mahayana, Buddhist Philosophy</keywords>

text:
{D4377}
In the language of India: <term>Arya Bhadracarya Pranidhana Raja</term> <gloss>The Noble King of Prayers for Excellent Conduct</gloss>
In the language of Tibet: <term>Phags pa bzang po spyod pa'i smon lam gyi rgyal po</term>

I pay homage to the youthful and noble Manjushri <note>the bodhisattva of wisdom</note>.

To all the lions among men <note>an epithet for Buddhas</note>, those who have gone before in the three times <note>past, present, and future</note> throughout the worlds of the ten directions, I pay homage to every one of them without exception, with body, speech, and a devoted mind.

By the power of this prayer for excellent conduct, I manifest all the Victorious Ones <note>Buddhas</note> clearly in my mind. With bodies as numerous as the atoms of the world, I bow deeply and pay homage to all the Victorious Ones.

Upon every single atom are Buddhas as numerous as all atoms, each sitting in the midst of the sons of Buddhas <note>bodhisattvas</note>. In this way, I am convinced that the entire sphere of phenomena <note>the <term>dharmadhatu</term></note> is entirely filled with Victorious Ones.

With an ocean of inexhaustible praise, through the sounds of an ocean of melodic parts, I express the qualities of all the Victorious Ones and praise all those who have gone to bliss <note>the <term>Sugatas</term></note>.

With the finest flowers and the finest garlands, with music, scented ointments, and supreme parasols, with the best lamps and the finest incense, I make offerings to those Victorious Ones.

With the finest garments and supreme fragrances, with powdered incense piled high as Mount Meru <note>the central mountain of Buddhist cosmology</note>, and with all kinds of supreme and extraordinary arrays, I make offerings to those Victorious Ones.

Whatever offerings are unsurpassed and vast, I have faith in them for all the Victorious Ones. Through the power of my faith in excellent conduct, I pay homage and make offerings to all the Victorious Ones.

Whatever negative actions I have committed through the influence of attachment, hatred, and ignorance, whether by body, speech, or likewise by mind, I individually confess every one of them.

In the merit of all the Victorious Ones of the ten directions, the sons of Buddhas, the solitary realizers <note><term>Pratyekabuddhas</term></note>, those in training, those beyond training <note><term>Arhats</term></note>, and all wandering beings, I rejoice.

To those who are the lights of the worlds in the ten directions <unclear>...</unclear>

<summary>This page contains the opening verses of the King of Prayers, a fundamental Mahayana text focusing on the seven-limb practice including homage, offering, and confession. It establishes the practitioner's intent to honor all Buddhas across time and space.</summary>
<keywords>King of Prayers, Samantabhadra, Bhadracarya, homage, offerings, confession, seven-limb practice, Manjushri, Bodhisattva conduct</keywords>

text:
The lamps of the world <note>a poetic epithet for Buddhas</note>, through the stages of enlightenment, have attained non-attachment and Buddhahood. I urge all those protectors to turn the supreme wheel of Dharma. To those who intend to demonstrate the final passing into nirvana, I pray with palms pressed together: please remain for as many eons as there are atoms in the world, for the sake of the benefit and happiness of all wandering beings.

Whatever slight virtue I have accumulated through prostrating, offering, confessing, rejoicing, urging, and praying, I dedicate it all toward the attainment of enlightenment.

May offerings be made to the Buddhas of the past and to those residing in the worlds of the ten directions. May those who have not yet arrived quickly fulfill their intentions and come as Buddhas through the stages of enlightenment. May all the world realms in the ten directions become vast and completely pure. May they be filled with victors who have gone to the foot of the king of trees <note>the Bodhi tree where enlightenment is attained</note> and by the sons of the Buddhas <note>Bodhisattvas</note>.

May all the many sentient beings in the ten directions always be healthy and happy. May the meaningful Dharma goals of all beings be met, and may their hopes be fulfilled. As I practice the conduct of enlightenment, may I remember my births in all states of existence. In all successive lives, through death, transition, and birth, may I always renounce worldly life <note>take monastic vows</note>.

Following in the footsteps of all the victors, may I bring the <term>Samantabhadra-charya</term> <gloss>Conduct of Excellence</gloss> to perfection. May I always practice a flawless and stainless moral conduct, never declining and remaining free from faults.

In the languages of the gods, the <term>nagas</term> <gloss>serpent-beings</gloss>, and the <term>yakshas</term> <gloss>nature spirits</gloss>, in the languages of <term>kumbhandas</term> <gloss>ghoulish spirits</gloss> and of humans, in as many sounds as there are of all wandering beings, I shall teach the Dharma in all their tongues.

Through that, may I be diligent in the perfections and never forget the <term>bodhicitta</term> <gloss>the mind of enlightenment</gloss>. May whatever misdeeds act as obscurations be completely purified without exception. May I be liberated from karma, mental afflictions, and the works of demons <note>the four Maras</note>, and in all worldly wanderings...

<keywords>Samantabhadra-charya, dedication of merit, Bodhicitta, seven-limb prayer, rebirth, multilingual teaching</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>in all worlds, just as a lotus is unsullied by water, and like the sun and moon move unhindered through the sky, I shall act. Throughout the entire extent and all directions of the worlds, I shall thoroughly pacify the suffering of the lower realms. I shall place all beings in happiness and act for the benefit of every living creature. I shall complete the conduct of enlightenment and engage in harmony with the activities of sentient beings. I shall demonstrate the conduct of excellence <note>original: "bhadracarya", referring to the practice of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra</note> and practice it throughout all future eons.

May I always be in the company of those whose actions are similar to my own. Through body, speech, and also mind, may our actions and aspirations be as one. May I always meet those friends who wish to help me and who thoroughly demonstrate the conduct of excellence. May I never disappoint them. 

I shall always behold the Victorious Ones <gloss>Buddhas</gloss>, the Protectors surrounded by the Sons of the Buddha <gloss>Bodhisattvas</gloss>. Without ever growing weary throughout all future eons, I shall make vast offerings to them. I shall uphold the holy Dharma <gloss>teachings</gloss> of the Victorious Ones and cause the conduct of enlightenment to appear everywhere. I shall purify the conduct of excellence and practice it throughout all future eons.

While wandering through all the states of existence <note>original: "bhava", the cycle of rebirth</note>, I shall find inexhaustible merit and wisdom. May I become an inexhaustible treasury of all qualities, including skillful means, wisdom, meditative absorption, and liberation.

Upon a single atom are worlds as numerous as atoms; in those worlds sit inconceivable Buddhas in the midst of the Sons of the Buddha. I shall behold them as I practice the conduct of enlightenment. In this way, in every direction without exception, even in the space of a single hair, there are oceans of Buddhas of the three times, oceans of worlds, and oceans of eons; I shall engage in their practice.

With the sounds of the ocean of branches of a single speech, which possesses the pure melody of all the Victorious Ones, and with melodies that accord with the intentions of all beings, I shall always engage with the speech of the Buddha. The Victorious Ones who depart in the three times <note>the past, present, and future</note>

<keywords>Samantabhadra, Bodhisattva path, Conduct of Excellence, Merit and Wisdom, Infinite Buddhas, Three Times, Pure Speech</keywords>

text:
<meta>This text is a section of the Samantabhadra Charya Pranidhana, popularly known as the King of Aspiration Prayers, found within the Derge Tengyur. It focuses on the bodhisattva's mastery over time, space, and spiritual powers.</meta>

All these things are pure. Through the way the <term>Chakra</term> <gloss>Wheel of Dharma</gloss> is turned, 
their melodic speech is inexhaustible; 
by the power of my intellect, I shall also enter into them.
I shall enter into all future eons,
and in a single instant, I shall also enter them.

Whatever measurement of time exists in the three periods of the eons,
I shall engage with them through a fraction of a single moment.
Those lions among men <note>a title for the Buddhas</note> who travel through the three times,
I shall behold them in a single instant.
Constantly, within their field of activity,
I shall enter by the power of liberation that is like an illusion.

Furthermore, the array of pure realms of the three times,
I shall manifest even upon a single atom.
In that way, throughout all directions without exception,
I shall enter into the array of the realms of the Conquerors.
Whosoever are the future lamps of the world <note>the future Buddhas</note>,
they will successively attain enlightenment and turn the wheel.

They demonstrate the ultimate peace of <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>the state beyond suffering</gloss>;
I shall go into the presence of all those protectors.
Through the powers of swift miraculous emanations,
the powers of the vehicle which is a door in every direction,
the powers of conducting virtuous activities everywhere,
and the powers of love that pervades all;

Through the powers of merit that is universally virtuous,
the powers of primordial wisdom that is free from attachment,
and the powers of analytical wisdom, skillful means, and meditative concentration,
I shall perfectly accomplish the powers of enlightenment.
I shall completely purify the powers of <term>Karma</term> <gloss>intentional action and its results</gloss>,
and I shall utterly destroy the powers of the <term>Kleshas</term> <gloss>disturbing emotions</gloss>.

I shall render the powers of the <term>Maras</term> <gloss>demonic obstructions</gloss> powerless,
and I shall complete the power of the Conduct of the Good <note>refers to the Samantabhadra's conduct</note>.
I shall purify oceans of realms,
and I shall liberate oceans of sentient beings.
I shall perceive oceans of <term>Dharmas</term> <gloss>phenomena and teachings</gloss>,
and I shall realize oceans of primordial wisdom.

I shall purify oceans of conduct,
and I shall fulfill oceans of aspirational prayers.
I shall make offerings to oceans of Buddhas,
and I shall practice without weariness throughout oceans of eons.

text:
As for the specific prayers for the conduct of the enlightened ones, those Victors who have gone before: through the conduct of the <term>Samantabhadra</term> <gloss>the Universal Goodness</gloss>, after I attain the awakening of a Buddha, I shall fulfill them all completely without exception.

The eldest son of all the Victors, whose name is called <term>Samantabhadra</term> <gloss>Ever-Excellent</gloss>; in order to practice in a way equal to that wise one, I dedicate all these virtues. 

May my body, speech, and mind also be completely pure; may my conduct be pure, and the realms be entirely pure. Just as the wise one is in his excellent dedication, may I also become equal to him.

In order to practice the excellent virtue in all ways, I shall practice the prayer of <term>Manjushri</term> <gloss>Gentle Glory, the Bodhisattva of Wisdom</gloss>. Without becoming weary throughout all future eons, I shall fulfill his activities completely without exception.

May my conduct be without any limit. May my qualities also be beyond measure. By remaining within this limitless conduct, I shall come to know all their miraculous transformations.

To whatever extent the limits of space reach, the limits of sentient beings are likewise without exception. To whatever extent <term>karma</term> <gloss>actions and their effects</gloss> and <term>kleshas</term> <gloss>mental afflictions</gloss> reach their limit, so shall be the limit of my prayers.

Whoever takes the infinite realms of the ten directions, adorns them with jewels, and offers them to the Victors—and even offers the supreme joys of gods and humans for eons as numerous as the atoms of those realms—if they should hear this King of Dedications and, being greatly inspired toward supreme awakening, feel faith for even a single moment, they will gain a merit far more supreme and holy than that.

Whoever makes this Prayer of Excellent Conduct will abandon all lower realms of existence. Such a person has abandoned negative friends and will quickly see <term>Amitabha</term> <gloss>the Buddha of Boundless Light</gloss>. 

They will gain great findings and live in happiness. Even in this human life, things will go well for them. In a short time, they will become just like <term>Samantabhadra</term> himself.

Whatever sins of the five inexpiable crimes <note>The five most serious sins in Buddhism: killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an Arhat, drawing the blood of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Sangha.</note> were committed under the power of ignorance, by reciting this Excellent Conduct <unclear>it is purified.</unclear>

<summary>This passage continues the Prayer of Samantabhadra, emphasizing the dedication of merit and the immense spiritual benefits of reciting the prayer. It promises the purification of even the heaviest sins and the eventual attainment of Buddhahood through the imitation of Samantabhadra and Manjushri.</summary>
<keywords>Samantabhadra, Manjushri, Bodhisattva Path, Dedication of Merit, Amitabha, Five Inexpiable Crimes, Universal Goodness, Enlightenment</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
If spoken, one will quickly and completely become purified without exception. One will possess primordial wisdom, a physical form, and the marks of excellence, along with the proper family and complexion. Many demons and <term>tirthikas</term> <gloss>non-Buddhist extremists</gloss> will be unable to overcome such a person. They will be honored throughout all the three worlds.

They will quickly go to the foot of the king of Bodhi trees. Having gone there, they will sit for the benefit of sentient beings, attain enlightenment as a Buddha, and turn the wheel of Dharma. They will subdue all the demons together with their hosts.

The ripening result for anyone who holds, teaches, or reads this Prayer of Excellent Conduct is known only by the Buddha. Do not have any doubt regarding supreme enlightenment.

Just as the heroic Manjushri knows, and Samantabhadra does as well, I will train myself following after them and dedicate all these virtues completely. With that dedication which is praised as supreme by all the Victors who have departed in the three times, I also dedicate all these roots of my virtue for the sake of excellent conduct.

When the time comes for me to die, by clearing away all obscurations and perceiving Amitabha <note>original: "Snang ba mtha' yas", the Buddha of Infinite Light</note> directly, may I go to that realm of Sukhavati <note>original: "Bde ba can", the Land of Bliss</note>.

Having gone there, may all these prayers be manifest without exception. I will fulfill them all entirely and act for the benefit of sentient beings as long as the world remains.

In that excellent and joyful mandala of the Victor, born from a most beautiful and holy lotus, may I receive a prophecy directly from the Victor Amitabha. Having received that prophecy there, may I bring much benefit to sentient beings in the ten directions through the power of the mind, using hundreds of millions of numerous emanations.

Through whatever slight virtue I have accumulated by reciting the Prayer of Excellent Conduct, may all the virtuous prayers of beings be accomplished in a single instant.

<summary>This page contains the concluding verses of the Prayer of Excellent Conduct, focusing on the benefits of the practice and the aspiration to be reborn in the pure land of Amitabha.</summary>
<keywords>Samantabhadra, Amitabha, Sukhavati, dedication of merit, Bodhisattva vow, enlightenment, Manjushri</keywords>

text:
What could be said to bring about auspicious goodness?
If those words are heard,
the <term>Relative of the World</term> <gloss>an epithet for the Buddha</gloss> has commanded:
Listen to that which I always recite
to bring about my own auspicious goodness.
Whatever wondrous and vast supreme jewels exist
in this world, in others, or in the higher realms,
none can ever compare, in number or in measure,
to the jewel of the Perfect Buddha.
This wonder is truly marvelous and immeasurable.
The jewel of the Perfect Buddha is the supreme thing in the world.
Since these words of mine are the supreme truth,
through this truth, may there be great auspicious goodness.

The peaceful cessation, the nectar that is truly exquisite,
which the Sage of the <term>Shakyas</term> <gloss>the Buddha's clan</gloss> realized in meditative absorption,
there is nothing comparable to that <term>Dharma</term> <gloss>the Buddhist teachings</gloss>.
If one realizes it, there will be no more suffering from that point on.
This wonder is truly marvelous and immeasurable.
The jewel of the Sublime Dharma is the supreme thing in the world.
Since these words of mine are the supreme truth,
through this truth, may there be great auspicious goodness.

Those whom the Victorious One described as the eight types of persons,
they comprise the four pairs of noble beings.
Those worthy of offerings are extremely rare upon this earth.
Giving to them results in immeasurable merit.
This wonder is truly marvelous and immeasurable.
The jewel of the <term>Sangha</term> <gloss>the spiritual community</gloss> is the supreme thing in the world.
Since these words of mine are the supreme truth,
through this truth, may there be great auspicious goodness.

The sublime one, the chief, the bestower of the supreme and exquisite,
the supreme light, the hero, the sublime supreme dwelling,
the supreme wisdom, the highest of the high.
The Blessed One alone is the knower of the supreme among all things.
This wonder is truly marvelous and immeasurable.
The jewel of the Perfect Buddha is the supreme thing in the world.
Since these words of mine are the supreme truth,
through this truth, may there be great auspicious goodness.

That supreme concentration which is without interruption,
which the infinite, wise <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>the Thus-Gone One, the Buddha</gloss> described,
the stable and blissful concentration compared to a diamond,
there is no concentration equal to that concentration.
This wonder is truly marvelous and immeasurable.
The jewel of concentration is the supreme thing in the world.
Since these words of mine are the supreme truth,
through this truth, may there be great auspicious goodness.

Just as a door bolt <note>The text breaks here at the start of a new metaphorical comparison.</note>

text:
Firm and most firm, like a pillar unmoved by the four great winds; so is the wise one who remains seeing the <term>Four Truths</term> <gloss>the fundamental principles of Buddhism regarding suffering and its cessation</gloss>. Worldly speakers do not sway such a person here. This is a wonder, most marvelous and immeasurable. The Jewel of the <term>Sangha</term> <gloss>the spiritual community</gloss> is the supreme of the world. Just as this of mine is the supreme truth, by this truth may there be great well-being.

The conqueror of all, the omniscient who sees all; the one possessing all knowledge and all powers. The supreme of all who has grasped the holy and is free from all attachments. This omniscient intention is the unique <term>Bhagavan</term> <gloss>the Blessed One or Buddha</gloss>. This is a wonder, most marvelous and immeasurable. The Jewel of the perfect Buddha is the supreme of the world. Just as this of mine is the supreme truth, by this truth may there be great well-being.

It stops existence, is immovable and unchanging. Faultless and completely liberated from all fears. Utterly ceased, excellent, and definitive in its emergence. Perfectly stainless, peaceful, and not to be stolen by the intellect. This is a wonder, most marvelous and immeasurable. The Jewel of the <term>Dharma</term> <gloss>the sacred teachings</gloss> is the supreme of the world. Just as this of mine is the supreme truth, by this truth may there be great well-being.

The conscientious ones who see the truths that reveal suffering and bestow happiness, those who are without doubt regarding the Jewels of Truth, they shall not take an eighth birth <note>referring to the 'stream-enterer' who is destined to reach enlightenment within seven lifetimes</note>. This is a wonder, most marvelous and immeasurable. The Jewel of the Sangha is the supreme of the world. Just as this of mine is the supreme truth, by this truth may there be great well-being.

Knowing the ultimate truth, the supreme among the holy. Knowing the superior and the non-superior, striving for the ultimate meaning. Realizing the holy through one's own mind, not to be led away by others. The supreme protector of those in extreme suffering. This is a wonder, most marvelous and immeasurable. The Jewel of the perfect Buddha is the supreme of the world. Just as this of mine is the supreme truth, by this truth may there be great well-being.

Having generated aspiration and becoming endowed with <term>yoga</term> <gloss>spiritual practice</gloss>, always striving in the teaching of <term>Gautama</term> <gloss>the historical Buddha</gloss> and being thoroughly liberated. Those who are not led by others touch that pure field <unclear>...</unclear>

text:
This will not be counted among those things touched.
It is an immeasurable and most marvelous wonder:
The Precious Community <note>original: "dge 'dun rin chen", referring to the Sangha</note> is the supreme in the world.
By the supreme truth of these words of mine,
May there be great well-being through this truth!
If one has seen the truth and spoken it, even if some sin
Has been committed on the path,
It is not appropriate to conceal it;
Because this nature of things <term>dharmata</term> <gloss>the intrinsic nature of reality</gloss> remains unmoving.
It is an immeasurable and most marvelous wonder:
The Precious Community is the supreme in the world.
By the supreme truth of these words of mine,
May there be great well-being through this truth!
In all the worlds including the realms of the gods,
There is none superior or equal to the Buddha.
He is the unsurpassed teacher of gods and men,
The supreme teacher, the caravan leader, and the physician.
It is an immeasurable and most marvelous wonder:
The Precious Perfect Buddha is the supreme in the world.
By the supreme truth of these words of mine,
May there be great well-being through this truth!
In the first month of summer, the Sage <note>referring to the Buddha, Shakyamuni</note>
Found the supreme Dharma in the forest groves.
There is none superior or equal to that Dharma.
This will not be counted among those things touched.
It is an immeasurable and most marvelous wonder:
The Precious Sublime Dharma is the supreme in the world.
By the supreme truth of these words of mine,
May there be great well-being through this truth!
Sins are withered and exhausted, and no new ones are made.
Without the disease of infectious fever, one is fearless and free from sorrow.
With the root ceased, existence is no longer produced;
The teaching will burn bright like a lamp.
It is an immeasurable and most marvelous wonder:
The Precious Community is the supreme in the world.
By the supreme truth of these words of mine,
May there be great well-being through this truth!

The Verses of Well-being Requested by a Deity are complete.

{D4401} In the language of India: <term>Svastayana-gatha</term> <gloss>Verses of Well-being</gloss>.
In the language of Tibet: <term>Bde legs su gyur pa'i tshigs su bcad pa</term>.
Homage to the All-Knowing One!
A certain deity approached
The Presence of the Leader of the World,
And asked: "What is that
Which is always well-being?"

text:
<meta>This page provides a philosophical commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom, likely from a sub-commentary in the Tengyur. It focuses on the transcendence of duality and the conceptualization of phenomena like form.</meta>

Through such means, one is disciplined, and by attaining <term>siddhi</term> <gloss>accomplishment</gloss>, the characteristics of abiding in discipline are shown. This discipline of the noble Dharma is known as the Perfection of Wisdom <note>original: "Prajnaparamita"</note>. Regarding the phrase "this is the destruction of the meditation on all phenomena," the meaning is that it eliminates the meditation on all phenomena such as form and the like.

The statement "one does not meditate that form is an existing entity" means one does not meditate with the thought that form possesses an essential nature of being an existing thing. As for the phrase "clinging to the two extremes by thinking: this is the self regarding the entity," it refers to those who possess the perception of entities. This means thinking "this is the self, existing separately," or "the self is form," or "the self is feeling," and so forth. The meaning is that one clings to the two extremes of nihilism and eternalism.

Subhuti, the statement "perceiving form is duality" means that for whoever has the perception of "form," conceptualizations of existence and non-existence, or entity and non-entity, will inevitably arise. Alternatively, it is called "duality" because it results in the duality of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject. 

The phrase "as long as there is an entity, to that extent there is formative action" <note>original: "samskara"</note> means that through the conceptualization of entities, formative actions such as merit and non-merit are produced. Regarding "one thoroughly relinquishes entities," this means not relinquishing the results of maturation <note>original: "vipaka"</note>.
